labs.title: Why seasons happen
labs.hook: Earth’s tilted axis changes the angle of sunlight and the length of the day as Earth travels around the Sun.
labs.objective: Explain how axial tilt changes daylight and solar angle, then predict which hemisphere experiences summer at a chosen point in the year.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Keep Orbit stretch at 0 and set Axial tilt to 0°. Play a year and read the two 12-hour daylight values. Switch to Earth close-up to inspect the terminator and axis.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Axial tilt to 23.44° and pause at the June solstice, then the December solstice. Compare New York with Sydney and trace the fixed axis direction.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why do the hemispheres experience opposite seasons, even though both are nearly the same distance from the Sun?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: What would happen to seasons if axial tilt were 0°?
choices: Seasons would reverse, so June would become winter in New York.
Seasons would grow stronger because the orbit would stretch.
The equator would freeze while the poles warmed up.
Almost no seasons: day length and noon Sun would barely change.
questions.explain: With zero axial tilt, solar declination would stay at the equator, so each latitude would have nearly constant day length and noon solar altitude. Earth's varying orbital distance would still cause a smaller annual change in incoming sunlight.

questions.prompt: Why is December summer in Sydney?
choices: The Southern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun in December.
Australia is closer to the Sun in December than in June.
Ocean currents reverse their direction every December.
The Moon pulls the southern oceans toward the Sun.
questions.explain: In December the Southern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, giving Sydney longer days and a higher noon Sun. The Northern Hemisphere experiences the opposite geometry.

questions.prompt: Earth is slightly nearer the Sun in early January. Does that cause northern winter?
choices: Yes. Being closer to the Sun makes the north colder.
No. Northern winter comes from tilt; the south has summer then.
Yes. Perihelion always brings winter to both hemispheres at once.
No. Earth is at aphelion, its farthest point, in January.
questions.explain: A change in Earth–Sun distance affects both hemispheres at the same time, whereas their seasons are opposite. Axial tilt therefore explains northern winter despite Earth being near perihelion.

questions.prompt: At the equator, how do day length and solar altitude change through the year compared with New York?
choices: The equator has long days in June and short days in December, like New York.
Both places change by the same amount; only temperature differs.
Equator days stay near 12 h; New York’s range from about 9 to 15 h.
The equator’s noon Sun is always directly overhead, all year.
questions.explain: Near the equator, the day–night boundary divides each daily path into almost equal halves throughout the year. New York’s higher latitude produces much larger seasonal changes in day length and noon solar altitude.

questions.prompt: On the June solstice, which places have 24 hours of daylight?
choices: Places on the equator, such as Quito
Every place in the Northern Hemisphere
Places south of the Antarctic Circle
Places north of the Arctic Circle
questions.explain: In June the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, so places north of the Arctic Circle (about 66.6° N) turn all the way round without leaving the sunlit half. South of the Antarctic Circle it is dark all day.

why: Earth’s tilted axis changes the angle of sunlight and the length of the day as Earth travels around the Sun. The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer while the other has winter.

The axis keeps pointing the same way in space. At the June solstice the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, so its noon Sun is higher, the same sunlight is concentrated on less ground, and days are longer. Six months later Earth is on the other side of the Sun and the Southern Hemisphere leans toward it.
Orbit stretch is a what-if setting for separating tilt from distance; its dates do not match Earth’s real orbit.

misconceptions.claim: Summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun.
misconceptions.truth: Earth’s axial tilt changes both the angle of sunlight and the length of daylight. The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer while the other has winter. Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, so orbital distance cannot explain their opposite seasons.

misconceptions.claim: In a US summer the Sun is directly overhead at midday.
misconceptions.truth: The Sun can only be overhead between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, so it is never directly overhead anywhere in the contiguous United States; of the 50 states, only Hawaii lies inside the tropics. Even at the June solstice, New York’s noon Sun reaches only about 73° above the horizon.

teacher.script:
Keep Orbit stretch at 0 and set Axial tilt to 0°. Play a year and read the two 12-hour daylight values. Switch to Earth close-up to inspect the terminator and axis.

Set Axial tilt to 23.44° and pause at the June solstice, then the December solstice. Compare New York with Sydney and trace the fixed axis direction.
pitfalls: Use the model’s position in the year to compare seasonal geometry rather than to identify an exact calendar date.
Distinguish the pattern of incoming sunlight from a prediction of local temperature.
Explain that Earth and its axis are enlarged in the display so students can see the geometry.

modelNotes: Orbit stretch changes a hypothetical eccentricity from 0 to 0.4.
Earth’s real eccentricity is about 0.0167, with perihelion in early January; this experiment starts in March and does not reproduce that timing.
With Axial tilt and Orbit stretch both at 0, every place except the poles has 12-hour days.

predict.prompt: If Earth's axis had no tilt at all, what would happen to the length of a June day in New York? Explain your guess.

cer.prompt: Does the changing distance between Earth and the Sun, or the tilt of Earth's axis, cause the seasons?
cer.claim: The tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons; the small change in distance does not.
cer.evidence: With Axial tilt at 0° and Orbit stretch at 0, every place except the poles has 12-hour days all year. At 23.44° tilt, New York's daylight changes from about 9 hours in December to about 15 hours in June, while Sydney has the opposite pattern. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter.
cer.reasoning: When a hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun it gets longer days and a higher noon Sun, so each square meter of ground receives more energy. Both hemispheres are the same distance from the Sun at any moment, so distance cannot explain why they have opposite seasons.

labs.title: Earth rotation and the terminator
labs.hook: Earth turns eastward, carrying each location into sunlight and then darkness.
labs.objective: Explain how Earth’s eastward rotation produces day and night, and relate a 15° difference in longitude to one hour of solar time.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Watch Earth turn eastward and follow a marked city from daylight into darkness. Identify the terminator before turning on Time zones.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Pause and move the Day slider. Check that a quarter-turn takes six hours, then explain why time zones do not cause day and night.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does following one city across the terminator help explain the relationship between rotation and local solar time?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Which way does Earth rotate, viewed from above the North Pole?
choices: Clockwise (east to west).
It does not rotate; the Sun orbits Earth.
It alternates each six months.
Counterclockwise (west to east).
questions.explain: Earth turns from west to east, which appears counterclockwise when viewed from above the North Pole. This rotation makes the Sun appear to cross the sky from east to west.

questions.prompt: Why is 15° of longitude equal to one hour?
choices: Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, which is 15° each hour.
Because there are exactly 15 time zones around the world.
Because Greenwich was placed 15° east of the date line.
Because the metric system divides a circle into hours.
questions.explain: A mean solar day corresponds to 360° of rotation relative to the Sun, so 360° divided by 24 hours gives 15° per hour. Civil time-zone boundaries also reflect political and practical choices.

questions.prompt: Which statement explains day and night correctly?
choices: Earth’s orbit around the Sun causes day and night.
Earth’s rotation carries each place into and out of sunlight.
The Sun travels around Earth once each day.
Time zones decide the hours when each place on Earth gets daylight.
questions.explain: Rotation carries a location into and out of sunlight, producing day and night. Time zones assign clock readings to locations; they do not cause the illumination to change.

questions.prompt: If it is solar noon in Denver (~105°W), about what local solar time is it in New York (~74°W)?
choices: 10:00 — New York is west of Denver.
Midnight.
About 14:00 — 30° is two hours ahead.
The same, because they share a country.
questions.explain: New York lies about 30° east of Denver, so it reaches solar noon about two hours earlier because Earth turns through 15° each hour. Its local solar time is therefore about 14:00 when Denver’s is noon.

questions.prompt: Why does the Sun rise earlier in Boston than in Detroit on the same day?
choices: Earth turns eastward, so Boston rotates into sunlight first.
Boston is a little farther north, so it sees the Sun first.
Time zones move the sunrise earlier in New England.
Boston has a higher altitude, so it sees the Sun sooner.
questions.explain: Boston is about 12° east of Detroit, at almost the same latitude, and both cities use Eastern Time. Because Earth rotates from west to east, places farther east turn into sunlight first, by about 4 minutes for every degree of longitude, so Boston’s sunrise comes roughly 50 minutes earlier.

why: Earth turns eastward, carrying each location into sunlight and then darkness. The boundary between day and night is called the terminator; it separates the illuminated and unilluminated halves of Earth.

Relative to the Sun, Earth turns 360° in about 24 hours, so each place moves through 15° of longitude every hour. A quarter-turn of 90° therefore takes six hours: in the model, New York goes from sunrise to solar noon. Time zones only label clock times; they do not cause day and night.

The time-zone bands divide longitude into ideal 15° intervals; actual civil time zones follow local decisions and borders. The model shows equinox geometry, with Earth's axis upright to the sunlight, so the terminator passes through both poles and every place gets about 12 hours of daylight. At other times of year the tilted axis tilts the terminator and day length changes with latitude.

misconceptions.claim: Time zones determine where day and night occur.
misconceptions.truth: Earth’s rotation carries places into and out of sunlight. Time zones assign civil clock times to regions; their boundaries reflect political and practical choices. Changing a time-zone boundary would change the clock label, while sunrise and sunset would still follow Earth’s rotation and the Sun’s direction.

misconceptions.claim: The Sun moves across the sky because it travels around Earth each day.
misconceptions.truth: Earth spins from west to east once a day, so the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west. The Sun does not orbit Earth; Earth orbits the Sun once a year.

teacher.script:
Play the animation and watch Earth turn eastward and follow a marked city from daylight into darkness. Identify the terminator before turning on Time zones.

Pause and move the Day slider. Check that a quarter-turn takes six hours, then explain why time zones do not cause day and night.
pitfalls: Check that Earth rotates from west to east when students describe the motion.
Distinguish the approximately 24-hour solar day from the slightly shorter sidereal day.
Ask students to follow one location across the day–night boundary before discussing time zones.

modelNotes: Places farther east see the Sun rise first: Dallas, about 15° east of Phoenix, sees sunrise roughly an hour earlier.
Relative to the Sun, Earth turns 360° in about 24 hours: 15° per hour.
A sidereal day is about 23 h 56 min; a mean solar day is 24 h.

predict.prompt: Dallas is about 15° of longitude east of Phoenix. Will the Sun rise earlier or later in Dallas, and by about how much?

cer.prompt: What causes day and night, and why do places at different longitudes reach noon at different times?
cer.claim: Earth's eastward rotation carries each place into and out of sunlight, and every 15° of longitude east makes solar noon arrive about one hour earlier.
cer.evidence: Moving the Day slider through a quarter of the scale turns Earth 90° in 6 hours. A city followed across the terminator goes from daylight into darkness without the Sun moving. Turning Time zones on changes the clock labels but not where the day–night boundary is.
cer.reasoning: Earth turns 360° relative to the Sun in about 24 hours, so 360 ÷ 24 = 15° per hour. Places farther east rotate into sunlight first. Time zones are human labels for clocks, so they cannot cause day and night.

labs.title: Moon phases and Sun–Earth–Moon geometry
labs.hook: Sunlight illuminates half the Moon.
labs.objective: Use the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon to explain the changing illuminated shape we see during a lunar month.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Play a month in Orbit geometry and watch the Moon’s sunlit half. Then switch to Moon close-up to see the phase as it looks from Earth’s Northern Hemisphere.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Pause at first quarter and full Moon. Compare the solid orbit with the dashed line (Earth’s orbital plane): at most full Moons the Moon sits above or below it. Turn on Eclipse alignment to flatten the orbit, then explain why the 5° tilt usually prevents an eclipse.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why does the shape of the Moon’s visible bright region change while sunlight continues to illuminate roughly half its surface?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: At first quarter, where is the Moon relative to the Sun and Earth?
choices: Directly between the Sun and Earth.
Partly inside Earth’s shadow.
About 90° from the Sun–Earth line.
On the far side of Earth from the Sun.
questions.explain: At first quarter, the Moon appears about 90° from the Sun in Earth's sky. We see half of its illuminated hemisphere and half of its night side.

questions.prompt: Does Earth’s shadow cause the ordinary crescent Moon?
choices: Yes. Earth’s shadow always covers part of the Moon.
Yes, but only when the Moon is low in the sky.
Only during winter, when Earth’s shadow is longest.
No. The dark part is the Moon’s own night side.
questions.explain: An ordinary crescent shows only a small part of the Moon's sunlit hemisphere; the rest of the visible disc is its own night side. Earth's shadow darkens the Moon only during a lunar eclipse.

questions.prompt: Why are eclipses rarer than full and new Moons?
choices: The Moon’s orbit is tilted about 5°, so it usually misses alignment.
The Moon is too small to block sunlight most months.
Eclipses happen every month, but clouds usually hide them from our view.
Eclipses can only happen when Earth is at perihelion.
questions.explain: The Moon's orbital plane is tilted to Earth's orbital plane, so most new and full Moons do not form a close alignment. An eclipse requires the Moon to be near a node, where those planes intersect.

questions.prompt: A synodic month is about 29.5 days. What is it measuring?
choices: The time for Earth to orbit the Sun.
The time from one new Moon to the next.
The time for Earth to rotate once.
The time for the Moon to spin once.
questions.explain: A synodic month measures the return to the same Sun–Earth–Moon phase geometry. It exceeds the Moon's orbital period relative to the stars because Earth also moves around the Sun.

questions.prompt: A waxing crescent is low in the west just after sunset. Where is the Moon in its orbit?
choices: Directly behind Earth, opposite the Sun
A little way past the Sun–Earth line after new Moon
At right angles to the Sun, at last quarter
Partly inside Earth’s shadow, as in a partial eclipse
questions.explain: A few days after new Moon the Moon has moved only a small angle away from the Sun in our sky, so it sets soon after the Sun and shows a thin sunlit crescent.

why: Sunlight illuminates half the Moon. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different proportions of that illuminated half, producing the phases; Earth’s shadow is involved only in a lunar eclipse.

Because the Moon’s orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth’s orbital plane, most new and full Moons pass just above or below the Sun–Earth line. An eclipse happens only when a new or full Moon falls near a node, where the two planes cross.

Sizes and separations are enlarged for inspection, and the Sun is drawn small and close only to show where sunlight comes from. Switch to Physical scale to see how widely separated Earth and Moon really are.

misconceptions.claim: A crescent Moon forms when Earth’s shadow covers part of the Moon.
misconceptions.truth: Sunlight normally illuminates half the Moon. A crescent occurs when we see only a narrow part of that illuminated half from Earth; the rest of the visible disc is the Moon’s night side. Earth’s shadow darkens the Moon during a lunar eclipse.

misconceptions.claim: The Moon can only be seen at night.
misconceptions.truth: The Moon is above the horizon for about half of each day, so it is often visible in daylight. A first-quarter Moon, for example, rises around midday and can be seen in the afternoon sky.

teacher.script:
Play a month in Orbit geometry and watch the Moon’s sunlit half. Then switch to Moon close-up to see the phase as it looks from Earth’s Northern Hemisphere.

Pause at first quarter and full Moon. Compare the solid orbit with the dashed line (Earth’s orbital plane): at most full Moons the Moon sits above or below it. Turn on Eclipse alignment to flatten the orbit, then explain why the 5° tilt usually prevents an eclipse.
pitfalls: Explain phases as changing views of the Moon’s sunlit half; Earth’s shadow is involved in a lunar eclipse.
Remind students that the average Earth–Moon separation is about 30 Earth diameters, much larger than a compact classroom display suggests.
Keep the observer’s position on Earth clear when comparing the orbital view with the visible phase.

modelNotes: The Moon’s orbit is tilted about 5° to the ecliptic, so most months it misses Earth’s shadow.
Sizes are exaggerated so the model reads from the back of the room; the real Moon is about 30 Earth diameters away.
Synodic month, new to new, is about 29.53 days, longer than the sidereal month because Earth has moved.
Turn on Eclipse alignment (it sets the 5° tilt to zero, so every full Moon would line up with Earth’s shadow), then ask why real full Moons are usually not eclipses.
Without the 3D view: half the Moon is always sunlit; phases are the viewing angle from Earth; eclipses need the Moon near a node of its tilted orbit.
The Moon close-up shows the phase as seen from the Northern Hemisphere. From the Southern Hemisphere the view is rotated, so a waxing Moon is lit on the left.

predict.prompt: Does Earth's shadow cause the Moon's crescent phase? Write yes or no and give a reason.

cer.prompt: Why does the Moon's shape seem to change during a month?
cer.claim: The Moon's phases happen because we see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half as it orbits Earth, not because of Earth's shadow.
cer.evidence: In the orbit view, the Sun always lights half of the Moon. At new Moon the lit half faces away from Earth; at first quarter, about 90° from the Sun–Earth line, half of the lit half faces us; at full Moon, opposite the Sun, the whole lit half faces us. The phase cycle takes about 29.5 days.
cer.reasoning: The dark part of a crescent is the Moon's own night side. Earth's shadow only reaches the Moon during a lunar eclipse, when the full Moon lines up with the Sun and Earth near a node of its tilted orbit.

labs.title: Earth’s interior
labs.hook: Seismic waves reveal an Earth with layers that differ in composition and physical state.
labs.objective: Identify Earth’s main layers and explain how seismic waves provide evidence for a liquid outer core.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Rotate the cutaway, then change Cutaway and Separate layers. Identify the four layers and read their material states.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Separate layers back to 0%, then turn on P/S waves and press Play. Compare how the waves travel through the solid mantle and the liquid outer core.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does the behavior of P and S waves help us distinguish the mantle from the outer core?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Which layer is liquid metal?
choices: Crust
Outer core
Mantle
Inner core
questions.explain: The outer core is liquid iron alloy, but the inner core is solid: the much greater pressure at the center raises the temperature at which the metal melts.

questions.prompt: Why is there a direct S-wave shadow on the far side of Earth?
choices: S-waves fade out before they can cross the planet.
The solid inner core reflects all S-waves back.
S-waves cannot travel through the liquid outer core.
The crust absorbs S-waves on the far side.
questions.explain: S-waves deform material by shear, and a liquid cannot sustain the shear stress needed to carry them. The liquid outer core therefore blocks direct S-waves from reaching the far side through the core.

questions.prompt: Why does a liquid outer core matter for the magnetic field?
choices: It does not; the field comes from magnetic crustal rocks.
Its weight holds the solid inner core magnetized.
Its heat keeps the mantle permanently magnetized.
Convecting liquid metal sustains the geodynamo.
questions.explain: Convection in the electrically conducting liquid outer core generates and maintains electric currents. Those currents sustain much of Earth's magnetic field through the geodynamo.

questions.prompt: About how thick is continental crust compared with Earth’s radius (~6,371 km)?
choices: About 35 km
About 2,000 km
About 3,200 km
About 2,260 km
questions.explain: A typical continental crust thickness of about 35 km is well under 1% of Earth's 6371 km radius. Crustal thickness varies considerably, particularly beneath mountain belts.

questions.prompt: How do scientists know what Earth’s core is like?
choices: Drill cores have reached the core–mantle boundary.
Lava from volcanoes comes straight from the core.
Seismic waves change speed and path inside Earth.
Satellites photograph the core through the crust.
questions.explain: No borehole has passed through the crust. Seismic waves from earthquakes speed up, slow down and bend at boundaries, and S-waves cannot cross the liquid outer core; these patterns reveal the layers.

why: Seismic waves reveal an Earth with layers that differ in composition and physical state. The mantle is mainly solid rock, the outer core is liquid, and the inner core is solid.

P waves are compressional and pass through both solids and liquids. S waves are shear waves, and a liquid cannot resist shearing, so S waves recorded on the far side of Earth cannot have crossed the outer core. This S-wave shadow is the main evidence that the outer core is liquid.
The cutaway shows a reference structure. Its wave paths show which layers carry each wave; they do not calculate earthquake travel times.

misconceptions.claim: The mantle is a continuous layer of liquid magma.
misconceptions.truth: The mantle is predominantly solid rock that can deform slowly over geological time. Partial melting occurs in particular settings and supplies magma, but it does not make the whole mantle liquid. Earth’s liquid outer core is a separate layer composed mainly of metal.

misconceptions.claim: Earth’s interior is hot because heat from the Sun soaks down into it.
misconceptions.truth: Sunlight warms only the top few meters of ground. Earth’s internal heat comes from its formation and from the decay of radioactive elements in rocks, and it flows outward toward the surface.

teacher.script:
Rotate the cutaway, then change Cutaway and Separate layers. Identify the four layers and read their material states.

Set Separate layers back to 0%, then turn on P/S waves and press Play. Compare how the waves travel through the solid mantle and the liquid outer core.
pitfalls: Describe the mantle as predominantly solid rock that can deform slowly, rather than as a global magma ocean.
Use the wave illustration to discuss transmission through materials; it does not calculate seismic shadow zones.
Return the layers to their original spacing before comparing their depths or thicknesses.

modelNotes: This section uses a uniform 35 km reference crust, a core–mantle boundary at radius 3480 km and an inner-core radius of 1221 km.
Oceanic crust is commonly 5–10 km thick and continental crust commonly 30–50 km; real boundaries are not perfectly concentric spheres.

predict.prompt: Earthquake S-waves cannot travel through liquid. If part of Earth's core is liquid, where on the far side of Earth would you expect S-waves to be missing?

cer.prompt: How do earthquake waves show that Earth's outer core is liquid?
cer.claim: The outer core is liquid because S-waves cannot pass through it.
cer.evidence: With P/S waves on, P-waves travel through the solid mantle, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core, bending at each boundary. S-waves travel through the mantle but stop at the core–mantle boundary, about 2,900 km down (radius 3,480 km), leaving a large S-wave shadow on the far side of Earth.
cer.reasoning: S-waves are shear waves, and liquids cannot resist shearing, so S-waves cannot travel through a liquid. Their missing arrivals on the far side mean the layer below the mantle is liquid. P-waves are compression waves, which can cross liquids, so they still arrive, though refracted.

labs.title: Plate boundaries
labs.hook: At divergent boundaries plates separate, at convergent boundaries they approach, and at transform boundaries they slide past.
labs.objective: Compare the motion at three types of plate boundary and explain how each produces characteristic landforms.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Rotate the present-day globe. Teal marks divergent boundaries, coral convergent and sand transform. Turn on Boundary section and change Boundary type to compare their motion.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Time before present to step back toward Pangaea in 10 Ma snapshots. Return to 0 Ma and turn on Hawaiʻi hotspot to find Hawaiʻi.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Choose a boundary and explain how the direction of plate movement accounts for the landforms found there.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is which boundary type?
choices: Convergent
Divergent
Transform
Hotspot
questions.explain: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, plates separate and mantle material rises beneath the spreading center. Partial melting supplies magma that forms new oceanic crust.

questions.prompt: The Himalaya are rising at…
choices: An ocean–ocean transform fault.
A mantle hotspot beneath a plate.
Continent–continent convergence.
A passive continental margin.
questions.explain: India's collision with Eurasia shortened and thickened continental crust. This crustal thickening and continuing convergence helped raise the Himalaya.

questions.prompt: The San Andreas Fault is best described as…
choices: A divergent ridge where new oceanic crust is forming beneath California.
A subduction zone like the one beneath the Cascades.
A continental rift that is splitting California away.
A transform boundary between the Pacific and North American plates.
questions.explain: The San Andreas mainly accommodates horizontal motion between the Pacific and North American plates. Slip on the fault causes earthquakes but, unlike ridges and subduction zones, produces little magma.

questions.prompt: A hotspot track like Hawaiʻi is evidence that…
choices: A plate has moved over a long-lived plume, leaving older volcanoes.
Plates stay still while mantle plumes migrate steadily beneath them.
Volcanoes form only where plates pull apart at mid-ocean ridges.
Each island formed above its own separate subduction zone.
questions.explain: As a plate moves relative to a persistent melting region, new volcanoes form while older ones move away from the active source. An age progression therefore records relative plate motion, although hotspots need not remain perfectly fixed.

questions.prompt: Why are there no volcanoes along the Himalaya, even though plates are converging?
choices: The mountains and crust there are far too cold for magma to form.
Neither continent subducts deeply enough to melt the mantle.
Volcanoes there were all eroded away by glaciers.
Convergent boundaries never produce volcanoes.
questions.explain: Continental crust is too buoyant to sink far into the mantle. Without a descending oceanic plate releasing water, little magma forms, so a continental collision builds mountains rather than a volcanic arc.

why: At divergent boundaries plates separate, at convergent boundaries they approach, and at transform boundaries they slide past. These relative motions help explain the distribution of ridges, trenches and earthquakes.

Plates move only a few centimeters a year, but over tens of millions of years that rearranges the continents. About 200 million years ago most continental crust was joined in Pangaea; spreading at ridges such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge has since opened new oceans between the pieces.
Past views move modern coastlines using a plate model, so they show continental positions rather than ancient shorelines.

misconceptions.claim: Continents move through an ocean floor that stays still.
misconceptions.truth: Both continents and ocean floor are carried by lithospheric plates. A plate may include continental and oceanic crust, and its boundary need not follow a coastline. Relative plate motion produces spreading, convergence or sideways slip, with different landforms and geological activity at each type of boundary.

misconceptions.claim: Earthquakes and volcanoes can happen anywhere with equal likelihood.
misconceptions.truth: Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur in narrow belts along plate boundaries, such as the Pacific Ring of Fire. Some happen within plates, for example above hotspots like Hawaiʻi, but these are the exception.

teacher.script:
Rotate the present-day globe. Teal marks divergent boundaries, coral convergent and sand transform. Turn on Boundary section and change Boundary type to compare their motion.

Increase Time before present to step back toward Pangaea in 10 Ma snapshots. Return to 0 Ma and turn on Hawaiʻi hotspot to find Hawaiʻi.
pitfalls: Distinguish countries from tectonic plates; the United Kingdom lies on the Eurasian plate.
Check that arrows show the relative movement of the plates, including motion parallel to a transform boundary.
Ask students to connect each boundary type with its landforms before introducing a named example.

modelNotes: The globe uses Bird PB2002 present-day boundaries; past views use GPlates MULLER2019 coastlines reconstructed in a mantle reference frame.
Time before present steps through 10 Ma snapshots.
If 3D is unavailable, use the photographs and the World map studio.

predict.prompt: Volcanoes form where plates pull apart and where one plate sinks under another. Would you expect volcanoes along a transform boundary like the San Andreas Fault? Why?

cer.prompt: How does the motion at each type of plate boundary explain the landforms found there?
cer.claim: Divergent boundaries build ridges and rift valleys, convergent boundaries build mountains, trenches and volcanic arcs, and transform boundaries mainly produce earthquakes along faults.
cer.evidence: In Boundary section, divergent plates move apart and new crust forms at the ridge; at a convergent boundary one plate descends beneath another; at a transform boundary the plates slide past each other. On the globe, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is divergent, the boundary along the Andes and Cascades is convergent, and the San Andreas is transform.
cer.reasoning: Separation lets mantle rock rise and partly melt, making new crust. Subduction carries water into the mantle, which helps rock melt and feed volcanoes. Sliding plates create or destroy little crust, so they produce faults and earthquakes but little magma.

labs.title: Contours ↔ 3D terrain
labs.hook: A contour joins places at the same elevation.
labs.objective: Relate contour spacing and shape to the height and slope of a landscape, then distinguish a valley from a spur.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Turn 3D hill off and on to compare the contour map with the hill. Follow a valley and a spur, then compare the direction in which their contours bend.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Change Contour interval while keeping the terrain fixed. Compare tightly spaced and widely spaced contours and explain the difference in slope.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How can the same contour interval represent a gentle slope in one place and a steep slope in another?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Contour lines that form a V pointing uphill usually mark a…
choices: Spur of high ground
Steep cliff face
Valley or stream
Spot height marker
questions.explain: A contour crosses a valley farther uphill near the stream than on the adjacent slopes, making its V point upstream. Water flows downhill in the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: A spur is…
choices: A closed hollow shown by rings of falling height.
A valley between two ridges; its contour Vs point uphill.
A steep slope where contours crowd together.
A ridge of high ground; its contour Vs point downhill.
questions.explain: A spur projects outward from higher ground into lower terrain. Contours curve around that projection, with their V or U pointing downslope.

questions.prompt: The contour interval is 10 m. If you cross five intervals between two points, the height difference is…
questions.explain: The height difference equals the number of elevation intervals multiplied by the contour interval. Five intervals of 10 m give 50 m.

questions.prompt: Widely spaced contours mean…
choices: A steep slope
A gentle slope
A cliff face
Land at sea level
questions.explain: Widely spaced contours show that a given rise in elevation occurs over a long horizontal distance. That smaller rise-to-distance ratio means a gentler slope.

questions.prompt: On a map, contour rings get higher toward a small closed loop in the middle. What is it?
choices: A hollow with water in it
A hilltop or summit
A river valley
A cliff edge
questions.explain: Closed contours that increase in height toward the center mark a hill or summit. If the heights decreased inward instead, the loop would mark a hollow.

why: A contour joins places at the same elevation. Closely spaced contours indicate a steep slope, while wider spacing indicates a gentler slope; their patterns reveal valleys, ridges and summits.

Where a contour crosses a valley, it has to travel uphill along the valley floor before it finds ground of the same height, so its V points uphill. Around a spur the higher ground sticks out, so the contour's V or U points downhill.
The same constructed terrain appears in both views, so changing the contour interval changes the map’s detail, not the hill.

misconceptions.claim: The V-shaped bend of a contour always points downhill.
misconceptions.truth: Where a contour crosses a stream valley, its bend generally points uphill and upstream. Around a projecting spur, the bend points downhill. Follow the height labels and nearby drainage to distinguish the two; the shape of a single line without context can be misleading.

misconceptions.claim: Contour lines are paths or boundaries you could see on the ground.
misconceptions.truth: Contours are imaginary lines joining points of equal height above sea level. You cannot see them in the landscape, but walking along one would keep you at the same height.

teacher.script:
Turn 3D hill off and on to compare the contour map with the hill. Follow a valley and a spur, then compare the direction in which their contours bend.

Change Contour interval while keeping the terrain fixed. Compare tightly spaced and widely spaced contours and explain the difference in slope.
pitfalls: Count the height intervals between contour lines when calculating a change in elevation.
Use the contour values to identify uphill; north on the map does not necessarily point up the slope.
Ask students to match the same ridge or valley in both the map and the three-dimensional terrain.

modelNotes: On USGS topographic maps and OS 1:25 000 maps, features smaller than the contour interval can fall between the lines and disappear.
You can change two things: Contour interval and the 3D hill view.
Height is exaggerated 2.5 times so the relief is easy to read; Compare physical scale removes this.
Switching between the map and the 3D hill does not change the landscape: a V that marks a valley on the map is still a valley in 3D.
Change Contour interval from 5 m to 20 m and ask which details disappear.
Click any point on the hill to read its height and draw the A–B cross-section.
On a flat map, close lines mean steep ground, widely spaced lines mean gentle ground, a V pointing uphill marks a valley and a spur bends the other way.
These rules are enough for the Check questions and for reading a USGS or OS map extract without the 3D view.
Choose Landscape → Real: Sugarloaf Mountain, MD to read contours on real USGS elevation data (heights above sea level); the model hill is idealized.

predict.prompt: On a contour map, would you expect the lines to be closer together on a steep slope or a gentle one? Why?

cer.prompt: How can you tell a steep slope from a gentle one, and a valley from a spur, using contour lines?
cer.claim: Closely spaced contours mean a steep slope, widely spaced contours mean a gentle slope, and a contour V that points uphill marks a valley while one pointing downhill marks a spur.
cer.evidence: Turning the 3D hill on shows the steepest part of the hill where the contours crowd together. Following a stream valley, the contour bends point upslope; along a ridge spur they point downslope. Changing the contour interval from 5 m to 20 m removes detail but keeps the same pattern.
cer.reasoning: Each contour joins points of equal height and neighboring lines differ by the contour interval. Where the height changes quickly over a short distance, the lines must be closer together. Contours bend upstream where they cross a valley because the land falls toward the stream.

labs.title: River long profile
labs.hook: A river’s long profile usually becomes gentler downstream.
labs.objective: Follow a river from source to mouth and explain how its gradient, channel shape and flow change downstream.
standards: OCR GCSE A Landscapes of the UK

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Follow the bed from the steeper upper reach through bends to the gentler lower reach. These are parts of one river.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Raise Discharge and compare the water level and the width of the wet channel. Play follows the water downstream; the channel itself does not erode.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why does raising discharge change the water level even when the channel shape stays fixed?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Where is vertical erosion most important?
choices: The delta
The floodplain
Upper course
The estuary
questions.explain: In the upper course, steep gradients commonly favor channel incision into the bed. Weathering and slope movement then help shape the sides of a V-shaped valley.

questions.prompt: An oxbow lake forms when…
choices: A waterfall retreats upstream and leaves a plunge pool.
Levees trap floodwater permanently on the floodplain.
A tributary is captured and its old channel dries out.
A meander neck is cut through, abandoning the old loop.
questions.explain: Erosion can narrow the land between neighboring meander bends until floodwater cuts a shorter channel through it. Deposition can then seal the abandoned loop, leaving an oxbow lake.

questions.prompt: Raising discharge typically…
choices: Raises competence and can flood the floodplain.
Lowers competence because the water spreads out.
Leaves competence unchanged; only speed increases.
Stops meandering by straightening the channel.
questions.explain: Increasing discharge often increases flow depth and bed shear stress, allowing larger particles to move. The response also depends on channel shape, slope and roughness.

questions.prompt: A delta needs…
choices: A steep waterfall just before the river finally reaches the sea.
Sediment deposited at the mouth faster than waves and tides remove it.
Strong tides that carry most of the sediment back upstream.
A coastline sinking faster than the river’s sediment arrives.
questions.explain: A delta grows when sediment supplied at a river mouth accumulates faster than waves, tides and currents remove it. Slower flow on entering a lake or sea encourages deposition.

questions.prompt: How does a river channel usually change from upper to lower course?
choices: It becomes narrower, shallower and rockier.
It stays the same width but becomes steeper.
It becomes wider and deeper, with more discharge.
It loses water downstream, so the channel gets smaller.
questions.explain: Tributaries add water downstream, so discharge increases. The channel usually becomes wider and deeper, while the gradient becomes gentler.

why: A river’s long profile usually becomes gentler downstream. Channel shape, water supply and sediment change along its course, helping explain why steep valleys and broad floodplains occur in different reaches.
Raise Discharge and compare the water level and the width of the wet channel. Play follows the water downstream; the channel itself does not erode.

The channel shape stays fixed while the water level changes; the displayed wet margins are an illustration rather than a mapped flood extent. As in real rivers, the model channel becomes wider and deeper downstream and carries deeper water there, because tributaries add discharge along the way.

misconceptions.claim: A river’s upper, middle and lower courses are separate kinds of river.
misconceptions.truth: These terms describe reaches along one river system. Gradient, channel form, discharge and sediment can change downstream, often gradually and with local interruptions. They help compare patterns along a long profile, but they do not divide every river into three sharply bounded sections.

misconceptions.claim: A river flows fastest near its source because the slope is steepest there.
misconceptions.truth: Mountain streams look fast, but rocks and shallow water create a lot of friction. Further downstream the channel is deeper and smoother, so average velocity often stays the same or increases even though the gradient is gentler.

teacher.script:
Follow the bed from the steeper upper reach through bends to the gentler lower reach. These are parts of one river.

Raise Discharge and compare the water level and the width of the wet channel. Play follows the water downstream; the channel itself does not erode.
pitfalls: Trace the upper, middle and lower courses as connected parts of one river system.
Distinguish a delta from a tidal estuary when discussing a river mouth.
Compare changes in gradient and channel form without assuming every river follows an identical profile.

predict.prompt: As a river flows from its source to the sea, do you expect it to get steeper or gentler? Wider or narrower?

cer.prompt: How do a river's gradient and channel change downstream, and why?
cer.claim: Downstream a river usually becomes less steep, with a wider and deeper channel that carries more water.
cer.evidence: The long profile is steep near the source and gentle near the mouth. The channel is narrow and rocky upstream and wide with bends in the lower course. Raising Discharge widens the wet channel and raises the water level.
cer.reasoning: Tributaries add water downstream, so discharge increases and the river needs a larger channel to carry it. In the upper course the river cuts down into its bed; downstream more energy goes into moving sediment sideways and depositing it, which builds a wider valley floor.

labs.title: Water cycle stores and flows
labs.hook: Water moves between the atmosphere, land and ocean through evaporation, precipitation and flows at and below the surface.
labs.objective: Trace water between stores and explain how changes in rainfall or human use affect the amount held in a reservoir.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify the ocean, atmosphere, snow and ice, soil and groundwater stores. Choose a process in Follow a transfer and trace the highlighted route between stores.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Turn on Drainage basin, then increase Abstraction. Watch the reservoir level and the budget in the readout, and explain how taking water from a local store changes the water available in the catchment.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How can a local water store shrink even though water continues to circulate through the global system?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The largest store of fresh water is…
choices: Rivers and freshwater lakes
Groundwater in aquifers
Ice sheets and glaciers
Moisture held in soil
questions.explain: Ice sheets and glaciers hold the largest share of Earth's fresh water. Groundwater is another major fresh-water store, while rivers contain a much smaller fraction.

questions.prompt: Infiltration is…
choices: Water vapor condensing into cloud.
A river flowing out into the sea.
Tree leaves intercepting falling rain.
Water soaking into the soil surface.
questions.explain: Infiltration is the entry of water through the ground surface into soil. When rainfall exceeds the soil's infiltration capacity, or the soil is saturated, more water can become surface runoff.

questions.prompt: Abstraction in this lab lowers the reservoir because…
choices: Water is taken out faster than rain and inflow replace it.
Abstraction reduces the total water in the global cycle.
Pumping stops evaporation from the reservoir surface.
Pumping draws water into the aquifer from the sea.
questions.explain: A local reservoir loses storage when withdrawals and other outflows exceed precipitation and inflow. Global water conservation does not prevent a particular lake, reservoir or aquifer from being depleted.

questions.prompt: A drainage basin is…
choices: The river channel and its banks only.
The land drained by a river and its tributaries.
The area that floods during a 100-year event.
The sea area where a river deposits its load.
questions.explain: A drainage divide separates land whose surface runoff reaches different river systems. The basin includes all the land contributing water to the selected river and its tributaries.

questions.prompt: Which change would most increase surface runoff after a storm?
choices: Paving over fields with tarmac and roofs
Planting trees across the catchment
A long dry spell that leaves soils unsaturated
Light drizzle falling over several days
questions.explain: Impermeable surfaces stop rain soaking in, so more of it runs straight off into drains and rivers. Trees and dry soils increase interception and infiltration, while gentle rain gives water time to soak in.

why: Water moves between the atmosphere, land and ocean through evaporation, precipitation and flows at and below the surface. Naming the stores first makes it easier to trace where water comes from and where it goes.

A reservoir is a local store. Its volume rises or falls with the balance between inputs (precipitation and inflow) and outputs (evaporation, releases and abstraction). When outputs exceed inputs the store shrinks, even though the total amount of water on Earth does not change.
The tracers show transfer routes; their size and spacing do not show how much water moves along each route.

misconceptions.claim: Because the global water cycle conserves water, a local reservoir cannot run out.
misconceptions.truth: Water can leave a local store faster than it is replenished. Withdrawals, evaporation and downstream releases may exceed inflow, so the stored volume falls even though the water still exists elsewhere on Earth. A regional water balance therefore needs both the amounts and the timing of inputs and outputs.

misconceptions.claim: Clouds are made of water vapor.
misconceptions.truth: Water vapor is an invisible gas. Clouds are made of tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals that form when moist air cools and the vapor condenses.

teacher.script:
Identify the ocean, atmosphere, snow and ice, soil and groundwater stores. Choose a process in Follow a transfer and trace the highlighted route between stores.

Turn on Drainage basin, then increase Abstraction. Watch the reservoir level and the budget in the readout, and explain how taking water from a local store changes the water available in the catchment.
pitfalls: Name each water store before tracing the transfers between them.
Distinguish the amount of water stored in a river from the volume passing through it over time.
Ask students to explain where water goes during each transfer rather than only memorizing the process names.

modelNotes: Abstraction moves up to 6,000 m³ from an invented 10,000 m³ reservoir into a human-use store.

predict.prompt: If people take water out of a reservoir faster than rain and rivers refill it, what happens to the total amount of water on Earth?

cer.prompt: How can a reservoir run low even though the total amount of water on Earth stays the same?
cer.claim: A reservoir shrinks when its outputs are larger than its inputs, but the water is moved to other stores rather than lost from Earth.
cer.evidence: Raising Abstraction moves up to 6,000 m³ from the 10,000 m³ reservoir into a human-use store, and the reservoir level falls, while the budget in the readout shows the combined total staying the same.
cer.reasoning: Water moves between stores by processes such as precipitation, runoff, evaporation and abstraction. A local store depends on the balance between these flows. Water taken out still exists elsewhere in the cycle, but it may not be available in the same place at the same time.

labs.title: Solar system
labs.hook: Planets differ enormously in size, orbital distance and period.
labs.objective: Compare the sizes and orbital periods of planets, and explain why planets farther from the Sun take longer to orbit.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Play the inner orbits and compare periods and speed around each ellipse.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Turn on All eight orbits, then switch to Physical scale (the ×N button, or press T) and compare planet radii with the distances between their orbits.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does orbital distance affect a planet’s period, and why is that difficult to show alongside its true size?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Why does a planet speed up near perihelion?
choices: The solar wind pushes it along whenever it is near the Sun.
Angular momentum is conserved, so it moves faster when closer.
The Sun’s gravity only acts strongly close to perihelion.
It is heated more near the Sun, which gives it extra speed.
questions.explain: In a two-body orbit, angular momentum is conserved and the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. It must therefore travel faster near perihelion, where its distance from the Sun is smaller.

questions.prompt: In the orbital view, physical scale means…
choices: Orbits are drawn on a logarithmic scale.
Every planet is drawn the same size.
Bodies and orbit distances share one scale.
Orbits shrink but planets stay enlarged.
questions.explain: Physical scale applies the same distance conversion to planetary radii and orbital separations. Because radii are tiny compared with those separations, most planets become difficult to see in a whole-system view.

questions.prompt: The radius-comparison arrangement shows…
choices: The planets’ current positions in their orbits.
Correct distances, with enlarged planets.
Planets drawn with equal volumes.
Correct relative sizes, with artificial spacing.
questions.explain: The comparison preserves the ratios between planetary radii but places the bodies at convenient display positions. Their spacing in this view does not represent orbital distance.

questions.prompt: Saturn’s rings are…
choices: Many particles in orbit.
A solid platform.
A shell attached to its surface.
A single sheet of solid ice.
questions.explain: Saturn's rings consist of many separate orbiting particles, mostly water ice with some rocky material. A continuous rendered disc represents particles too small to resolve individually.

questions.prompt: Which planets are the rocky, terrestrial planets?
choices: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune
Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars
Earth, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn
Venus, Earth, Uranus and Neptune
questions.explain: The four inner planets are small and rocky. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, while Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

why: Planets differ enormously in size, orbital distance and period. Kepler’s laws connect distance with orbital period and explain why a planet moves faster near the Sun than farther away.

Kepler’s third law (T² ∝ a³) means period grows faster than distance: Mars, at about 1.5 au, takes about 1.9 years, while Neptune, at about 30 au, takes about 165 years. Farther planets travel a longer path and also move more slowly.
The orbital experiment uses fixed reference elements and chosen starting positions, so it does not show the planets’ locations today.

misconceptions.claim: A picture comparing planet sizes also shows their correct spacing.
misconceptions.truth: Planet radii and orbital distances differ across such large ranges that many illustrations use separate scales for them. A size-comparison view may preserve relative radii while arranging planets close together. Check the stated scale before using a displayed gap as a physical distance.

misconceptions.claim: Outer planets take longer to orbit only because their orbits are bigger.
misconceptions.truth: Their orbits are longer, but they also move more slowly because the Sun’s gravity is weaker far away. Both effects together explain Kepler’s third law: Neptune takes about 165 years to orbit, far more than 30 times Earth’s year.

teacher.script:
Play the inner orbits and compare periods and speed around each ellipse.

Turn on All eight orbits, then switch to physical scale and compare planet radii with the distances between their orbits.
pitfalls: Orbit spacing in the orbital view uses one au scale, but in teaching scale the Sun and planets are enlarged by different amounts; in the radius comparison the spacing is only a display arrangement.
Describe planetary rings as collections of particles rather than solid discs.
Distinguish a model’s surface or cloud colors from measurements made by an observing instrument.

modelNotes: Orbital motion uses JPL J2000 semi-major axes, eccentricities, inclinations and orbital orientations, held fixed.
Mercury’s 4096-pixel MESSENGER map uses enhanced color, not human-eye color.
Jupiter uses a 6000-pixel NASA map; Mars and Saturn use NASA geometry and mapped materials.

predict.prompt: Neptune is about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth. Do you think its year is 30 times longer, more than 30 times longer, or less? Why?

cer.prompt: Why do planets farther from the Sun take longer to complete an orbit?
cer.claim: Farther planets take longer to orbit because they have a longer path to travel and also move more slowly.
cer.evidence: In Orbital motion, Mercury completes an orbit in about 88 days, Earth in a year, Mars in about 1.9 years and Neptune in about 165 years, which is far more than 30 Earth years. The inner planets visibly move faster along their orbits.
cer.reasoning: The Sun's gravity weakens with distance, so a distant planet needs less speed to stay in orbit. Kepler's third law (T² ∝ a³) combines the longer path and the slower speed, so the period grows faster than the distance.

labs.title: Sun and Earth
labs.hook: The same sunlight spreads across a larger area when it strikes a surface at a shallow angle.
labs.objective: Explain how latitude and the Sun’s declination affect the solar energy received at noon and across a whole day.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Set Solar declination to 0° and use Latitude to compare the equator, 60° and a pole.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Move Solar declination to ±23.44° (the solstices) and compare the noon and daily-mean values.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can two places receive different amounts of solar energy even on the same day?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The 1361 W/m² reference applies to…
choices: Any horizontal patch of ground on Earth at noon.
A surface facing the Sun at 1 AU, above the air.
The ground at either pole in midsummer.
The glowing surface of the Sun itself.
questions.explain: The solar irradiance reference measures incoming power per unit area on a surface perpendicular to the beam at 1 AU. A tilted surface receives less per unit area, and Earth's atmosphere further alters surface sunlight.

questions.prompt: At zero declination, the noon flux at 60° latitude is…
choices: Twice the equatorial value.
Zero all year.
Half the equatorial value.
The same as at the equator.
questions.explain: At zero solar declination, noon sunlight strikes a horizontal surface at 60° latitude with an incidence factor of cos 60°, or 0.5. Its top-of-atmosphere input is therefore half the equatorial noon value.

questions.prompt: Why can a pole in summer have a large daily-mean energy input?
choices: The pole is much closer to the Sun in summer.
Sunspots direct extra energy at the poles.
The atmosphere is thinnest over the poles.
Continuous daylight makes up for the low Sun.
questions.explain: A daily mean adds up energy received over the full day, including the duration of daylight. Continuous summer daylight can partly compensate for the low solar elevation at a pole.

questions.prompt: Turning on Sunspot observation changes…
choices: Only the photograph, not the fixed irradiance calculation.
Earth’s axial tilt, which the model then recalculates.
The calculation, which turns into a solar forecast.
The irradiance value, which doubles when spots appear.
questions.explain: The photograph is an observation selected for comparison, while this calculation keeps its reference solar irradiance fixed. Selecting another image therefore does not change the calculated energy input.

questions.prompt: Why is it usually colder at the poles than at the equator, averaged over a year?
choices: The poles are further from the Sun than the equator is, all year.
Sunlight arrives at a low angle and spreads over more ground.
The poles have no daylight for half of every year.
Snow at the poles creates cold air on its own.
questions.explain: At high latitudes the Sun is low, so each beam of sunlight is spread over a larger area and passes through more atmosphere. Bright snow and ice then reflect much of what does arrive.

why: The same sunlight spreads across a larger area when it strikes a surface at a shallow angle. Latitude, solar declination and day length therefore affect the energy received by a horizontal surface.

When the solar declination is +23.44°, the noon Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. Northern latitudes then receive more energy per square meter at noon, and long or continuous daylight raises their daily mean further, while the southern hemisphere receives less.
The calculation describes sunlight above the atmosphere; clouds and atmospheric absorption would change the energy reaching the ground.

misconceptions.claim: Sunlight above the atmosphere supplies the same energy to every square meter of ground.
misconceptions.truth: The angle of the rays changes how incoming energy is spread over a horizontal surface. At a lower Sun angle the same beam covers more ground, and day length also changes daily energy receipt. Clouds, reflection and atmospheric absorption further modify the energy reaching the surface.

misconceptions.claim: The Sun is a huge ball of burning fire.
misconceptions.truth: Nothing is burning in the Sun: there is no oxygen fire. Its energy comes from nuclear fusion in the core, where hydrogen nuclei join to form helium and release energy.

teacher.script:
Set Solar declination to 0° and use Latitude to compare the equator, 60° and a pole.

Move Solar declination to ±23.44° (the solstices) and compare the noon and daily-mean values.
pitfalls: Distinguish sunlight measured perpendicular to a beam from energy received by a horizontal surface.
Include the night-time interval when interpreting a daily average of incoming solar energy.
Explain the seasons through Earth’s axial tilt rather than changes in visible sunspots.

modelNotes: The fixed reference here is 1361 W/m² at 1 AU, near the top of Earth’s atmosphere.
For a horizontal surface at local noon, the geometric input is 1361 × max(0, cos(latitude − solar declination)).
Declination moves the subsolar latitude between about 23.44° south and north over a year.

predict.prompt: At an equinox, the noon Sun is overhead at the equator. Do you think a place at 60° latitude gets more or less than half as much noon sunlight per square meter? Why?

cer.prompt: Why does a place at high latitude receive less solar energy per square meter at noon than a place near the equator?
cer.claim: Sunlight strikes high latitudes at a lower angle, so the same beam spreads over a larger area of ground.
cer.evidence: At 0° declination the noon input is about 1,361 W/m² at the equator and half of that, about 680 W/m², at 60°, because the factor is cos 60° = 0.5. At the poles it is zero. At the June solstice (+23.44°) the subsolar point moves to the Tropic of Cancer.
cer.reasoning: A beam of sunlight carries a fixed amount of energy. When it arrives at a slant, it covers more ground, so each square meter gets less. The input is proportional to the cosine of the angle between the Sun's rays and the vertical.

labs.title: Universe scale
labs.hook: Distances within the Solar System are commonly measured in astronomical units; distances between stars are more conveniently measured in light-years.
labs.objective: Compare distances within and beyond the Solar System, using light-travel time to make their scale easier to understand.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Read the mean Earth–Moon distance, then press Play to send a light signal.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Switch to physical scale, then use Distance comparison to jump to the Sun–Earth reference and the nearest stellar neighbor.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain what a light-travel time tells you about distance. How does changing the display scale affect the comparison?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A light-year measures…
choices: A duration.
A stellar mass.
A distance.
A light intensity.
questions.explain: A light-year is the distance light travels in vacuum during one Julian year. The word year describes the travel time used to define the distance, not the type of quantity measured.

questions.prompt: If an interstellar diagram uses one scale for everything, it can show…
choices: Stars as large neighboring balls.
True star sizes, but distances squashed together.
Stars and planets at one readable size.
True separations, but stars smaller than a pixel.
questions.explain: The distances between stars greatly exceed their radii. A diagram that fits interstellar separations at one scale may therefore render the stellar discs smaller than a screen pixel.

questions.prompt: The 1 AU reference is…
choices: Exactly 149597870.7 km.
Exactly one light-year.
A fixed distance between Earth and the Sun every day.
The average Earth–Moon distance.
questions.explain: The astronomical unit is a defined length of exactly 149597870.7 km. Earth's actual distance from the Sun changes around its elliptical orbit, so it is not always exactly 1 AU.

questions.prompt: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. What does this tell us?
choices: We see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago.
The Sun is 8 light-years away from Earth.
Sunlight slows down as it passes through space.
The Sun rises 8 minutes before we can see it.
questions.explain: Light travels at about 300,000 km per second, and the Sun is about 150 million km away. The light we see left the Sun about 8 minutes earlier, so we always see it slightly in the past.

questions.prompt: Which list is in order from smallest to largest?
choices: Galaxy, Solar System, star, planet
Planet, star, galaxy, Solar System
Solar System, planet, galaxy, star
Planet, star, Solar System, galaxy
questions.explain: A planet orbits a star; a star and everything orbiting it form a planetary system such as the Solar System; and a galaxy contains billions of stars and their systems.

why: Distances within the Solar System are commonly measured in astronomical units; distances between stars are more conveniently measured in light-years. Changing scale helps separate an object’s size from its distance away.

Light crosses the mean Earth–Moon distance in about 1.28 seconds and 1 AU in about 499 seconds (8.3 minutes), but takes about 4.24 years to reach Proxima Centauri. Because light travels at a fixed speed in a vacuum, each travel time is a direct measure of distance.

Each comparison uses its own straight-line (linear) scale, so the same screen gap stands for 384,400 km in one view and about 40 trillion km in another. In teaching scale the bodies are enlarged so they can be seen; in physical scale they shrink to dots, showing that the gaps between bodies are far larger than the bodies themselves.

misconceptions.claim: A light-year is a length of time, so a star 4.24 light-years away is about time rather than distance.
misconceptions.truth: A light-year is a distance: how far light travels in one Julian year, about 9.46 trillion km. Proxima Centauri is about 4.24 light-years away, so its light takes about 4.24 years to reach us; the travel time is how the distance is defined, not the quantity being measured.

misconceptions.claim: The stars in a constellation are close together in space.
misconceptions.truth: Stars in a constellation only appear close in our sky. They can lie at very different distances: in Orion, Betelgeuse is roughly 500–600 light-years away, while Rigel is around 860.

teacher.script:
Read the mean Earth–Moon distance, then press Play to send a light signal.

Switch to physical scale, then use Distance comparison to jump to the Sun–Earth reference and the nearest stellar neighbor.
pitfalls: Define a light-year as a distance before using it to compare objects.
Use the stated measurements rather than the width of a locator symbol to compare stellar sizes.
Explain that the sequence compares scales; it does not show the objects’ actual arrangement in the sky.

sources.label: NASA Exoplanet Archive: published Proxima radius estimates

modelNotes: One astronomical unit is exactly 149597870.7 km.
A light-year is the distance light travels in a Julian year of 365.25 days, at 299792.458 km/s in vacuum.
The first view uses the mean Earth–Moon center distance of 384400 km; actual separation varies.
The second uses 1 AU as a Sun–Earth reference.
The third uses a rounded 4.24 light-years to Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun.
At 1× speed, every full playback lasts 24 seconds, while the readout gives the corresponding physical travel time: about 1.28 seconds, 499 seconds or 4.24 years.

predict.prompt: Light takes about 1.3 seconds to reach Earth from the Moon. Guess how long it takes light to reach us from the Sun, and from the nearest star.

cer.prompt: What does a light-year measure, and how does light-travel time show the scale of space?
cer.claim: A light-year is a distance: how far light travels in one year. Light-travel times show that stars are vastly farther away than anything in the Solar System.
cer.evidence: Light crosses the Earth–Moon distance (384,400 km) in about 1.28 seconds and 1 AU in about 499 seconds (8.3 minutes), but takes about 4.24 years to reach Proxima Centauri.
cer.reasoning: Light travels at a fixed speed in a vacuum, about 300,000 km/s, so its travel time is a direct measure of distance. A time of years rather than minutes means the nearest star is about 270,000 times farther away than the Sun.

labs.title: Geologic time
labs.hook: Earth’s history spans about 4.54 billion years.
labs.objective: Read dates in millions of years and compare the unequal durations of major intervals in Earth’s history.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Set Time window to Earth history and move Oldest → present to the oldest end.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Move toward the present, then switch Time window to Phanerozoic or Quaternary.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Choose two intervals and compare their durations. How does enlarging a time window change which details you can see?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Ma means…
choices: Minutes ago
Million years ago
Meters of altitude
Million years from now
questions.explain: Ma is the geological abbreviation for a million years. An age of 100 Ma therefore refers to about 100 million years before the present.

questions.prompt: On the timeline, Pangaea sits…
choices: Near Earth’s formation, about 4500 Ma
At the very start of the long Precambrian eon
Within the last few hundred million years
In the last few thousand years
questions.explain: Pangaea assembled during the late Paleozoic and began breaking apart during the Mesozoic. These events occurred billions of years after Earth formed.

questions.prompt: Human history on this coil is…
choices: About half of the whole spiral
The whole of the final coil
A section before the first life
A thin mark at the very end
questions.explain: Recorded human history spans only a few thousand years compared with Earth's roughly 4.54 billion years. On a uniformly scaled geological timeline it occupies an extremely small interval near the present.

questions.prompt: The full 4540 Ma viewing window begins at…
choices: An approximate age of Earth itself.
The K–Pg boundary, when dinosaurs died out.
The assembly of the supercontinent Pangaea.
The start of the Quaternary ice ages.
questions.explain: The 4540 Ma window approximates Earth's age, based on radiometric evidence. Pangaea assembled much later, within the last few hundred million years.

questions.prompt: Which happened first?
choices: The extinction of the non-bird dinosaurs
The formation of the first oceans
The assembly of Pangaea
The appearance of the first trilobites
questions.explain: Oceans existed on early Earth more than 4 billion years ago. Trilobites appeared about 520 million years ago, Pangaea assembled around 335 million years ago and the dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago.

why: Earth’s history spans about 4.54 billion years. Placing events on a proportional timeline shows how recent human history is and why a short interval near the present can hide much older events.

Equal distance along the coil always stands for equal time, so the long Precambrian fills most of the full window. Choosing a shorter window stretches recent time along the coil and reveals events that are crowded together near the present; it does not change how long any interval lasted.
The timeline is a scale for comparing ages; event dates have different uncertainties and should not all be read as equally precise.

misconceptions.claim: The Grand Canyon is as old as the rocks exposed in its walls.
misconceptions.truth: The rocks formed before erosion exposed them in the canyon. Rock formation, deformation, uplift and river incision belong to different parts of the geological history and require different evidence to date. An old rock can therefore form the wall of a much younger landform.

misconceptions.claim: Dinosaurs and early humans lived at the same time.
misconceptions.truth: Non-bird dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. Our species appeared only about 300,000 years ago, so tens of millions of years separate them. Birds are the dinosaurs’ living descendants.

teacher.script:
Set Time window to Earth history and move Oldest → present to the oldest end.

Move toward the present, then switch Time window to Phanerozoic or Quaternary.
pitfalls: Read the numerical dates rather than the width of an event marker to judge its duration.
Distinguish the coiled time display from a column showing the thickness of real rocks.
Explain that enlarging a time window changes the display scale without changing how long the events lasted.

modelNotes: Earth is approximately 4.54 billion years old.
The 4540 Ma start is not the exact base of the Hadean, which the ICS chart places at 4567 Ma.
The Phanerozoic begins at 538.8 Ma on the ICS 2026/06 chart.
Evidence of life extends back at least about 3.5 billion years, while human history occupies a minute part of the full window.

predict.prompt: If Earth's whole history were one 24-hour day, how long ago in that day do you think humans appeared?

cer.prompt: Why does recorded human history look so small on a timeline of Earth's history?
cer.claim: Human history is a tiny fraction of Earth's 4.54-billion-year history, so on an evenly scaled timeline it is only a thin mark at the very end.
cer.evidence: In the Earth history window (4,540 Ma) the long Precambrian fills most of the coil. Our species appears only about 300,000 years ago and recorded history a few thousand years ago, which only becomes visible in the Quaternary window (2.58 Ma).
cer.reasoning: On a proportional timeline, equal distances stand for equal time. A few thousand years is about one millionth of 4.54 billion years, so it shrinks to almost nothing. Zooming to a shorter window spreads recent time out without changing how long any interval lasted.

labs.title: Eclipses
labs.hook: An eclipse requires the Sun, Earth and Moon to align closely enough for one body to enter another’s shadow.
labs.objective: Explain how the Sun, Earth and Moon must align for an eclipse, and identify the regions of total and partial shadow.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Start with the lunar shadow close-up and follow the Moon through the penumbra and umbra. Then set Node direction to 60° and compare the miss.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: With Shadow close-up on, set Eclipse close-up to Lunar — full Moon and Node direction to 0°. Drag the Transit slider through the shadow. Then choose Solar — new Moon and compare the nearest and farthest Moon distance: is the Moon's umbra long enough to reach Earth?

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why does changing the direction of the Moon’s orbital nodes turn an eclipse into a miss?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The umbra is…
choices: The dark core of the shadow
The faint outer part of a shadow
The half of the Moon lit by the Sun
The night side of Earth
questions.explain: Inside the umbra, the eclipsing body blocks the entire solar disc. In the surrounding penumbra, only part of the Sun is obscured.

questions.prompt: Eclipses are rare because…
choices: The Moon is too small to cover the Sun
The Moon’s orbit is tilted about 5°
Clouds usually hide them
The Moon orbits too slowly
questions.explain: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5° to Earth's orbital plane, so the bodies usually fail to align closely enough at new or full Moon. Eclipses occur when that phase happens near an orbital node.

questions.prompt: A lunar eclipse needs…
choices: New Moon close to an orbital node
Any full Moon, wherever the Moon is
Full Moon close to an orbital node
First quarter close to an orbital node
questions.explain: At full Moon, Earth lies between the Sun and Moon. A lunar eclipse also requires the Moon to pass near a node so that it enters Earth's shadow.

questions.prompt: At full Moon away from an orbital node, what normally happens?
choices: A lunar eclipse, because the Moon is full
A solar eclipse, because the Moon is aligned
A partial lunar eclipse, because the Moon’s orbit is tilted
Usually a miss: the Moon passes above or below the shadow
questions.explain: Away from an orbital node, the Moon's tilted orbit carries it above or below Earth's shadow at full Moon. The full phase alone is therefore insufficient to produce a lunar eclipse.

questions.prompt: Why can a total solar eclipse only be seen from a narrow path on Earth?
choices: The Moon’s umbra is small where it reaches Earth.
Clouds hide the eclipse from most other places.
Only people on the equator can see the Sun at noon.
Earth’s shadow covers everywhere else at that time.
questions.explain: The Moon’s dark umbra narrows to at most a few hundred kilometers across by the time it reaches Earth. Outside this path observers are in the penumbra and see only a partial eclipse.

why: An eclipse requires the Sun, Earth and Moon to align closely enough for one body to enter another’s shadow. The Moon’s orbital tilt usually carries it above or below the necessary alignment.

Distance matters for solar eclipses. Near its closest point the Moon looks slightly larger than the Sun, so its umbra reaches Earth and the eclipse can be total. Near its farthest point the Moon looks slightly smaller than the Sun, the umbra ends before reaching Earth, and a ring of Sun stays visible: an annular eclipse.
The shadow experiment isolates alignment and angular size; it is not a calendar of future eclipses.

misconceptions.claim: Every full Moon produces a lunar eclipse.
misconceptions.truth: A lunar eclipse requires the full Moon to pass through Earth’s shadow. The Moon’s orbital plane is tilted by about five degrees relative to Earth’s orbital plane, so it usually passes above or below that shadow. An eclipse occurs only when the alignment is sufficiently close to an orbital node.

misconceptions.claim: It is safe to look at the Sun during a partial solar eclipse because most of it is covered.
