misconceptions.truth: Even a thin crescent of the Sun is bright enough to damage your eyes. Use certified eclipse glasses or project the Sun’s image through a pinhole. Only during totality, when the Moon covers the whole disc, is it briefly safe without protection.

teacher.script:
Predict whether every full Moon enters Earth’s shadow. Keep the real tilt and set Node direction to 60°. Observe the miss.

With Shadow close-up on, set Eclipse close-up to Lunar and Node direction to 0°. Drag the Transit slider through the shadow. Then choose Solar and compare the nearest and farthest Moon distance.
pitfalls: Distinguish ordinary lunar phases from eclipses caused by one body entering another’s shadow.
Use the Moon’s orbital tilt of about 5° to explain why an eclipse does not occur every month.
Check whether the Moon is near an orbital node when testing the alignment for an eclipse.

modelNotes: The close view spans 8.5 hours around full or new Moon; Play and the Transit slider follow that interval.

predict.prompt: There is a full Moon every month. Do you expect a lunar eclipse every month? Why or why not?

cer.prompt: Why is there not an eclipse at every new Moon and full Moon?
cer.claim: Eclipses are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°, so the Sun, Earth and Moon line up only when a new or full Moon happens near an orbital node.
cer.evidence: With Node direction at 0°, the full Moon passes through Earth's umbra and the readout shows a total lunar eclipse. At 60°, the full Moon passes above or below the shadow and misses. Turning on Eclipse alignment removes the tilt, and then every full Moon enters the shadow.
cer.reasoning: A shadow can only fall on a body that lies on the line from the Sun. The tilted orbit carries the Moon above or below that line most months. Only near the two places where the orbits cross, the nodes, can the alignment be close enough for an eclipse.

labs.title: Tides
labs.hook: The Moon’s gravitational attraction varies across Earth, creating a tide-generating effect with two broad bulges.
labs.objective: Explain how the relative positions of the Moon and Sun produce the difference between spring and neap tides.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Play the month and identify the two broad tidal bulges, one toward the Moon and one on the opposite side of Earth.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Drag the Month slider to New Moon or Full Moon, then to Quarter Moon. Compare the blue tidal lobes and the relative range in the readout, then describe the difference between spring and neap tides.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why is the tidal range larger when the Sun and Moon align than when they are at right angles?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Why two bulges?
choices: The Moon’s pull differs across Earth
Two moons pull from opposite sides
Winds pile water on both sides
Earth’s rotation flings water outward
questions.explain: The Moon's gravitational pull varies across Earth, producing tidal accelerations directed away from Earth's center on both the near and far sides. The two bulges describe an ideal equilibrium response; real ocean tides also depend on basin shape and motion.

questions.prompt: Spring tides occur when…
choices: It is the spring season
Sun and Moon line up with Earth
Sun and Moon are at right angles
The Moon is farthest from Earth
questions.explain: Near new and full Moon, the solar and lunar tidal effects reinforce one another along the same axis. This generally produces the larger high-to-low tidal range called a spring tide.

questions.prompt: Neap tides are…
choices: The smallest range, occurring only in winter
The largest range, at new and full Moon
The smallest range, Sun and Moon at right angles
Tides caused by onshore winds
questions.explain: Near first and third quarter, the Sun and Moon lie in roughly perpendicular directions from Earth. Their tidal effects partly offset, producing a smaller range called a neap tide.

questions.prompt: If you pause when the Sun and Moon are at right angles, the range is…
choices: Spring — the two pulls add, so a larger range
Zero — the pulls of the Sun and Moon cancel out exactly
Unchanged — the Sun has no effect on tides
Neap — the pulls partly cancel, so a smaller range
questions.explain: At this right-angle arrangement, the solar contribution partly reduces the lunar tidal range. The resulting neap range is smaller rather than zero, and the term does not refer to a season.

questions.prompt: Why is high tide about 50 minutes later each day?
choices: Earth’s rotation is slowing down each day.
The Sun pulls the tide back by 50 minutes.
The Moon moves along its orbit, so Earth must turn further.
Ocean water takes about 50 minutes longer to cross each basin.
questions.explain: While Earth spins once, the Moon moves about 13° along its orbit in the same direction. Earth has to rotate a little further, roughly 50 minutes, to bring a place back under the Moon.

why: The Moon’s gravitational attraction varies across Earth, creating a tide-generating effect with two broad bulges. The Sun also contributes: aligned effects produce spring tides, while roughly perpendicular effects produce neap tides.

At new and full Moon the Sun and Moon lie on one line, so their tidal lobes point the same way and add: the range is large (spring tides). At the quarters they are at right angles, so the Sun's lobes fill the Moon's lows: the range is smaller (neap tides), but never zero, because the Moon's effect is about twice the Sun's.
These are equilibrium tides; coastlines, ocean depth and basin resonance strongly affect actual tidal heights and timing.

misconceptions.claim: Spring tides occur only during the spring season.
misconceptions.truth: Spring tides are periods of relatively large tidal range around new and full Moon, when solar and lunar tide-generating effects reinforce each other. They occur throughout the year. The height and timing at an actual coast also depend on water depth, basin shape and local conditions.

misconceptions.claim: Every coast has two high tides a day at the same times each day.
misconceptions.truth: Many coasts, including most of the US Atlantic coast and Britain, have two highs and two lows a day, but parts of the Gulf of Mexico have only one, and the US Pacific coast has two unequal highs. High tide also arrives about 50 minutes later each day, because the Moon moves along its orbit.

teacher.script:
Play the month and identify the two broad tidal bulges, one toward the Moon and one on the opposite side of Earth.

Pause at New Moon or Full Moon, then at Quarter Moon, and compare the blue tidal lobes. Describe the difference between spring and neap tides.
pitfalls: Explain that spring tides refer to an increased tidal range and can occur in any season.
Include both sides of the equilibrium tidal pattern when discussing the Moon’s influence.
Distinguish astronomical tides from wind-driven storm surge and tsunami waves.

predict.prompt: Do you expect the biggest difference between high and low tide when the Sun and Moon line up with Earth, or when they are at right angles? Why?

cer.prompt: Why are tidal ranges larger at new and full Moon than at the quarter Moons?
cer.claim: When the Sun and Moon line up with Earth, their tidal effects add together and make spring tides with a large range; when they are at right angles, they partly cancel and make smaller neap tides.
cer.evidence: At new and full Moon the solar and lunar tidal lobes point the same way and the readout shows the largest relative range. At the quarter Moons the Sun's lobes fill the Moon's lows and the range is smaller, but never zero.
cer.reasoning: Tides come from the difference in the Moon's and Sun's pull across Earth, which stretches the oceans into two bulges. The Moon's tidal effect is about twice the Sun's, so lined-up effects add to a large range, while effects at right angles subtract but leave the Moon's tide in place.

labs.title: Solar altitude and sun path
labs.hook: Solar altitude is the Sun’s angle above the horizon.
labs.objective: Compare the Sun’s daily path at different latitudes and explain how the season changes noon altitude and day length.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Locate the horizon, solar path and selected Sun position. Move Local solar time from morning to afternoon and follow the Sun across the sky.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Change Latitude and the Year slider, then compare the highest solar altitude and length of daylight. Find the longest and shortest days the model allows.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do noon solar altitude and day length work together to change the energy received during a day?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Noon solar altitude is lowest in New York around…
choices: June
December
March only
Every day the same
questions.explain: Near the December solstice, the Sun’s declination is farthest south. This gives New York its lowest noon solar altitude and shortest daylight period of the year.

questions.prompt: At the equator day length is…
choices: Short in June, long in December
24 hours at the equinoxes
Near 12 hours all year
Longest at the solstices
questions.explain: At the equator, the day–night boundary divides the daily rotation into nearly equal illuminated and dark portions. Day length therefore stays close to 12 hours through the year.

questions.prompt: In winter, moving to a higher latitude…
choices: Raises the noon Sun and lengthens the day
Lowers the noon Sun but lengthens the day
Leaves noon altitude and day length unchanged
Lowers the noon Sun and shortens the day
questions.explain: Moving poleward in the hemisphere's winter increases the angular distance from the Sun's declination. The Sun follows a lower, shorter path above the horizon, eventually producing polar night at sufficiently high latitude.

questions.prompt: If you drag Latitude from 40.7° toward 0°, how does the Sun’s path change?
choices: The winter noon Sun climbs higher and days stay nearer 12 h
The noon Sun drops lower and the winter days get even shorter
The Sun is directly overhead at noon every day
Day length swings more between summer and winter
questions.explain: Moving from New York toward the equator reduces the seasonal variation in daylight and raises the noon Sun in winter. Equatorial day length remains near 12 hours, while the noon Sun still changes with solar declination.

questions.prompt: New York is at about 40.7° N. What is its noon solar altitude at an equinox?
choices: About 90°
About 23.5°
About 40.7°
About 49.3°
questions.explain: At an equinox the Sun is overhead at the equator, so noon altitude equals 90° minus latitude: 90° − 40.7° = 49.3°.

why: Solar altitude is the Sun’s angle above the horizon. It changes through the day and year, while latitude determines how high the Sun can climb and whether it rises or sets at all.

Earth’s axis is tilted by about 23.4°, so the Sun’s declination moves between about 23.4° N and 23.4° S during the year. When the Sun is over your own hemisphere its path is higher and longer, giving longer days; in your winter the path is lower and shorter. The further a place is from the equator, the larger this seasonal swing.
The model shows geometric solar directions; local terrain and atmospheric refraction can change an observed sunrise or sunset.

misconceptions.claim: The Sun is directly overhead at local noon everywhere on Earth.
misconceptions.truth: Local solar noon is when the Sun reaches its daily highest position, but that position need not be overhead. Noon altitude depends on latitude and solar declination. The Sun can be directly overhead only between the tropics, and only on dates appropriate to the latitude.

misconceptions.claim: The Sun always rises due east and sets due west.
misconceptions.truth: That happens only near the equinoxes. In a US summer the Sun rises in the north-east and sets in the north-west, giving a long, high path; in winter it rises in the south-east and sets in the south-west.

teacher.script:
Locate the horizon, solar path and selected Sun position. Move Local solar time from morning to afternoon and follow the Sun across the sky.

Change Latitude and the Year slider, then compare the highest solar altitude and length of daylight. Find the longest and shortest days the model allows.
pitfalls: Use geographic north and south when describing the Sun’s path; a magnetic compass may require a local correction.
Explain that an overhead noon Sun is possible only within the tropics.
Compare both noon solar altitude and daylight duration when changing the latitude or season.

modelNotes: Comparing 40.7° (New York) with about 0° (Nairobi) challenges the idea that the noon Sun is overhead everywhere.
Noon altitude is 90° minus the absolute difference of latitude and declination: 90° − |φ − δ|.
Toward the equator: noon stays high, day length sits near 12 h.
Drag Latitude to about 0° for Nairobi, 26° for Miami, or below 0° for the Southern Hemisphere.

predict.prompt: Is the noon Sun directly overhead everywhere on Earth? Predict the noon Sun's height in New York on the March equinox.

cer.prompt: How do latitude and the time of year change the Sun's noon altitude and the length of the day?
cer.claim: The noon Sun is highest and days are longest when the Sun's declination is close to your latitude; moving away from the equator increases the seasonal swing.
cer.evidence: In New York (40.7° N) the noon altitude is 90° − 40.7° = 49.3° at the equinoxes, about 73° in June and about 26° in December, with day length from about 9 to 15 hours. Near the equator, day length stays close to 12 hours all year.
cer.reasoning: Noon altitude equals 90° minus the difference between latitude and solar declination. Because Earth's axis is tilted 23.44°, the declination moves between 23.44° N and S over the year, changing the Sun's path most at high latitudes.

labs.title: Continental drift
labs.hook: Continents move with tectonic plates.
labs.objective: Compare reconstructed continental positions through time and use fossil and coastline evidence to discuss the former arrangement of Pangaea.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Begin with the older reconstruction and identify the major continental blocks. Compare their positions with the present-day globe.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Move Ma before present toward 0 and follow India northward. Use geological evidence as well as coastlines when explaining how earlier positions are reconstructed.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Set 250 Ma and turn on Fossil evidence. Where do the Mesosaurus, Glossopteris, Lystrosaurus and Cynognathus sites sit, and which other evidence would you use to test this arrangement?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Pangaea was…
choices: A late Paleozoic supercontinent, one of several
Earth’s first continental crust
The only supercontinent in all of Earth’s history
A supercontinent of the last million years
questions.explain: Pangaea was assembled by plate convergence long after Earth formed, and other supercontinents existed before it. Its later breakup produced the arrangement from which today's continents developed.

questions.prompt: Wegener’s fit argument is strongest when…
choices: You match today’s coastlines
You match the continental shelves
You match the continents’ interiors
You match mountain heights
questions.explain: Modern shorelines shift with sea level, erosion and sediment deposition. The submerged continental margins therefore provide a better guide to matching former continental edges.

questions.prompt: Continents move because…
choices: They plow through a static ocean floor
Tides drag them
They are passengers on plates
Earth’s spin flings them
questions.explain: Continents are embedded in lithospheric plates that can also include oceanic crust. Their movement is part of plate motion rather than continents independently pushing through stationary ocean floor.

questions.prompt: The Himalaya record…
choices: A hotspot track like Hawaiʻi
A mid-ocean ridge like Iceland
A transform fault like San Andreas
A collision between India and Eurasia
questions.explain: India moved north as part of its plate and eventually collided with Eurasia. Continued convergence shortened and thickened the crust, building the Himalayan mountain belt.

questions.prompt: Fossils of the reptile Mesosaurus are found in both southern Africa and South America. What do they suggest?
choices: It swam thousands of kilometers across the open Atlantic.
The two continents were once joined together.
The same species evolved separately on each continent.
Birds carried its eggs across the ocean.
questions.explain: Mesosaurus lived in fresh or brackish water and could not cross a wide ocean. Its fossils on both continents, together with matching rocks, support the idea that Africa and South America were once joined.

why: Continents move with tectonic plates. Matching geological evidence across oceans helped establish continental drift, and plate reconstructions combine evidence to estimate earlier continental positions.

Plates move only a few centimeters a year, but over tens of millions of years that adds up to thousands of kilometers: India crossed the Tethys Ocean and collided with Eurasia, and the Atlantic opened as the Americas separated from Europe and Africa.
Modern coastlines are moved by a reconstruction model; ancient coastlines also depended on sea level, erosion and sedimentation.

misconceptions.claim: Matching modern coastlines is enough to prove how the continents once fitted together.
misconceptions.truth: Coastlines change with sea level, erosion and deposition, so their fit is approximate. Reconstructions also use continental margins, matching rock sequences and structures, fossils, and magnetic evidence. Agreement among different kinds of evidence provides a stronger basis for estimating past continental positions.

misconceptions.claim: Continents moved apart quickly, over a few thousand years.
misconceptions.truth: Plates move only a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Opening the Atlantic Ocean took around 180 million years.

teacher.script:
Begin with the older reconstruction and identify the major continental blocks. Compare their positions with the present-day globe.

Move Ma before present toward 0 and follow India northward. Use geological evidence as well as coastlines when explaining how earlier positions are reconstructed.
pitfalls: Explain that Pangaea was one of several supercontinents and that oceanic crust moves with the plates.
Use continental margins and geological evidence rather than matching modern beaches alone.
Distinguish a tectonic plate from a country; the United Kingdom moves with the Eurasian plate.

modelNotes: Maps that treat today’s coastlines as permanent hide 250 million years of continental movement.
Pangaea stayed assembled from about 300 Ma until it began to break apart around 200–180 Ma.
The globe uses EarthByte’s Müller 2019 plate reconstruction at 10 Ma intervals.
Set Ma before present to 250 Ma, then compare the 10 Ma snapshots toward the present.
At about 250 Ma the continental shelves fit together as Pangaea.
Fossil evidence shows a few representative published sites for each species, moved with their plates by the same model. The dots mark where fossils are found, not each species’ full range.

predict.prompt: Fossils of the same freshwater reptile, Mesosaurus, are found in Brazil and in southern Africa. How could that happen?

cer.prompt: What evidence shows that the continents were once joined in Pangaea?
cer.claim: The continents were once joined, because matching fossils and coastlines line up when the continents are moved back to their positions about 250 million years ago.
cer.evidence: At 250 Ma with Fossil evidence on, the Mesosaurus sites in Brazil and Namibia sit side by side, and Glossopteris and Lystrosaurus sites cluster across South America, Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia. Moving toward 0 Ma, the Atlantic opens and India moves north to collide with Asia.
cer.reasoning: Mesosaurus lived in fresh or brackish water and could not have crossed an ocean, so the land must have been connected. A reconstruction that fits fossils, rock belts and coastlines together at once is stronger evidence than any one clue alone.

labs.title: Hotspots
labs.hook: A moving plate can carry older volcanoes away from a long-lived region of melting.
labs.objective: Use the direction of increasing volcanic age to infer relative plate motion in the Hawaiian and Yellowstone examples.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the young and old ends of the Hawaiian track. Then press Play and watch the plate carry the active volcano away from the plume while a new seamount starts to grow.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Turn on Yellowstone and compare the direction in which its volcanoes get older.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does the direction of increasing volcanic age indicate the plate’s motion relative to the melting region?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Older volcanoes in the main Hawaiian chain generally lie…
choices: Southeast of the youngest active island.
Next to a deep subduction trench.
Scattered randomly along the chain.
Northwest of the active southeastern end.
questions.explain: The Pacific Plate carries older Hawaiian volcanoes northwest relative to the active melting region. Newer volcanic centers form near the southeastern end of the chain.

questions.prompt: Older centers in the Yellowstone track lie…
choices: Southwest along the Snake River Plain.
Northwest, as in Hawaiʻi.
Along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
At the same location as every modern eruption.
questions.explain: Volcanic centers become progressively older southwest of Yellowstone along the Snake River Plain. This pattern records motion of the North American Plate relative to the underlying magmatic system.

questions.prompt: A mantle plume is best described here as…
choices: A hollow pipe full of liquid lava.
Hot, mostly solid mantle rising slowly.
A crack running up from the inner core.
One pipe feeding Hawaiʻi and Yellowstone.
questions.explain: Mantle rock can rise slowly while remaining mostly solid. As pressure falls during ascent, some of that hot rock may cross its melting threshold and generate magma.

questions.prompt: Where does Yellowstone sit relative to plate boundaries?
choices: On a subduction zone, like the Cascades
On a spreading ridge, like Iceland
On a transform fault, like San Andreas
Inside the North American Plate
questions.explain: Yellowstone is far from any plate boundary. Like Hawaiʻi it is an intraplate volcanic system, fed by a long-lived source of heat beneath the moving plate.

questions.prompt: Volcanoes on Hawaiʻi’s Big Island are active, but those on Kauaʻi are not. Why?
choices: Kauaʻi’s magma froze when the climate cooled.
Kauaʻi lies over a cooler part of the ocean.
Kauaʻi has been carried away from the hotspot.
Kauaʻi’s volcanoes are blocked by coral reefs.
questions.explain: Kauaʻi formed over the hotspot about 5 million years ago. The Pacific Plate has since carried it north-west, away from its magma supply, so its volcanoes are extinct and eroding.

why: A moving plate can carry older volcanoes away from a long-lived region of melting. Comparing the direction of increasing age along a volcanic track helps explain relative plate motion.

The active volcano sits above the region of melting. As the plate moves, it carries that volcano away, the volcano becomes extinct, cools, subsides and erodes, and a new one forms above the melting region. Volcanoes therefore get older in the direction the plate is moving.
The sections illustrate motion and age direction; they do not calculate eruption dates or reproduce the full structure of a mantle plume.

misconceptions.claim: A hotspot must remain perfectly fixed while its plate moves.
misconceptions.truth: A volcanic age track records motion of a plate relative to a region of melting. Plate motion is important, but the source can also shift as the mantle moves. Track direction and age therefore constrain relative motion without requiring an exactly stationary source.

misconceptions.claim: Hawaiian volcanoes form above a subduction zone, like the volcanoes of Japan.
misconceptions.truth: Hawaiʻi lies near the middle of the Pacific Plate, thousands of kilometers from the nearest plate boundary. Its magma comes from melting of hot mantle beneath the plate, not from a sinking oceanic plate.

teacher.script:
Start with Hawaiʻi only. Ask students to find the youngest (black, glowing) and oldest (atoll, drowned seamount) ends, then press Play: the plate carries the active volcano away and a new seamount begins over the plume.

Turn on Yellowstone. In both sections the arrow points the way the plate moves, so ask which compass direction that is in each case (northwest for the Pacific Plate, southwest for the North American Plate) and why the older centers lie in that direction.
pitfalls: Treat the selected hotspot examples as separate volcanic systems rather than one continuous plume.
Describe the warm mantle region as mostly solid material that can produce partial melting.
Use the illustrated landforms to explain the process; do not read dates or real sizes from them.

sources.label: USGS: hot but not molten plume material

modelNotes: In the main Hawaiian island chain, older volcanoes generally lie northwest of the currently active southeastern end; Kauaʻi preserves rocks about 5–5.5 Ma old.
The Yellowstone track becomes older southwestward along the Snake River Plain and extends back roughly 17 Ma.

predict.prompt: Kauaʻi is an old Hawaiian island and the Big Island is young. If the hotspot stays in one place, which way do you think the Pacific Plate is moving?

cer.prompt: How do the ages of volcanoes along a hotspot track show the direction a plate is moving?
cer.claim: The plate moves away from the hotspot toward the older volcanoes: the Pacific Plate moves northwest over the Hawaiian hotspot and the North American Plate moves southwest over Yellowstone.
cer.evidence: In the Hawaiian track the youngest, active volcano is at the southeastern end and the islands get older northwestward; Kauaʻi is about 5 million years old. Playing the model carries the active volcano off the plume while a new seamount grows. The Yellowstone track gets older southwestward along the Snake River Plain, back about 17 million years.
cer.reasoning: A hotspot is a long-lived source of melting beneath the plate. Each volcano forms over it and is then carried away as the plate moves, so the line of volcanoes ages in the direction of plate motion.

labs.title: Seafloor spreading
labs.hook: New oceanic crust forms at a spreading ridge and moves away on both sides.
labs.objective: Explain how new oceanic crust forms at a ridge and how magnetic stripes record spreading on either side.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the ridge axis and the age labels at each end of the section. Set Full spreading rate to 25 mm/year and work out the half rate for each flank.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Press Play to run the reversal sequence and follow the paired markers. Compare wide and narrow stripes; reversals do not happen at regular intervals.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why do matching magnetic stripes appear on opposite sides of a ridge, and what can their widths tell us?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Newest crust is…
choices: At the continents
At the trench only
In the inner core
At the ridge axis
questions.explain: Magma rises and solidifies at a spreading ridge, forming new oceanic crust. Continued spreading moves that crust away from the axis, so it generally becomes older with distance.

questions.prompt: Stripes are symmetrical because…
choices: Both sides of the ridge add crust
Ocean currents sort the stripes
Only one plate moves away
Reversals happen at regular intervals
questions.explain: New crust forms on both sides of the ridge and records the same sequence of magnetic polarity changes. Spreading carries those records outward into broadly matching bands, although their widths can differ if spreading is asymmetric.

questions.prompt: Magnetic stripes record…
choices: Changes in ocean temperature
Magnetic reversals frozen in basalt
The age of the sediment layers on top
Variations in seawater salinity
questions.explain: As basalt cools, magnetic minerals lock in a record of the prevailing geomagnetic field. Successive reversals and continued spreading create bands of normal and reversed polarity.

questions.prompt: Old ocean floor is destroyed at…
choices: Mid-ocean ridges
Transform faults
Subduction trenches
Continental rift valleys
questions.explain: At a subduction trench, oceanic lithosphere bends and descends into the mantle. Transform boundaries mainly accommodate sideways motion and do not perform that recycling process.

questions.prompt: Where is the oldest oceanic crust usually found?
choices: At the crest of a mid-ocean ridge
Close to the ridge axis, under a thin cover of sediment
Spread evenly across every ocean floor
Far from ridges, near some trenches and margins
questions.explain: Crust forms at the ridge and is carried away on both sides, so it gets older with distance. The oldest crust lies furthest from the ridge, often near trenches where it will eventually be subducted.

why: New oceanic crust forms at a spreading ridge and moves away on both sides. Its age generally increases with distance, while magnetic stripes record changes in Earth’s magnetic polarity.

Each strip of new crust keeps the magnetic polarity it had when it cooled at the axis, so the same sequence of stripes is carried out on both flanks. Reversals happen at irregular intervals, so stripe widths vary even when the spreading rate stays the same.
The experiment uses a selected spreading history; real ridges change speed and can spread asymmetrically.

misconceptions.claim: Every magnetic stripe on the ocean floor represents the same amount of time.
misconceptions.truth: Geomagnetic reversals occur at irregular intervals, and spreading rates can change. A stripe’s width depends on both the duration of its polarity interval and the rate at which crust moved away from the ridge. Matching sequences are stronger evidence than an assumption of equally spaced reversals.

misconceptions.claim: The ocean floor is the oldest part of Earth’s surface.
misconceptions.truth: Almost all ocean floor is less than about 200 million years old, because oceanic crust is recycled at subduction zones. Some continental rocks are over 4 billion years old.

teacher.script:
Find the ridge axis and the age labels at each end of the section. Set Full spreading rate to 25 mm/year and work out the half rate for each flank.

Press Play to run the reversal sequence and follow the paired markers. Compare wide and narrow stripes; reversals do not happen at regular intervals.
pitfalls: Explain magnetic stripes as records preserved in cooling crust, rather than as waves moving across the seabed.
Compare the age of crust on either side of the ridge, and distinguish spreading from movement along the San Andreas transform system.
Account for the model’s twelvefold vertical exaggeration when interpreting the shape of the ridge.

modelNotes: A full spreading rate of 25 mm/year means each flank moves 12.5 mm/year, or 12.5 km per million years.
Change Full spreading rate and compare the ages labeled at the two ends of the section.

predict.prompt: If new seafloor forms at a mid-ocean ridge, where would you expect to find the oldest seafloor?

cer.prompt: How do magnetic stripes and rock ages show that the seafloor is spreading?
cer.claim: New oceanic crust forms at the ridge and moves away on both sides, so the youngest rock is at the ridge and matching magnetic stripes mirror each other across it.
cer.evidence: The age labels increase with distance from the ridge on both flanks. At a full spreading rate of 25 mm/year each flank moves 12.5 mm/year, or 12.5 km per million years. The stripe pattern is symmetrical, with wide and narrow stripes because reversals happen at irregular times.
cer.reasoning: As lava cools at the ridge, magnetic minerals record the direction of Earth's magnetic field. When the field reverses, newly formed crust records the new direction, so each stripe is a time band carried away on both sides.

labs.title: Atmosphere as a thin film
labs.hook: Atmospheric layers are distinguished mainly by how temperature changes with altitude.
labs.objective: Identify the main atmospheric layers and explain how changes in temperature with height help distinguish them.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Open Layer globe and name regions 1–4 using the key. Use Separate layers to pull the regions apart, then set it back to 0%. Switch to Physical scale and compare the thickness of the atmosphere with Earth’s radius.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Open Temperature profile. At a lapse rate of 6.5 °C/km, the air at 12 km is 15 − 12 × 6.5 = −63 °C. Set the lapse rate to 4 °C/km and check that it becomes 15 − 12 × 4 = −33 °C.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does the temperature profile distinguish atmospheric layers that have no solid boundary between them?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Where does almost all weather happen?
choices: Thermosphere
Mesosphere
Troposphere
Exosphere
questions.explain: The troposphere contains most atmospheric water vapor and supports strong vertical mixing. These conditions concentrate clouds, precipitation and most familiar weather in the lowest atmospheric layer.

questions.prompt: A lapse rate of 6.5 °C/km means…
choices: Temperature rises 6.5 °C each kilometer up.
Pressure falls 6.5 hPa per kilometer up.
The stratosphere warms 6.5 °C per kilometer.
Temperature falls about 6.5 °C per kilometer up.
questions.explain: A lapse rate of 6.5 °C/km means temperature falls by about 6.5 °C for each kilometer you climb. This is an average; real profiles vary with weather, place and season.

questions.prompt: Why is the stratosphere warmer as you go up?
choices: Ozone absorbs ultraviolet and heats that layer.
Heat rising from the ground collects there.
Clouds high up trap heat in that layer.
It is closer to the Sun than the ground.
questions.explain: Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and converts part of that energy into heat. This absorption produces the characteristic temperature increase with height through much of the stratosphere.

questions.prompt: Denver is a mile high. Is its weather still troposphere weather?
choices: No. At that height it is in the stratosphere.
Yes. The tropopause is still many km above.
Only in winter, when the tropopause is higher.
No. Weather happens only near sea level.
questions.explain: Denver is about 1.6 km above sea level, but the tropopause there is usually more than 10 km up. Its weather is still troposphere weather.

questions.prompt: About how much of the atmosphere’s mass is in the troposphere?
choices: About 10%
About 33%
About 75%
All of it
questions.explain: Air is compressed by the weight above it, so it is densest near the ground. Although the troposphere is only about 8–17 km deep, it holds roughly three-quarters or more of the atmosphere’s mass.

why: Atmospheric layers are distinguished mainly by how temperature changes with altitude. Most weather occurs in the troposphere, while absorption of ultraviolet radiation helps warm the stratosphere above it.

The troposphere is warmed mainly from the ground below, so its temperature usually falls with height, by about 6.5 °C per kilometer on average. Each layer boundary is where that trend reverses: temperature stops falling at the tropopause, rises through the stratosphere, falls again in the mesosphere and rises in the thermosphere.
Layer boundaries vary with place and season; the atmosphere is drawn thicker so its vertical structure can be inspected.

misconceptions.claim: The tropopause is the top of the atmosphere.
misconceptions.truth: The tropopause is only the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere. Air continues far above it, getting steadily thinner. Its height changes with latitude, season and weather.

misconceptions.claim: The higher you climb, the warmer it gets, because you are closer to the Sun.
misconceptions.truth: In the troposphere temperature usually falls with height, by about 6.5 °C per kilometer on average. The air is heated mainly from the ground, and a few kilometers makes no real difference to the distance from the Sun.

cases.label: UK sea breeze: air in the lowest layer

teacher.script:
Open Layer globe and name regions 1–4 using the key. Use Separate layers to pull the regions apart, then set it back to 0%. Switch to Physical scale and compare the thickness of the atmosphere with Earth’s radius.

Open Temperature profile. At a lapse rate of 6.5 °C/km, the air at 12 km is 15 − 12 × 6.5 = −63 °C. Set the lapse rate to 4 °C/km and check that it becomes 15 − 12 × 4 = −33 °C.
pitfalls: Set Separate layers back to 0% before comparing layer thicknesses.
Explain that the tropopause separates layers within the atmosphere; air continues above it.
Connect stratospheric warming with the absorption of ultraviolet radiation rather than proximity to the Sun.

modelNotes: The reference globe uses boundaries at 12, 50 and 85 km, and shows the thermosphere only as far as 500 km; real boundaries vary.
The troposphere is commonly about 8 km deep near the poles and 16–18 km in the tropics.
At 6.5 °C/km, a 15 °C surface gives −63 °C at 12 km.
If 3D is unavailable, use the ISS limb photograph, definitions and the teacher note.

predict.prompt: Do you think it gets warmer or colder as you climb a high mountain, even though you are closer to the Sun? Why?

cer.prompt: How do changes in temperature with height show the boundaries between atmospheric layers?
cer.claim: Each layer boundary is a height where the temperature trend reverses: temperature falls through the troposphere, rises through the stratosphere, falls in the mesosphere and rises in the thermosphere.
cer.evidence: At a lapse rate of 6.5 °C/km a 15 °C surface gives −63 °C at 12 km, the model's tropopause. Above it the profile warms to about 50 km, cools to about 85 km and then warms again.
cer.reasoning: The troposphere is heated mainly from the ground, so it cools with height. Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation in the stratosphere and warms it. A few kilometers make no real difference to the distance from the Sun, so height above the ground, not closeness to the Sun, sets the pattern.

labs.title: Earth’s energy budget
labs.hook: Earth reflects some incoming sunlight and absorbs the rest.
labs.objective: Trace energy entering and leaving Earth, and explain how reflection and atmospheric absorption affect the surface temperature.
standards: OCR GCSE A Environmental threats to our planet

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Set Albedo to 0.3 and turn Greenhouse return off. Read the surface temperature, then explain why the incoming 1361 W/m² is divided by four.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Turn Greenhouse return on. Compare what the surface emits with what leaves to space at the top of the atmosphere. Is the top-of-atmosphere balance still zero?

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain why a change in reflected sunlight or infrared absorption changes the temperature needed for energy balance.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: What hits the ground first from the Sun?
choices: Longwave from the air
Earth’s own infrared
Only ultraviolet
Shortwave sunlight
questions.explain: The Sun is very hot, so it emits mostly short wavelengths, such as visible light. The much cooler ground absorbs this sunlight and then emits its own longwave infrared.

questions.prompt: Albedo is…
choices: The fraction of sunlight reflected
The fraction of sunlight absorbed
The heat a surface emits
The heat trapped by clouds
questions.explain: Albedo compares reflected shortwave energy with incoming shortwave energy. A high-albedo surface reflects a larger fraction and absorbs less of the incident sunlight.

questions.prompt: Why can a snowy Rocky Mountain meadow heat the air less than bare dark soil?
choices: Snow is colder, so it absorbs more.
Higher albedo, so less is absorbed.
Dark soil reflects more than snow.
Snow emits more longwave radiation.
questions.explain: Snow reflects much more sunlight than dark soil, so less energy is absorbed to warm the surface and the air above it. Some of the energy snow does absorb goes into melting rather than heating.

questions.prompt: Greenhouse return in this lab is…
choices: Sunlight reflected back by clouds.
Sunlight absorbed by ozone in the stratosphere.
Infrared from the atmosphere to the surface.
Heat carried up by convection.
questions.explain: Greenhouse gases and clouds absorb infrared and emit it in all directions, including back down. This downward infrared adds energy to the surface, which also emits its own infrared upward.

questions.prompt: As Arctic sea ice shrinks in summer, what happens to the region’s albedo?
choices: It rises, so more sunlight is reflected.
It is unchanged because water is blue.
It stops mattering because water is cold.
It falls, so more sunlight is absorbed.
questions.explain: Ice and snow reflect much of the sunlight that reaches them, while dark open water absorbs most of it. Less ice means a lower albedo and more absorbed energy, which can cause further melting.

why: Earth reflects some incoming sunlight and absorbs the rest. Its temperature adjusts as outgoing thermal radiation balances absorbed energy; greenhouse gases change the exchange of thermal radiation.

With Greenhouse return on, the surface receives sunlight plus infrared emitted back down by the layer, so it must emit more, and be warmer, than without the layer. Only part of the surface infrared escapes directly, yet once balance is reached the infrared leaving to space still equals the sunlight absorbed.
This simple model includes only radiation; it leaves out convection, evaporation and weather.

misconceptions.claim: Greenhouse gases mainly warm Earth by trapping incoming visible sunlight.
misconceptions.truth: Greenhouse gases let most visible sunlight through, and much of it is absorbed at the surface. The warmed surface emits infrared, which greenhouse gases and clouds absorb and re-emit, partly back downward. The surface therefore has to be warmer before enough energy escapes to space to balance the sunlight absorbed.

misconceptions.claim: The greenhouse effect is caused by the hole in the ozone layer.
misconceptions.truth: They are separate issues. The ozone hole is a thinning of stratospheric ozone that lets more ultraviolet reach the ground. The greenhouse effect is the absorption and re-emission of infrared by gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapor.

teacher.script:
Set Albedo to 0.3 and turn Greenhouse return off. Read the surface temperature, then explain why the incoming 1361 W/m² is divided by four.

Turn Greenhouse return on. Compare what the surface emits with what leaves to space at the top of the atmosphere. Is the top-of-atmosphere balance still zero?
pitfalls: Make clear that the model shows energy transfers; it does not predict future climate.
Explain albedo as the fraction of incoming sunlight reflected, and distinguish shortwave sunlight from outgoing longwave radiation.
When checking the budget, use the model’s own values; published diagrams use different numbers because they include convection and evaporation.

sources.label: University of Washington one-layer radiation balance

modelNotes: Averaging 1361 W/m² over the globe gives 340.25 W/m² before reflection.
With Greenhouse return on, infrared absorptivity and emissivity are both 0.78.

predict.prompt: If Earth's surface became more reflective, for example covered by more snow and ice, would the surface get warmer or cooler? Why?

cer.prompt: How do albedo and greenhouse gases change Earth's surface temperature?
cer.claim: A higher albedo cools the surface because less sunlight is absorbed, and greenhouse gases warm the surface because they send infrared energy back down.
cer.evidence: The incoming 1,361 W/m² averages to 340.25 W/m² over the globe. Raising Albedo above 0.3 lowers the absorbed sunlight and the surface temperature. Turning on Greenhouse return makes the surface emit more infrared than before, while the energy leaving at the top of the atmosphere still balances the sunlight absorbed.
cer.reasoning: In balance, Earth must emit as much energy as it absorbs. Reflecting more sunlight leaves less to absorb. A layer that absorbs and re-emits infrared returns part of the surface's emission, so the surface must be warmer to emit enough energy to escape.

labs.title: Thermal circulation
labs.hook: Unequal heating can create pressure differences and a circulation.
labs.objective: Explain how unequal heating creates a circulation, then apply that reasoning to a coastal breeze and an urban heat island.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Drag the Day slider until the readout shows local hour 15, then compare the sea and land temperatures. Trace the surface flow toward the warmer land and the return flow aloft.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Move to local hour 3: has the surface flow reversed? Then turn on Urban heat (it replaces the coast) and compare the city with the countryside around it.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does the temperature contrast between land and sea produce a circulation that may reverse overnight?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A sea breeze at the surface blows…
choices: From land to sea
From sea to land
Straight up
Only at night
questions.explain: During the day, land commonly warms faster than the adjacent sea, helping air rise over the land. The resulting pressure differences can draw cooler surface air inland as a sea breeze.

questions.prompt: At night the land often cools faster. The surface flow…
choices: Stays onshore
Turns to blow straight upward
Can reverse as a land breeze
Stops completely
questions.explain: If land cools below the sea's temperature at night, the local pressure pattern can reverse and drive surface air offshore. Background winds and cloud cover can weaken or prevent this land breeze.

questions.prompt: An urban heat island is…
choices: A city cooled by sea breezes.
A warm patch of sea near a coast.
A dome of cold air trapped over a valley.
A city warmer than the land around it.
questions.explain: Urban materials store and release heat, while reduced vegetation often limits evaporative cooling. These changes can keep a city warmer than its surroundings, especially at night.

questions.prompt: Why does this lab leave out the Coriolis effect?
choices: To focus on heating; rotation can still turn real breezes.
The Coriolis effect is exactly zero along every single coastline.
The sea does not rotate along with Earth.
Pressure differences cannot form near a coast.
questions.explain: Leaving out the Coriolis effect lets the lab show only the circulation driven by local heating. Real breezes are also turned by Earth’s rotation and shaped by background winds and terrain.

questions.prompt: Why does warm air rise?
choices: Heat naturally rises and carries the warm air up with it.
The Sun pulls warm air toward it.
Warm air contains less water vapor.
It is less dense than the cooler air around it.
questions.explain: Heating makes air expand, so a given volume has less mass. Surrounded by denser, cooler air, it is buoyant and rises.

why: Unequal heating can create pressure differences and a circulation. Warm air expands and rises, and a return flow aloft completes the loop.

Land heats and cools faster than water, so by afternoon the land is warmer than the sea and surface air flows onshore; at night the land can become cooler and the loop reverses. A city stores heat in concrete and has less evaporative cooling, so it stays warmer than its countryside, most strongly at night, and draws surface air inward.
The model shows only the effect of uneven heating; real winds also depend on Earth’s rotation, friction and larger weather systems.

misconceptions.claim: A sea breeze always blows from sea to land, by day and by night.
misconceptions.truth: A sea breeze blows onshore by day, when the land is warmer than the sea. At night the land can cool below the sea’s temperature, and a land breeze may blow offshore instead. Background winds, cloud and coastal hills can weaken or stop either breeze.

misconceptions.claim: Hot air rises because heat itself rises.
misconceptions.truth: Warm air rises because it is less dense than the cooler air around it. The denser cooler air sinks and pushes the warm air upward, just as a cork floats up in water.

teacher.script:
Drag the Day slider to local hour 15 and compare the sea and land temperatures. Trace the surface flow toward the warmer land and the return flow aloft.

Move to hour 3: has the surface flow reversed? Then turn on Urban heat and compare the city with the countryside around it.
pitfalls: The land and sea temperatures are set by the model, not measured at a real coast.
Explain that local temperature contrasts favor breezes, while larger weather systems can change or suppress them.
Explain that the Coriolis effect is left out because the circulation is small and short-lived, not because it is zero near coasts.

modelNotes: The loop is drawn four times taller than true; Physical scale shows the true proportions of a model area 20 km wide and 2 km deep.

predict.prompt: On a sunny afternoon at the beach, which heats up faster, the land or the sea? Which way do you think the wind will blow at ground level?

cer.prompt: Why does a sea breeze blow onshore by day and often reverse at night?
cer.claim: Uneven heating of land and sea makes a circulation: by day the surface wind blows from the cooler sea toward the warmer land, and at night it can reverse into a land breeze.
cer.evidence: At local hour 15 the readout shows the land warmer than the sea, with surface flow onshore and a return flow aloft. At hour 3 the land is cooler than the sea and the surface flow reverses. With Urban heat on, the city is warmer than the countryside and air flows in toward it.
cer.reasoning: Land heats and cools faster than water. Warmer air is less dense and rises, lowering surface pressure, so cooler, denser air flows in underneath. When the heating pattern reverses at night, the pressure difference and the flow reverse too.

labs.title: Wind, PGF and Coriolis
labs.hook: Air accelerates in response to pressure differences.
labs.objective: Explain how pressure differences start air moving and how Earth’s rotation and surface friction change its direction.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the lower-pressure side and predict which way the pressure-gradient arrow points. Then turn Southern hemisphere on and off and compare the steady wind.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Turn on Friction: does the wind now cross the isobars, and toward which side? Then turn on Release from rest and drag the Process slider to watch the wind develop.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why does adding friction change both the speed and direction of the wind?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The pressure-gradient force (PGF) points…
choices: Along the isobars
Always east
From low to high pressure
From high to low pressure
questions.explain: A pressure difference exerts a net force from higher toward lower pressure. A steeper pressure gradient produces a stronger force per unit mass of air.

questions.prompt: In the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis effect deflects moving air…
choices: Right
Left
Up
Not at all
questions.explain: Seen from the rotating Earth, moving air is deflected to the right of its direction of travel in the Northern Hemisphere. 'Right' is relative to the direction of travel, not a fixed compass direction.

questions.prompt: Friction near the surface makes wind…
choices: Faster and more geostrophic
Cross isobars toward low pressure
Lose all Coriolis deflection
Blow straight from high to low pressure
questions.explain: Surface friction slows the wind and weakens its Coriolis deflection. The pressure-gradient force then gives the flow a component across the isobars toward lower pressure.

questions.prompt: The horizontal Coriolis parameter f is zero at…
choices: The poles
Chicago
The equator
The tropopause only
questions.explain: For horizontal motion, the Coriolis parameter is proportional to the sine of latitude. It is zero at the equator and changes sign between the two hemispheres.

questions.prompt: A westerly wind blows…
choices: From the east toward the west
Toward the west, out to sea
From the west toward the east
Only along a country’s west coast
questions.explain: Wind direction always names where the air comes from. Across the midlatitude United States, the prevailing westerlies carry air and weather systems from west to east.

why: Air accelerates in response to pressure differences. Earth’s rotation deflects its motion, while surface friction changes both wind speed and the angle at which it crosses pressure contours.

Air released from rest starts moving toward lower pressure, but Coriolis turns it to the right in the Northern Hemisphere (left in the Southern) until the wind runs along the isobars, with Coriolis balancing the pressure-gradient force: the geostrophic wind. Friction slows the air, which weakens Coriolis, so the pressure-gradient force wins slightly and the wind crosses the isobars toward lower pressure.
The fixed pressure field and simple drag isolate these forces; the model does not predict the wind at any real place.

misconceptions.claim: Wind always blows straight from high pressure to low pressure.
misconceptions.truth: The pressure-gradient force pushes air toward lower pressure, but Earth’s rotation deflects moving air and friction slows it near the ground. Above the surface layer, winds blow almost along the isobars; near the ground they cross them at an angle toward lower pressure.

misconceptions.claim: A wind is named after the direction it is blowing toward.
misconceptions.truth: Winds are named after the direction they come from. A westerly wind blows from the west toward the east, and a north wind comes from the north.

teacher.script:
Find the lower-pressure side and predict which way the pressure-gradient arrow points. Then turn Southern hemisphere on and off and compare the steady wind.

Turn on Friction: does the wind now cross the isobars, and toward which side? Then turn on Release from rest and drag the Process slider to watch the wind develop.
pitfalls: Explain Coriolis as an apparent deflection in Earth’s rotating reference frame and check the direction in each hemisphere.
Use large-scale atmospheric examples rather than sinks or toilets to demonstrate the Coriolis effect.
Distinguish the pressure-gradient force that accelerates air from friction that slows it and changes its direction.

modelNotes: The fixed northward pressure-gradient acceleration is 0.001 m/s².
Coriolis parameter f is ±0.0001 s⁻¹; surface friction uses a linear drag coefficient of 0.00005 s⁻¹.
Turn on Release from rest, then press Play or drag the Process slider to see the first 24 hours.

predict.prompt: Air flows from high to low pressure. Do you think the wind blows straight across the isobars from high to low? Why or why not?

cer.prompt: Why does the wind above the ground blow along the isobars instead of straight toward low pressure?
cer.claim: Earth's rotation turns moving air until the Coriolis effect balances the pressure-gradient force, so the wind blows along the isobars; near the ground, friction makes it cross them toward low pressure.
cer.evidence: With Release from rest, air starts toward lower pressure and turns right in the Northern Hemisphere (left with Southern hemisphere on) until it runs parallel to the isobars. Turning on Friction slows the wind, and it then crosses the isobars at an angle toward lower pressure.
cer.reasoning: The Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and grows with wind speed. A steady wind is reached when it exactly balances the pressure-gradient force. Friction slows the air and weakens the deflection, so the pressure force wins slightly.

labs.title: Three-cell circulation
labs.hook: Unequal solar heating and Earth’s rotation organize broad atmospheric circulation.
labs.objective: Locate the Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells and relate their circulation to broad patterns of winds and rainfall.
standards: OCR GCSE A Environmental threats to our planet

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells on the globe. Follow the surface easterlies and westerlies.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Turn Three cells off to see a single heat-driven loop, then on again. Compare the Ferrel cell, kept going by weather systems, with the heat-driven Hadley and Polar cells. Press Play to move the ITCZ through a year, then explain why the real ITCZ moves less neatly.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do rising and sinking air help explain broad rainfall patterns, and why does the Ferrel cell need a different explanation?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The Hadley cell has rising air near…
choices: The poles
The subtropics, near 30°
The equator / ITCZ
The polar front, near 60°
questions.explain: Strong tropical heating and surface convergence support rising air near the ITCZ. This ascent forms the rising branch of the idealized Hadley circulation.

questions.prompt: The ITCZ shifts north and south during the year because…
choices: The Moon’s pull shifts the trade winds
Ocean tides move the zone of rising air
Earth’s rotation speed changes from season to season
Seasonal heating moves the zone of convergence
questions.explain: Seasonal changes in heating and differences between land and ocean shift the zone where tropical surface winds converge. Its position varies with longitude and does not simply follow the latitude directly beneath the Sun.

questions.prompt: The Ferrel cell is called ‘indirect’ because…
choices: Midlatitude weather eddies maintain it.
It is driven directly by local surface heating.
It runs opposite to Earth’s rotation.
It exists only over the oceans.
questions.explain: Midlatitude weather systems carry heat and momentum and keep the average Ferrel circulation going. Its air rises on the colder, poleward side and sinks on the warmer side: the opposite of what heating alone would drive.

questions.prompt: Why does Earth differ from a simple one-cell circulation?
choices: Earth is heated equally at all latitudes.
Rotation and weather eddies reshape the flow.
The oceans block air moving toward the poles.
Mountains split the single cell into three.
questions.explain: Earth's rotation constrains large-scale motion, while weather systems redistribute heat and momentum. Their combined effects produce a circulation more complex than a single direct equator-to-pole loop.

questions.prompt: Why are many of the world’s hot deserts near 30° N and 30° S?
choices: The Sun is overhead there all year.
Trade winds bring rain there from the sea.
They are the furthest places from oceans.
Air sinks there, warming and drying.
questions.explain: Air that rose at the ITCZ descends in the subtropics. Sinking air warms by compression and its relative humidity falls, so clouds struggle to form.

why: Unequal solar heating and Earth’s rotation organize broad atmospheric circulation. Rising and sinking regions help explain the trade winds, westerlies and major pressure belts.

Air rising at the ITCZ cools and condenses, giving heavy tropical rain; air sinking near 30° warms and dries, giving subtropical highs and deserts. Rising air near 60° brings frequent midlatitude rain. As Earth rotates, air moving across latitudes is turned, so equatorward surface flow becomes the easterly trades and polar easterlies, while poleward flow becomes the westerlies.
The three-cell pattern is an average framework; actual circulation shifts with seasons, continents and changing weather.

misconceptions.claim: The three atmospheric cells are fixed loops followed by individual air parcels.
misconceptions.truth: The three-cell model shows average circulation across latitudes. Real air moves through changing weather systems and mixes between regions. Continents, seasons and oceans disturb the pattern, and the Ferrel cell is kept going mainly by midlatitude weather systems, not by a simple convection loop.

misconceptions.claim: The biggest hot deserts lie on the equator because it is the hottest place.
misconceptions.truth: The equator is mostly wet, because air rises there and forms heavy rain. The Sahara, Arabian and Australian deserts lie near 30° N and S, where air sinks in the Hadley cell, warms and dries out.

teacher.script:
Find the Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells on the globe. Follow the surface easterlies and westerlies.

Compare the Ferrel cell, kept going by weather systems, with the heat-driven Hadley and Polar cells. Play a year to shift the ITCZ, then explain why the real ITCZ moves less neatly.
pitfalls: Use the three-cell model as a broad circulation pattern rather than three equal, fixed cells.
Locate the United Kingdom in the midlatitudes rather than in the Hadley cell, and allow the ITCZ to shift seasonally.
Explain that the Ferrel cell is an indirect circulation influenced by midlatitude weather systems.

modelNotes: Play a year to move the model ITCZ between 10° S and 10° N.
Physical scale (T) shrinks the cells to their true 12 km depth against Earth’s 6371 km radius.

predict.prompt: Many of the world's hot deserts lie near 30° N and 30° S. What do you think the air is doing there: rising or sinking?

cer.prompt: How does the three-cell circulation explain where the world's rainforests and hot deserts are?
cer.claim: Rainforests lie near the equator where air rises in the Hadley cell, and hot deserts lie near 30° N and S where that air sinks.
cer.evidence: In the model, air rises at the ITCZ near the equator, flows poleward aloft, and sinks near 30°, then returns as the easterly trade winds. Playing a year moves the model ITCZ between 10° S and 10° N.
cer.reasoning: Rising air expands and cools, so its water vapor condenses into cloud and heavy rain. Sinking air is compressed and warms, which lowers its relative humidity and stops clouds forming, giving the subtropical highs and deserts.

labs.title: Fronts as wedges
labs.hook: A weather front separates air masses with different temperature and density.
labs.objective: Compare warm, cold and occluded fronts, and explain how the movement of contrasting air masses produces cloud and rain.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the cold air, the warm sector and the cool air ahead. Compare the slopes of the cold front and the warm front.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Drag the Process slider to 0.70, where the cold front catches the warm front and the warm sector disappears from the ground. Keep going and read in the results panel how high the warm air has been lifted.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain how the slopes and motion of contrasting air masses affect where warm air rises.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A cold front is…
choices: A vertical wall of cold air
Warm air sliding over cold air
A line where air stops moving
Cold air undercutting warmer air
questions.explain: Advancing cold air is denser than the warmer air ahead and pushes beneath it. The forced ascent can produce cloud and precipitation along a relatively steep frontal boundary.

questions.prompt: A warm front typically has…
choices: A gentle slope, with cloud ahead
A steeper slope than a cold front
A vertical boundary with no cloud
Heavy showers behind the front only
questions.explain: At a warm front, advancing warm air gradually rises over a retreating colder air mass. Its gentler slope often spreads cloud and precipitation over a broader area ahead of the surface front.

questions.prompt: Occlusion means…
choices: The warm front catches up with the cold front ahead
The cold front lifts the warm sector off the ground
Two warm air masses merge together at the surface
The front stops moving and slowly dissolves away
questions.explain: An occlusion develops when a cold front catches a warm front and lifts the warm sector away from the ground. The resulting structure depends on the temperatures of the two colder air masses.

questions.prompt: The front drawn on a National Weather Service chart is…
choices: A vertical wall of air from ground to space
The edge of the cloud band on satellite images
Where a sloping boundary meets the ground
The place where all the rain falls
questions.explain: A weather-map front marks where the sloping boundary between air masses meets Earth's surface. Cloud and precipitation can extend well away from that line because air is lifted along the boundary above it.

questions.prompt: After a cold front passes over the Midwest, the weather usually becomes…
choices: Warmer and more humid, with drizzle
Calm and foggy for several days
Cooler and clearer, with showers
Unchanged until the next warm front
questions.explain: Behind a cold front, colder and drier air arrives. Skies often clear, with bright spells and scattered showers, and the wind usually shifts, often to the northwest.

why: A weather front separates air masses with different temperature and density. A colder air mass can undercut warmer air, while a warm front rises more gradually over cold air ahead.

The cold front moves faster than the warm front, so the warm sector narrows. When the cold air catches the cool air ahead, the warm air is squeezed upward and no longer touches the ground: this is an occlusion. The occluded front on a chart marks where the two colder air masses meet at the surface.
The front slopes and speeds are set to show the geometry; the clouds do not predict rainfall.

misconceptions.claim: A front is a solid wall that keeps two air masses completely separate.
misconceptions.truth: A front is a transition zone across which properties such as temperature and humidity change. Its slope and movement affect how air is lifted, with cloud and precipitation depending on moisture and stability. Mixing occurs, and real fronts have more complex shapes than a single dividing line.

misconceptions.claim: A warm front brings warm, sunny weather.
misconceptions.truth: A warm front usually brings thickening cloud and a long spell of steady rain as warm air rises gently over cold air. Temperatures rise once the front has passed, but the warm sector is often cloudy too.

teacher.script:
Find the cold air, the warm sector and the cool air ahead. Compare the slopes of the cold front and the warm front.

Drag the Process slider to 0.70, where the cold front catches the warm front and the warm sector disappears from the ground. Keep going and read in the results panel how high the warm air has been lifted.
pitfalls: Use the three-dimensional slope of a front to explain cloud and rainfall patterns beyond its line on a map.
Compare the slopes of warm and cold fronts without drawing either as a perfectly vertical wall.
Distinguish rainbands associated with midlatitude fronts from the structure of a tropical cyclone.

modelNotes: The model uses a cold-front slope of 1:50 and a gentler warm-front slope of 1:150 across a 600 km section.

predict.prompt: When cold air pushes into warm air, which do you think goes underneath, and what happens to the warm air?

cer.prompt: Why do fronts bring cloud and rain?
cer.claim: At a front, warm air is lifted over colder, denser air; as it rises it cools and its water vapor condenses into cloud and rain.
cer.evidence: The cold front slopes steeply (1:50 in the model) and the warm front gently (1:150), with cloud over both sloping boundaries. At Process 0.70 the cold front catches the warm front and the warm sector is lifted off the ground, and the results panel gives how high it has been lifted.
cer.reasoning: Cold air is denser, so it stays underneath and wedges the warm air upward. Rising air expands and cools; once it reaches its dew point, water vapor condenses. A steep cold front lifts air quickly, giving short heavy showers; a gentle warm front gives wider, steadier rain.

labs.title: Cyclone and anticyclone
labs.hook: Around a low-pressure system, air tends to converge near the surface; around a high it tends to diverge.
labs.objective: Compare pressure and airflow around a cyclone and an anticyclone, then relate each pattern to the weather it can bring.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the low and trace how surface air converges on it. Note the direction of spin seen from above, then turn on Southern hemisphere.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Turn on Anticyclone. How is air spreading out (divergence) different from air spinning (rotation)? Name the vertical motion shown by the exaggerated center arrow.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do surface convergence and divergence differ from the rotation around a pressure system?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: In the Northern Hemisphere, a midlatitude cyclone spins…
choices: Counterclockwise
Clockwise
Not at all
Only vertically
questions.explain: The pressure-gradient force draws air toward the low, while Northern Hemisphere Coriolis deflection acts to the right of its motion. The resulting circulation is counterclockwise, with surface friction adding inward flow.

questions.prompt: An anticyclone is associated with…
choices: A surface low with rising air and cloud
High pressure, sinking air, clearer skies
A surface high with strongly rising air
Low pressure with strong fronts and rain
questions.explain: Air commonly descends within an anticyclone and warms as it is compressed, reducing relative humidity. Clearer skies are common, although low cloud or fog can persist beneath an inversion.

questions.prompt: A nor’easter, a winter storm on the US East Coast, is…
choices: A tropical cyclone from warm seas
An anticyclone with weather fronts
A midlatitude cyclone with fronts
A thermal low over heated land
questions.explain: Nor’easters, like most winter storms over the United States and Europe, develop in midlatitudes along strong horizontal temperature contrasts and have fronts. Tropical cyclones draw much of their energy from warm-ocean heat and moisture and have a different structure.

questions.prompt: Clockwise, outward surface flow in the Northern Hemisphere marks…
choices: A midlatitude cyclone
A tropical cyclone
A depression filling in
An anticyclone
questions.explain: In the Northern Hemisphere, the pressure-gradient force points away from a high and Coriolis deflects the moving air to its right. The resulting anticyclonic circulation is clockwise, with outward flow near the surface.

questions.prompt: On a weather chart, isobars packed closely around a low pressure center mean…
choices: Light, calm winds
High pressure building quickly
Strong winds near the low
Clear, settled skies
questions.explain: Closely spaced isobars show a steep pressure gradient, which drives strong winds. Widely spaced isobars, common in anticyclones, mean light winds.

why: Around a low-pressure system, air tends to converge near the surface; around a high it tends to diverge. Rotation and friction determine the circulation direction and cross-isobar flow.

Air cannot pile up or empty out at the surface. Where surface air converges on a low it must rise, cooling and often forming cloud; where it diverges from a high, air sinks from above to replace it and warms, which tends to clear the skies. Rotation is a separate property: the spin direction depends on the hemisphere, but convergence and divergence do not.
These idealized pressure systems show circulation patterns; cloud and rainfall depend on moisture and stability as well as pressure.

misconceptions.claim: High pressure always brings hot, sunny weather.
misconceptions.truth: High pressure usually means sinking air and settled weather, but what that feels like depends on the season and moisture. An anticyclone can bring clear skies or days of fog and low cloud, and in winter its calm, clear nights can bring hard frost.

misconceptions.claim: Water always drains the opposite way down plugholes in the Southern Hemisphere, because of the Coriolis effect.
misconceptions.truth: The Coriolis effect matters for systems hundreds of kilometers across that last for days, such as depressions. In a sink it is far too weak; the shape of the basin and how the water was moving decide which way it swirls.

cases.label: Katrina and Sandy: tropical cyclones, for comparison

teacher.script:
Find the low and trace how surface air converges on it. Note the direction of spin seen from above, then turn on Southern hemisphere.

Turn on Anticyclone. How is air spreading out (divergence) different from air spinning (rotation)? Name the vertical motion shown by the exaggerated center arrow.
pitfalls: Check the hemisphere before describing the direction of circulation around high and low pressure.
Distinguish a midlatitude cyclone with fronts from a tropical cyclone driven by warm-ocean conditions.
Explain that an anticyclone can bring fog or low cloud, so high pressure does not guarantee sunshine.

predict.prompt: In the Northern Hemisphere, do you think air spins clockwise or counterclockwise around a low-pressure center? Why?

cer.prompt: Why are low-pressure systems often cloudy and wet while high-pressure systems are often clear?
cer.claim: Air converges and rises in a low, which makes cloud and rain; air sinks and spreads out in a high, which suppresses cloud.
cer.evidence: Around the low, surface air spirals inward counterclockwise (clockwise with Southern hemisphere on) and the center arrow points up, with cloud bands and rain. With Anticyclone on, surface air spirals outward clockwise, the center arrow points down, and the sky has only scattered cumulus.
cer.reasoning: Air that converges near the ground has to go somewhere, so it rises; rising air cools and its vapor condenses. Sinking air warms as it is compressed, so clouds evaporate. The Coriolis effect turns the moving air, which sets the direction of spin.

labs.title: Climate types
labs.hook: Compare the world’s climate families through long-term temperature and rainfall patterns.
labs.objective: Explore the five major climate families and explain how long-term temperature and rainfall patterns shape their global distribution.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Read the A–E legend and identify the highlighted family on the globe.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Choose Tropical, then Dry. Compare their distribution and explain why temperature alone cannot separate them.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why must rainfall be considered alongside temperature when comparing tropical and dry climates?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Köppen–Geiger classification primarily uses…
choices: Today’s weather at a weather station.
Latitude and height above sea level.
Long-term monthly temperature and rainfall.
Only the plants visible in one photograph.
questions.explain: Köppen–Geiger classes use thresholds based on long-term monthly temperature and precipitation, including when in the year they occur. Vegetation reflects those conditions but is not used to define the classes.

questions.prompt: A B climate can be…
choices: Only hot.
Only polar ice.
A guarantee of rain every day.
Dry and either hot or cold.
questions.explain: B climates are defined by dryness: rainfall below a threshold that depends on temperature and on when the rain falls. A final letter then separates hot (h) from cold (k) dry climates.

questions.prompt: Washington, DC’s Cfa label applies to…
choices: One sampled point, dataset and period.
Every location in the United States.
The weather expected tomorrow in DC.
All of the eastern US lowlands.
questions.explain: A climate label describes the data at the sampled location over the selected reference period. Other places in the same country can fall into different classes because of elevation, coastal influence or regional rainfall patterns.

questions.prompt: The polar family includes…
choices: Only landscapes covered by permanent ice.
Both tundra and ice-cap climates.
Every place with a cold winter.
Only locations in the Southern Hemisphere.
questions.explain: Both tundra and ice-cap climates have a warmest-month mean below 10 °C. Tundra reaches at least 0 °C in its warmest month, while an ice-cap climate remains below 0 °C.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes climate rather than weather?
choices: It is raining heavily in Chicago today.
Tomorrow will be windy in Denver.
Last night was the coldest night of the whole winter.
Seattle averages about 1,000 mm of rain a year.
questions.explain: An average over many years describes climate. The other statements describe conditions on particular days, which is weather.

why: Köppen–Geiger groups climates using long-term monthly temperature and rainfall. Tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar families describe different combinations of warmth, seasonality and moisture.

The families form a pattern because heat and moisture are delivered unevenly. Tropical climates sit near the equator, where it is warm all year. Dry climates cluster under the sinking air of the subtropics, in continental interiors and in rain shadows. Temperate, cold continental and polar climates follow as winters become colder toward the poles; cold continental climates are almost absent from the Southern Hemisphere because little land lies at those latitudes. High mountains can be polar even in the tropics.
The colors summarize the 1991–2020 reference period; a location’s climate class does not determine its current weather or exact vegetation.

misconceptions.claim: One unusual day of weather can change a place’s climate classification.
misconceptions.truth: Climate classes come from long-term statistics, such as 30 years of monthly temperature and rainfall. A heatwave or a very wet day is one event within that record. Only a lasting shift in those statistics can eventually change a place’s class.

misconceptions.claim: Weather and climate mean the same thing.
misconceptions.truth: Weather is the state of the atmosphere over hours or days. Climate is the long-term pattern of weather, usually averaged over 30 years: as the saying goes, climate is what you expect, weather is what you get.

teacher.script:
