Choose Tropical and ask students to describe where it occurs. Then choose Dry and discuss why rainfall matters as well as temperature.

Locate Washington, DC as a temperate example, then compare Saint Paul, Minnesota, and Nuuk. Ask students why a city’s classification should not be assigned to its whole country.

Finish by distinguishing climate from today’s weather. Discuss why vegetation also depends on soil, land use and disturbance, then use Check to test the explanation.
pitfalls: Use long-term temperature and rainfall patterns to explain climate classes rather than treating them as today’s weather.
Keep a reference point’s climate separate from the range of climates found across a whole country.
Explain that a climate family can support several vegetation types and does not determine one unique biome.

sources.label: Beck et al. classification and data

modelNotes: The classification uses Beck et al. V3 for 1991–2020. The globe groups the official 0.1° grid into five families.

Singapore, Cairo, Washington, DC and Saint Paul are reference points from the Atlas 1 km raster; Nuuk is sampled from the 0.1° globe grid. Different resolutions can change classifications near a boundary.

predict.prompt: The Sahara and the Amazon are both hot. What do you think separates a tropical climate from a hot desert climate?

cer.prompt: Why can't temperature alone tell you which climate family a place belongs to?
cer.claim: Climate families depend on both temperature and precipitation, so two equally hot places can belong to different families.
cer.evidence: Choosing Tropical highlights a band near the equator, including the Amazon and Congo basins. Choosing Dry highlights the Sahara, Arabia and central Australia near 30° N and S, and interiors and rain shadows elsewhere. Both include places that are hot all year.
cer.reasoning: The Köppen–Geiger system uses long-term monthly temperature and precipitation. A dry (B) climate is defined by too little precipitation for its temperature, whatever the temperature is. Rising air near the equator brings heavy rain, while sinking subtropical air keeps deserts dry.

labs.title: Drainage basin
labs.hook: A drainage basin collects water that flows toward a common outlet.
labs.objective: Trace water through a drainage basin and explain how the watershed connects the tributaries to a shared outlet.
standards: OCR GCSE A Landscapes of the UK

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Use Basin overlay to show the drainage divide and trace the edge of the basin. Identify which slopes drain toward the same outlet.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Feature to Tributary and press Play to follow water down a tributary to its confluence with the main river. Then hide the labels and ask a partner to find the source, confluence and outlet.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does the drainage divide determine which slopes supply water to the same river outlet?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A watershed is…
choices: The river mouth
The main river channel
The river source
The drainage divide
questions.explain: The drainage divide follows higher ground separating surface runoff that reaches different river systems. It forms the outer boundary of the selected basin.

questions.prompt: A confluence is…
choices: Where tributaries meet
Where a river meets the sea
Where a river begins
Where a river splits
questions.explain: A confluence is the meeting point of two or more river channels. Their flows combine and continue downstream in a shared channel.

questions.prompt: The mouth is…
choices: The spring, bog or lake where the river first begins
Where it enters the sea, a lake or a larger river
Always a delta built out into the sea
The steepest, fastest stretch of the river
questions.explain: The mouth is the downstream end where a river enters another body of water. Whether a delta forms there depends on how much sediment arrives and how quickly waves, tides or currents carry it away.

questions.prompt: The drainage basin includes…
choices: Only the river channels on the map
Only the floodplain beside the river
All the land draining to the river
The river and its groundwater only
questions.explain: Rain falling on basin slopes can reach the river by surface runoff, soil flow or groundwater flow. The drainage basin therefore includes the contributing land as well as the visible channels.

questions.prompt: Rain falls just beyond a basin’s watershed. Where does its runoff go?
choices: Into this river, but more slowly
Nowhere, because it all evaporates
Straight into this river’s main channel
Into a neighboring river system
questions.explain: The watershed is the boundary of the basin. Rain falling on the other side drains toward a different river, even if the two places are very close.

why: A drainage basin collects water that flows toward a common outlet. The watershed separates it from neighboring basins; tributaries connect hillslope inputs to the main river.

Rain falling anywhere inside the divide runs downslope into the nearest channel. Tributaries collect water from their own side slopes and deliver it to the main river at a confluence, so discharge increases downstream until all of it leaves at the outlet.
The terrain is an invented teaching catchment, and the moving traces show routes, not measured travel times.

misconceptions.claim: All rain falling within a drainage basin reaches its river immediately.
misconceptions.truth: Rainfall can be intercepted, infiltrate soil, replenish groundwater, evaporate or enter surface runoff. These pathways have different travel times, and some water remains stored or leaves through evapotranspiration. The river’s response depends on both rainfall and the basin’s existing conditions.

misconceptions.claim: Rivers flow from north to south.
misconceptions.truth: Rivers flow downhill, in whatever direction the land slopes. The Nile flows north to the Mediterranean, and the River Tay flows east; ‘north’ is only the top of the map.

teacher.script:
Use Basin overlay to show the drainage divide and trace the edge of the basin. Identify which slopes drain toward the same outlet.

Follow a tributary to its confluence with the main river. Hide the labels and ask a partner to find the source, confluence and outlet.
pitfalls: Trace the full land area draining toward the outlet, not only the river channels.
Clarify whether watershed means the drainage divide or the whole basin in the terminology being used.
Distinguish the river mouth from a delta, which forms only where sediment accumulates under suitable conditions.

modelNotes: Relief is exaggerated so the bowl shape is easy to see. A real divide, such as the low divide between the Great Lakes and Mississippi basins near Chicago, can be a barely noticeable rise.
Orbit the model: the catchment is a 3D landscape, not a flat colored area.
Without the 3D view, sketch a rim (the divide), a source, tributaries joining at a confluence, and an outlet.

predict.prompt: Rain falls on two sides of a hilltop ridge. Will the water from both sides end up in the same river? Why or why not?

cer.prompt: What decides which river the rain falling on a slope ends up in?
cer.claim: The drainage divide (watershed) decides it: all the rain that falls inside the divide drains to the same outlet, and rain just outside it goes to a neighboring river.
cer.evidence: With Basin overlay on, the divide follows the high ground around the basin rim. Following a tributary shows water flowing downhill to a confluence and then to the single outlet; slopes beyond the rim drain away from it.
cer.reasoning: Water flows downhill. The divide is the line of highest ground between basins, so it separates the slopes that drain toward one outlet from those that drain toward another.

labs.title: Storm hydrograph
labs.hook: A storm hydrograph shows how river discharge changes after rainfall.
labs.objective: Read the main features of a storm hydrograph and explain how urban surfaces can change the timing and size of peak discharge.
standards: OCR GCSE A Landscapes of the UK

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Play the storm and compare rainfall with the rising and falling limbs of river discharge. Locate the rainfall and discharge peaks.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Urban cover and compare peak discharge and lag time. Return to a less urban catchment and explain how infiltration and storage change the response.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why does the discharge peak occur after the rainfall peak, and how can urban cover change that delay?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: In this lab, lag time is…
choices: Start of rain to peak flow
Peak flow to base flow
Total length of the storm
Peak rain to peak discharge
questions.explain: In this lab, lag time is the interval between peak rainfall intensity and peak discharge. Water takes time to move through the catchment and reach the measurement point.

questions.prompt: Urban land use typically…
choices: Shortens lag and raises peak
Lengthens lag and lowers peak
Lowers the peak but keeps lag
Has no effect on runoff at all
questions.explain: Paved surfaces reduce infiltration, while drains can carry runoff rapidly to channels. Under comparable rainfall, these changes commonly raise the flood peak and shorten its lag.

questions.prompt: A falling limb is…
choices: Discharge rising after heavy rain
Discharge falling after the peak
The flow between storms
The time of peak rainfall
questions.explain: On the falling limb, discharge decreases after its peak as quick surface runoff drains away. Slower drainage from soil and groundwater keeps the river flowing.

questions.prompt: Stage and discharge are…
choices: The same number with two names
Flow speed versus the channel’s width at the gauge
Water height versus flow volume per second
Rainfall total versus surface runoff
questions.explain: Stage is the height of the water surface above a reference level, whereas discharge is the volume passing a cross-section each second. The link between them (a rating curve) is different at every site.

questions.prompt: Why might the same storm give a higher peak after a wet week?
choices: Rain falls faster and harder onto wet ground.
Rivers are always deeper in winter.
Saturated soil lets less water infiltrate.
Wet weather lowers the river’s bed.
questions.explain: When the soil is already full of water, little more can infiltrate. More of the rain becomes overland flow, reaching the river quickly and raising the peak.

why: A storm hydrograph shows how river discharge changes after rainfall. Infiltration, storage and routing delay the response. A greater runoff fraction raises the peak, and faster routing through drains and channels brings it earlier.

Paved surfaces let less rain soak into the soil, so more of it becomes surface runoff, and drains carry it straight to the river. More water arrives in less time, so the peak is higher and the lag time shorter. Soil, vegetation and groundwater store water and release it slowly, which flattens the peak and lengthens the falling limb.
The model uses an invented catchment and a set storm, so it compares processes; it is not a forecast for a real river.

misconceptions.claim: Peak river discharge occurs at exactly the same time as peak rainfall.
misconceptions.truth: Water takes time to move through a catchment and its stores, so the discharge peak commonly follows the rainfall peak. The delay depends on rainfall location and duration, catchment size, slopes, soil conditions and drainage. State which rainfall reference is used when measuring lag time.

misconceptions.claim: The same amount of rain always produces the same flood.
misconceptions.truth: The response depends on the catchment’s condition. Rain on soil that is already saturated or frozen runs off quickly and gives a higher, sharper peak than the same rain falling on dry ground.

teacher.script:
Play the storm and pause at the dashed lines that mark the rainfall peak (2 h) and the discharge peak; the gap between them is the lag time shown in the readout.

Set Urban cover to 0 and then 1 with Rain unchanged, and record peak discharge and lag time each time. Then change Rain alone: the peak scales with rainfall but the lag stays the same, because in this model timing depends on the catchment, not on how much rain falls.
pitfalls: Distinguish river stage, which is a water level, from discharge, which is a volume passing per unit time.
Compare the rainfall peak with the discharge peak and explain the processes that produce a time lag.
Use the timescale of the response to distinguish a rapid flood from a flood with a prolonged recession.

modelNotes: A four-hour triangular storm peaks at 20 mm/h multiplied by the Rain setting.
Urban cover raises the runoff fraction from 0.25 to 0.85 and shortens the delay and storage time. These are teaching assumptions, not values measured at a real site.

The graph shows 24 hours and so cuts off part of the long recession; the model keeps that water in storage. A constant baseflow of 0.05 m³/s stands for groundwater that keeps the river flowing between storms.

predict.prompt: If fields around a river are covered with roads and roofs, will the river flood sooner or later after a storm? Higher or lower?

cer.prompt: How does building a town in a catchment change a river's response to a storm?
cer.claim: Urban surfaces make the river peak sooner and higher, so the lag time shortens and the peak discharge rises.
cer.evidence: Raising Urban cover from 0 to 1 raises the share of rain that runs off from 0.25 to 0.85 and moves the discharge peak closer to the rainfall peak at 2 hours. The rising limb gets steeper and the peak discharge in the readout increases.
cer.reasoning: Roads and roofs stop water soaking into the soil, and drains carry it quickly to the river. Less water is stored and slowed, so more of the rain reaches the channel in a shorter time.

labs.title: River regime
labs.hook: A river regime describes the seasonal pattern of discharge.
labs.objective: Compare annual patterns of river discharge and explain how rainfall, snowmelt and dams can change their timing.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Read the gold (rain-fed) and blue (snow-fed) discharge curves. Drag the Year slider through winter and find where water is stored as snow.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Follow the spring melt and compare its flow peak with the rain-fed river's winter peak (the readout gives both dates). Turn on Dam on snow-fed river and compare the new peak with the dashed curve without the dam.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does storing precipitation as snow shift the timing of river flow?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A nival regime is driven by…
choices: Summer rainstorms
Tidal cycles
Snowmelt
Groundwater springs
questions.explain: A nival regime reflects water stored as seasonal snow and released when temperatures rise. This commonly produces a spring or early-summer increase in discharge rather than an immediate response to winter precipitation.

questions.prompt: A pluvial regime follows…
choices: Evaporation from the river
Snowmelt timing
Glacier melt
Rainfall seasonality
questions.explain: A pluvial regime is governed mainly by the seasonal distribution of rainfall. Evaporation, soil storage and groundwater can modify when that rainfall appears as river flow.

questions.prompt: The Mississippi’s year is…
choices: A huge basin of snowmelt and rain, managed by dams
A small upland stream’s flashy regime
A spring-fed flow that barely varies all year
A regime set mainly by glacier melt in the summer months
questions.explain: The Mississippi integrates runoff from a very large basin with contrasting rainfall and snowmelt patterns. Reservoirs, water use and river engineering also modify its seasonal flow.

questions.prompt: A storm hydrograph and a regime graph differ because…
choices: They are the same plot at different scales
One covers hours after a storm; the other a typical year
One plots rainfall totals; the other plots river discharge
One is measured; the other is always modeled
questions.explain: A storm hydrograph follows discharge during and after an individual rainfall event, often over hours or days. A regime graph summarizes the recurring seasonal pattern, usually using monthly values.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to a river’s flow below a large dam?
choices: The river stops flowing completely.
Peaks are lowered and low flows raised.
Floods become larger and more frequent.
The yearly pattern is left unchanged.
questions.explain: The reservoir stores water during high flows and releases it later. Downstream, flood peaks are reduced and dry-season flows are often higher, smoothing the regime.

why: A river regime describes the seasonal pattern of discharge. Rain may reach the river quickly, while snow stores water until melting; a reservoir can smooth and delay the resulting flow.

In the snow-fed catchment, winter precipitation falls below 0 °C and builds a snowpack, so discharge stays very low even though water is arriving. When temperatures rise above freezing the stored snow melts in a few weeks, giving a sharp late-spring peak. The rain-fed river instead peaks in winter, when rainfall is highest and evaporation lowest. A reservoir stores part of the melt peak and releases it over the following months, so the peak is lower, later and longer.
Both catchments repeat the same invented year, and the dam shows storage behavior, not a real operating rule.

misconceptions.claim: A river’s seasonal flow pattern depends only on the amount of rain each month.
misconceptions.truth: Rainfall matters, but snow accumulation and melt, evaporation, groundwater storage and reservoir operation can shift the timing of discharge. Water received in one season may reach the river in another. Explaining a regime therefore requires both the inputs and the processes that delay or remove water.

misconceptions.claim: A dam stops a river flowing.
misconceptions.truth: A dam stores water in a reservoir and releases it through the year. It usually lowers flood peaks and raises low flows, changing the river’s regime, but water still flows downstream.

teacher.script:
Read the gold (rain-fed) and blue (snow-fed) discharge curves. Drag the Year slider through winter and find where water is stored as snow.

Follow the spring melt and compare its flow peak with the rain-fed river's winter peak. Turn on Dam on snow-fed river and compare the peak and the delayed release.
pitfalls: Compare regimes across different climates rather than applying one annual pattern to every river.
Distinguish a monthly river regime from the short-term response shown by a storm hydrograph.
Use the graph’s stated scale and avoid reading exact discharge values from a curve that is only illustrative.

modelNotes: Two invented 100 km² catchments repeat the same 365-day weather every year.
The snow-fed case stores precipitation below 0 °C and melts up to 3 mm water equivalent per positive degree Celsius per day.

A fixed share of rain and meltwater is lost (40% for the rain-fed river, 25% for the snow-fed one). Of the rest, 70% reaches the river within days and 30% seeps into groundwater that drains slowly over months as baseflow, so both rivers keep flowing between peaks.
The 3D terrain is illustrative: relief is enlarged ten times unless you switch to Physical scale (T), and the channel width and dam are symbols.

predict.prompt: A mountain river is fed mainly by melting snow. In which season do you expect its highest flow?

cer.prompt: Why does a snow-fed river peak at a different time of year from a rain-fed river, and how does a dam change that?
cer.claim: A snow-fed river peaks in late spring, when stored snow melts, while a rain-fed river peaks in the wettest season; a dam lowers the peak, delays it and spreads it out.
cer.evidence: The blue snow-fed curve stays low through winter while snow builds up, then rises sharply in spring melt. The gold rain-fed curve peaks in winter. Turning on Dam on snow-fed river gives a lower, later and longer peak than the dashed curve without the dam.
cer.reasoning: Below 0 °C precipitation is stored as snow instead of running off, so it reaches the river only when temperatures rise. A reservoir stores part of the melt peak and releases it over the following months.

labs.title: Ocean currents
labs.hook: Surface winds and Earth’s rotation help organize subtropical ocean gyres.
labs.objective: Follow the major surface currents and explain how winds and ocean heat transport contribute to regional climate.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Choose North Atlantic and find its western and eastern boundary currents. Follow the arrows and name the Gulf Stream and the Canary Current.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Switch to South Atlantic and explain why it turns the opposite way. Then visit all five subtropical gyres.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do winds, Earth’s rotation and ocean-basin boundaries help organize the major surface gyres?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A gyre is…
choices: A deep current along the seabed
A current that flows only in winter
A tidal stream in a narrow strait
A large looping surface current system
questions.explain: A gyre is a broad system of linked ocean currents shaped by wind forcing, Earth's rotation and basin boundaries. Subtropical gyres form large circulating patterns rather than isolated straight streams.

questions.prompt: The Gulf Stream is…
choices: A warm western-boundary current
A cold coastal current off Peru
A cold current from the Arctic
A deep current along the seabed
questions.explain: The Gulf Stream carries warm water northward along the western side of the North Atlantic basin. It is a fast, concentrated boundary current within the wider Atlantic circulation.

questions.prompt: Seattle is farther north than Boston, yet its winters are milder. Why?
choices: The warm Gulf Stream flows past Seattle
Westerlies bring mild Pacific air onshore
Seattle is much closer to the equator
Warm desert air flows north from Mexico
questions.explain: Prevailing westerlies carry air that has crossed the Pacific onto the West Coast, and the ocean stores heat through the winter. Boston, on the east coast, mostly receives air that has crossed the cold continent, so the Gulf Stream offshore does less to warm it. The same setting helps explain the mild winters of western Europe.

questions.prompt: A western-boundary current is typically…
choices: Broad, slow and cold
Broad, fast and cold
Narrow, fast and warm
Narrow, slow and deep
questions.explain: Because the Coriolis effect strengthens with latitude, the return flow of a subtropical gyre is squeezed against its western boundary. This produces narrow, fast currents such as the Gulf Stream and Kuroshio.

questions.prompt: Why are the Atacama and Namib deserts beside cold ocean currents?
choices: Cold currents bring heavy rain to the coast.
Cold water evaporates faster than warm water, drying the air.
Cold currents cool the air, keeping it stable and dry.
The currents wash desert sand onto the coast.
questions.explain: Air cooled from below by cold water is stable and does not rise to form rain clouds. Little rain falls, although sea fog is common.

why: Surface winds and Earth’s rotation help organize subtropical ocean gyres. Warm western boundary currents generally carry water poleward, while cooler eastern boundary currents carry it toward the equator.

Earth’s rotation deflects moving water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. Together with the trade winds and westerlies, this turns northern gyres clockwise and southern gyres counterclockwise, and squeezes each gyre’s poleward return flow into a narrow, fast western boundary current.
The globe shows the broad routes and directions of currents; their width and tracer speed are exaggerated so they are easy to read.

misconceptions.claim: Ocean currents are driven only by differences in water temperature.
misconceptions.truth: Winds and pressure gradients drive much upper-ocean circulation, with Earth’s rotation and coastlines shaping the flow. Temperature and salinity affect density and contribute to overturning, while mixing connects different depths. Surface gyres and deep circulation are related but cannot be explained by temperature alone.

misconceptions.claim: Cold ocean currents make the coasts beside them wet and rainy.
misconceptions.truth: Cold currents cool the air above them, making it stable so it does not rise to form rain clouds. Coasts beside cold currents, such as the Atacama and Namib, are among the driest places on Earth, though often foggy.

teacher.script:
Choose North Atlantic and find its western and eastern boundary currents. Follow the arrows and name the Gulf Stream and the Canary Current.

Switch to South Atlantic and explain why it turns the opposite way. Then visit all five subtropical gyres.
pitfalls: Distinguish wind-driven surface gyres from the deeper overturning circulation.
Explain that the Gulf Stream transports heat as part of a wider ocean–atmosphere system.
Consider atmospheric circulation and maritime exposure as well as ocean currents when discussing the United Kingdom’s climate.

predict.prompt: Seattle is farther north than Boston, yet its winters are milder. What do you think could explain this?

cer.prompt: Why do the big ocean gyres turn the way they do, and why are their western currents fast and warm?
cer.claim: Winds and Earth's rotation drive gyres that turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counterclockwise in the Southern, with narrow, fast, warm currents along their western sides.
cer.evidence: The North Atlantic gyre turns clockwise, with the Gulf Stream flowing north along the US East Coast and the cooler Canary Current flowing south off Africa. The South Atlantic gyre turns the opposite way.
cer.reasoning: The trade winds and westerlies push surface water around each basin, and the Coriolis effect deflects it right in the north and left in the south. Because that effect strengthens with latitude, the return flow is squeezed against the western boundary, carrying tropical heat poleward.

labs.title: Thermohaline conveyor
labs.hook: Seawater density depends on temperature and salinity.
labs.objective: Explain how cooling and changes in salinity affect seawater density, then relate sinking and rising water to ocean overturning.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: In the basin section, trace the warm upper limb from the tropical coast to the icy polar coast, the sinking there, the deep return and the upwelling. Name winds and mixing as drivers as well as density.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Choose Density experiment and compare the parcel's density with the reference water. With Process at 0 the parcel is at mid-depth; at 4 °C and 35 g/kg, press Play and watch it sink.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can cooling and adding freshwater have opposing effects on whether a parcel of seawater sinks?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Thermohaline means…
choices: Circulation driven by wind alone
Circulation driven by tides alone
Circulation set by sea-ice cover
Density set by temperature and salt
questions.explain: Cooling generally increases seawater density, while adding salt also makes seawater denser. These temperature and salinity effects help determine whether surface water can sink beneath surrounding water.

questions.prompt: Deep water forms in…
choices: Cold, often salty high-latitude seas
The shallow seas along the equator
The warm tropical western Pacific
Shallow, sheltered coastal lagoons
questions.explain: Strong cooling at high latitudes can make surface seawater dense enough to sink, especially where salinity is high. Sea-ice formation can further increase the salinity of nearby seawater by rejecting salt.

questions.prompt: The conveyor is…
choices: A fast surface current
A slow global density circulation
A wind-driven surface gyre
A single deep river in the ocean
questions.explain: The conveyor image links regions of sinking, deep transport and return toward the surface. Actual overturning follows many pathways and also depends on winds and mixing, rather than a single continuous belt.

questions.prompt: Freshwater input at high latitude…
choices: Always shuts the circulation down quickly
Increases density and speeds sinking
Can lower density and reduce sinking
Has no effect on ocean density
questions.explain: Freshwater lowers surface salinity and usually lowers density, which can strengthen stratification and inhibit deep mixing. The overall circulation response also depends on temperature, winds and where the freshwater enters.

questions.prompt: Which water would sink beneath the others?
choices: Warm, fresh water
Warm, salty water
Cold, fresh water
Cold, salty water
questions.explain: Cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water is denser than fresh water. Cold, salty water is the densest, which is why it sinks in high-latitude seas.

why: Seawater density depends on temperature and salinity. Cooling and salinity changes can contribute to deep-water formation, connecting surface waters with slower circulation through the ocean interior.

Cooling a parcel from 10 °C to 4 °C makes it about 1.2 kg/m³ denser than the surrounding water, so it sinks. Freshening works the other way: lowering salinity from 35 to 32 g/kg makes it about 2.3 kg/m³ less dense, which outweighs that cooling, so a cold but fresh parcel stays near the surface. This is why meltwater, rain and river inflow at high latitudes can weaken deep-water formation.
The real circulation is driven by several mechanisms, including winds and mixing; it is not a single conveyor driven only by temperature and salinity.

misconceptions.claim: The ocean conveyor is one continuous pipe carrying water along a fixed route.
misconceptions.truth: The conveyor image simplifies a network of branching currents, mixing and exchanges between depths. Temperature and salinity influence density, while winds and mixing also help drive circulation. A parcel can follow many routes and take a range of times to move between ocean regions.

misconceptions.claim: Melting sea ice raises sea level as much as melting ice sheets.
misconceptions.truth: Sea ice already floats, displacing its own weight of water, so its melting changes sea level very little. Melting ice on land, such as the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, adds new water to the ocean and raises sea level.

cases.label: Mississippi: river water entering the sea

teacher.script:
In the basin section, trace the warm upper limb from the tropical coast to the icy polar coast, the sinking there, the deep return and the upwelling. Name winds and mixing as drivers as well as density.

Choose Density experiment and compare the parcel's density with the reference water. With Process at 0 the parcel is at mid-depth; at 4 °C and 35 g/kg, press Play and watch it sink.
pitfalls: Treat the conveyor image as a simplified representation of interconnected circulation rather than a single enclosed pipe.
Connect deep-water formation with seawater density and conditions at high latitudes.
Distinguish the timescales and uncertainties of real circulation change from dramatic fictional accounts.

modelNotes: The section is 6000 km long and 4 km deep; Teaching scale enlarges depth 500 times.
Reference water is 10 °C, 35 g/kg and 1027 kg/m³.
A simple linear formula uses a thermal expansion coefficient of 0.0002 per °C and a saline contraction coefficient of 0.00076 per g/kg at one reference pressure.
This is not the TEOS-10 equation of state; real coefficients and compressibility vary.
Compare 4 °C at 35 g/kg with the same temperature at 32 g/kg: the fresher parcel rises.

predict.prompt: Which seawater do you think sinks: warm and fresh, or cold and salty? Why?

cer.prompt: Why does cold, salty water sink, and how could melting ice weaken deep-water formation?
cer.claim: Cooling and adding salt both make seawater denser, so cold, salty water sinks; adding fresh meltwater lowers density and can stop it sinking.
cer.evidence: In the Density experiment, cooling a parcel from 10 °C to 4 °C at 35 g/kg makes it about 1.2 kg/m³ denser than the reference water and it sinks. Lowering salinity from 35 to 32 g/kg makes it about 2.3 kg/m³ less dense, so a cold but fresh parcel stays near the surface.
cer.reasoning: Density depends on temperature and salinity. Water denser than its surroundings sinks. At high latitudes, fresh water from melting ice, rain and rivers can outweigh the effect of cooling, which reduces sinking and slows the overturning circulation.

labs.title: Carbon cycle
labs.hook: Carbon moves among the atmosphere, organisms, soils, ocean and rocks.
labs.objective: Trace carbon between fast and slow stores, and explain how burning fossil fuels transfers carbon into the atmosphere.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Drag the Process slider to 0 and read the starting amount in each of the five carbon stores. Set the Fossil-fuel tap to 0 and press Play: the stores stay level because exchanges balance, not because nothing moves.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: In Follow a transfer, choose Photosynthesis, then Respiration / decay, and compare their rates. Raise the Fossil-fuel tap, drag the Process slider to 1 (model year 100), and compare the fall in the Fossil fuel store with the Burned total. Then find which stores gained that carbon.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain how balanced exchanges can continue without changing a store, and how fossil-fuel burning disrupts that balance.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Fossil fuels are…
choices: A fast store in living plants
A fast store in the upper ocean
A slow geological store we release quickly
A store that naturally refills within a century
questions.explain: Fossil fuels contain carbon stored in geological deposits over long timescales. Extraction and burning transfer that carbon rapidly into the atmosphere and other active stores.

questions.prompt: The ocean store…
choices: Holds carbon only as dissolved gas
Gains carbon only from rivers
Holds less carbon than the air
Exchanges carbon with the atmosphere
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide can dissolve into seawater and can also leave it for the atmosphere. The direction and rate of exchange depend on the conditions on both sides of the sea surface.

questions.prompt: Weathering is…
choices: A slow transfer toward rock and ocean stores
A fast daily exchange with plants
A fast release of carbon to the air
A transfer that only happens in hot, dry deserts
questions.explain: Chemical weathering carries dissolved material from rocks to rivers and the ocean. Silicate weathering uses up carbon dioxide, and the carbon is eventually buried as carbonate in ocean sediments over geological timescales.

questions.prompt: Burning fuel…
choices: Creates new carbon atoms
Moves geological carbon into the air
Destroys the carbon in the fuel
Moves carbon from the air back into rock
questions.explain: Combustion combines carbon in the fuel with oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide. The carbon atoms are transferred from the fuel store into the atmosphere rather than being newly created.

questions.prompt: Where does most of a tree’s dry mass come from?
choices: Minerals taken up from the soil
Water drawn up through the roots
Carbon dioxide taken in from the air
Sunlight turned into solid material
questions.explain: Photosynthesis uses light energy to combine carbon dioxide from the air with water, building sugars and then wood. Light supplies energy, not mass.

why: Carbon moves among the atmosphere, organisms, soils, ocean and rocks. Photosynthesis, respiration and other transfers connect stores that operate on very different timescales.

A store stays level when its inputs equal its outputs: at the start, photosynthesis takes 60 Pg C a year from the air and respiration and decay return 60. Burning fossil fuel adds an extra input to the air from a slow store that is not refilled on human timescales, so carbon builds up in the air and spreads into plants and the ocean while the total stays the same.
The budget tracks only a few stores and transfers with invented amounts, so it does not describe the whole global carbon cycle.

misconceptions.claim: Carbon released by burning fossil fuels is immediately removed by the natural carbon cycle.
misconceptions.truth: Burning fossil fuels transfers carbon from long-term geological stores into the atmosphere. Land and oceans absorb some of it, but uptake does not instantly match all emissions. Atmospheric carbon increases when inputs exceed removals, and different stores exchange carbon over very different timescales.

misconceptions.claim: Plants get most of their mass from the soil.
misconceptions.truth: Most of a plant’s dry mass is carbon compounds made from carbon dioxide taken from the air during photosynthesis. Soil supplies water and small amounts of minerals.

teacher.script:
Identify the five carbon stores and read their starting amounts. Close the Fossil-fuel tap and press Play: the stores stay level because exchanges balance, not because nothing moves.

In Follow a transfer, choose Photosynthesis, then Respiration / decay. Open the Fossil-fuel tap, drag the Process slider toward model year 100, and compare the fall in the fossil-fuel store with the total carbon burned.
pitfalls: Keep the carbon stores visible while explaining how each transfer changes their contents.
Explain that combustion moves existing carbon between stores rather than creating new carbon atoms.
Use the model’s stated quantities when checking conservation, and distinguish carbon mass from carbon dioxide mass.

modelNotes: Starting stores: atmosphere 600, biosphere 1200, ocean 3000, sediment / rock 6000 and fossil fuel 1200 Pg C.
One petagram of carbon is 10¹² kg of carbon, not of CO₂.
At the starting state, photosynthesis and respiration each transfer 60 Pg C/year, air–ocean exchange 40 in each direction, and the weathering–burial–degassing loop 0.2 on each leg.
The fossil-fuel tap adds 0–10 Pg C/year to air for up to 100 model years.

With the tap open, the fossil-fuel store falls and the fast stores change, while total carbon stays at 12000 Pg C. Extra CO₂ only partly speeds up uptake by plants and the ocean, so by model year 100 about half of the burned carbon is still in the air, close to what is seen on Earth today.

predict.prompt: When fossil fuels are burned, does the carbon disappear, stay in the air, or go somewhere else? Predict where it ends up.

cer.prompt: Where does the carbon from burning fossil fuels go, and why does the amount in the air keep rising?
cer.claim: Burning fossil fuels moves carbon from a slow geological store into the air; plants and the ocean take up part of it, but much stays in the atmosphere.
cer.evidence: At the start, photosynthesis and respiration each move 60 Pg C a year and the stores stay level. With the Fossil-fuel tap open to model year 100, the fossil-fuel store falls by the burned total, the atmosphere, biosphere and ocean stores all rise, and about half of the burned carbon is still in the air. The total stays at 12,000 Pg C.
cer.reasoning: A store stays level only when its inputs equal its outputs. Fossil carbon adds a new input to the air from a store that is not refilled on human timescales. Uptake by plants and the ocean speeds up but cannot keep pace, so the atmospheric store grows.

labs.title: ENSO and the Walker cell
labs.hook: Across the tropical Pacific, trade winds, warm surface water and the thermocline interact.
labs.objective: Compare normal Pacific conditions with El Niño and La Niña, and explain how changes in winds and ocean temperature affect rainfall.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Start at ENSO 0 (neutral) and find the west, the east and the thermocline. Trace the rising air in the west and the surface trade winds blowing toward it.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Move ENSO toward +1 (El Niño) and compare the eastern temperature and thermocline depth. Then try −1 (La Niña) and explain the stronger west–east contrast.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does a change in the trade winds affect Pacific surface temperatures and the location of rising air?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The Walker cell is…
choices: A north–south polar circulation
An east–west tropical Pacific loop
A north–south tropical Atlantic loop
An Atlantic surface current
questions.explain: Under typical neutral conditions, air rises over the warmer western tropical Pacific and descends farther east. Surface trade winds and an upper-level return flow form the broad east–west Walker circulation.

questions.prompt: El Niño’s warm pool…
choices: Disappears completely
Shifts further west toward Asia
Shifts east across the Pacific
Moves into the Indian Ocean
questions.explain: During El Niño, weakened trade winds reduce the normal westward accumulation of warm surface water. The central and eastern equatorial Pacific warm, and the pattern of convection shifts eastward.

questions.prompt: For a US winter, ENSO…
choices: Fixes the weather for the whole season
Has no link to US weather at all
Reverses the jet stream every winter
May shift the odds, but decides nothing
questions.explain: ENSO can alter large-scale atmospheric circulation and change the probabilities of some seasonal weather patterns; during El Niño, for example, the southern United States tends to be wetter than usual. Local weather also depends on other influences, so an ENSO phase cannot determine a particular month’s conditions.

questions.prompt: La Niña in this lab is…
choices: Cooler east Pacific, stronger Walker cell
Warmer water across the east Pacific
Weaker trade winds than in normal years
A shift of the warm pool eastward
questions.explain: La Niña is associated with cooler-than-average central and eastern equatorial Pacific surface water and often stronger trade winds. These changes strengthen aspects of the usual east–west tropical Pacific contrast.

questions.prompt: During a strong El Niño, which region often gets much more rain than usual?
choices: Coastal Peru and Ecuador
Indonesia and northern Australia
The central Sahara
Central Siberia
questions.explain: Warm water and rising air shift east during El Niño, bringing heavy rain and floods to the normally dry coasts of Peru and Ecuador, while Indonesia and Australia often turn drier.

why: Across the tropical Pacific, trade winds, warm surface water and the thermocline interact. El Niño and La Niña describe departures from the usual coupled ocean–atmosphere pattern.

Normally the easterly trade winds push warm surface water west, piling it up over a deep thermocline near Indonesia while cold water upwells off Peru. In El Niño the trades weaken, warm water spreads east, the thermocline flattens and the rising air and rain follow the warm water toward the central Pacific. In La Niña stronger trades exaggerate the usual west–east contrast.
The selected states illustrate these relationships; their effects on weather vary between events and places.

misconceptions.claim: El Niño causes the same weather in every affected place during every event.
misconceptions.truth: ENSO changes tropical Pacific ocean and atmospheric conditions, influencing weather probabilities in many regions. The response depends on season, event strength and other climate conditions. A regional tendency toward wetter or drier weather is not a guarantee for every location, day or event.

misconceptions.claim: El Niño is a single storm that hits South America.
misconceptions.truth: El Niño is a pattern of ocean warming and changed winds across the tropical Pacific. It lasts many months, returns every few years and shifts rainfall and temperature patterns far from the Pacific.

teacher.script:
Start at ENSO 0 (neutral) and find the west, the east and the thermocline. Trace the rising air in the west and the surface trade winds blowing toward it.

Move ENSO toward +1 (El Niño) and compare the eastern temperature and thermocline depth. Then try −1 (La Niña) and explain the stronger west–east contrast.
pitfalls: Locate the changing trade winds, warm water and rising air in the tropical Pacific before discussing effects elsewhere.
Describe ENSO as a pattern that changes the likelihood of regional conditions rather than a forecast for a specific day.
Ask students to explain the ocean–atmosphere interaction before connecting the model with a distant weather event.

sources.label: NOAA ENSO wind and thermocline changes

modelNotes: The ocean cross-section is 15,000 km wide and shows the upper 500 m.
Depth is enlarged 10,000 times unless you switch to Physical scale (T).

predict.prompt: If the trade winds across the Pacific weaken, what do you think happens to the warm water usually piled up near Indonesia?

cer.prompt: How do changes in the trade winds produce El Niño and change where heavy rain falls?
cer.claim: When the trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east across the Pacific and the rising air and heavy rain move east with it: this is El Niño.
cer.evidence: At ENSO 0, warm water and rising air sit in the west over a deep thermocline, while cooler water lies near the surface in the east. Moving ENSO to +1 warms the eastern surface water, flattens the thermocline and shifts the rising branch east. At −1 (La Niña) the west–east contrast strengthens.
cer.reasoning: Trade winds normally push warm surface water west and allow cold water to upwell in the east. Rising air and rain follow the warmest water, so when the winds weaken and the warm water spreads, rainfall shifts toward the central and eastern Pacific.

labs.title: Landform types
labs.hook: Elevation, relief, slope and shape describe different properties of terrain.
labs.objective: Compare the elevation and shape of mountains, hills, plateaus, plains and basins using a shared scale.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Compare Mountain with Plain at the common scale. Use the readout to distinguish elevation (highest point) from local relief (highest minus lowest point).

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Right landform to Plateau and explain its high, flat surface. Then compare Hill with Basin and rotate the view.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why is elevation alone insufficient to distinguish a plateau, a mountain and a plain?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A plateau is…
choices: A deep, narrow valley
A cone-shaped volcanic peak
A low, flat river floodplain
A raised area with a flat top
questions.explain: A plateau is elevated relative to surrounding terrain but retains a broad, comparatively level surface. Rivers may dissect it into valleys and canyons without removing its overall plateau setting.

questions.prompt: A basin is…
choices: A lower area surrounded by higher land
A high, isolated mountain peak
A flat, raised tableland
A narrow ridge between two deep valleys
questions.explain: A basin is a lower area relative to the land around it. Water may converge toward its floor, although not every basin is completely enclosed or internally drained.

questions.prompt: Mountains and hills differ mainly in…
choices: A fixed height of exactly 600 m
Relief and slope, along a continuum
The type of rock underneath them
Whether the summit holds snow
questions.explain: Mountains and hills differ in relative height, slope and relief, but those properties vary continuously. No single height threshold is used consistently in every country and context.

questions.prompt: The Grand Canyon is best described as…
choices: A folded mountain range
A glacial U-shaped trough
A canyon cut into a plateau
A basin with no river in it
questions.explain: The Colorado River and its tributaries incised the elevated Colorado Plateau. The canyon is therefore a deeply cut valley within a plateau, rather than a glacial trough or an isolated mountain.

questions.prompt: Which landform is built mainly by deposition?
choices: A broad river floodplain
A deep river canyon
A glacial cirque
A wave-cut cliff on a rocky coast
questions.explain: A floodplain is built from sediment that a river drops during floods and as its meanders migrate. Canyons, cirques and cliffs are carved mainly by erosion.

why: Elevation, relief, slope and shape describe different properties of terrain. A plateau can stand high above sea level while remaining relatively flat, and a basin is defined by its lower position relative to nearby land.

Elevation is height above sea level; local relief is the difference between the highest and lowest ground nearby. A plateau and a mountain can both be high, but the plateau has a broad, gently sloping top bounded by steep edges, while the mountain rises to a peak on steep slopes all round. A plain and a plateau can both be flat; the plateau stands well above the land around it. A basin is defined by being lower than its surroundings, not by its absolute height.
The five terrain samples use a shared scale for comparison; shape alone does not establish the process or rock type that formed a landscape.

misconceptions.claim: A landform’s shape tells us which single process created it.
misconceptions.truth: A landscape can record several processes acting at different times. A river may occupy a valley widened by ice, while rock structure influences both erosion and slope failure. Shape provides clues, but interpreting the history also needs evidence such as sediments, rock relationships and chronology.

misconceptions.claim: Mountains stay the same height for ever.
misconceptions.truth: Mountains are raised by tectonic uplift and worn down by weathering and erosion. The Himalaya are still rising, while older ranges such as the Appalachians and the Scottish Highlands were once much higher than they are today.

teacher.script:
Compare Mountain with Plain at the common scale. Use the readout to distinguish elevation (highest point) from local relief (highest minus lowest point).

Set Right landform to Plateau and explain its high, flat surface. Then compare Hill with Basin and rotate the view. Point out that the steepest slopes on the plateau are at its edges, and that the basin floor is the lowest point in its sample.
pitfalls: Use landform categories to organize observations without treating them as universal rules with sharp boundaries.
Distinguish a canyon cut into a landscape from a mountain range raised by tectonic processes.
Explain that the distinction between a hill and a mountain does not have one universally accepted height threshold.

predict.prompt: Can a high flat plateau have less local relief than a low hill? Explain your guess.

cer.prompt: How do elevation and relief help you tell mountains, plateaus, hills, plains and basins apart?
cer.claim: Landforms are distinguished by both elevation (how high) and relief (how much the height varies): mountains are high with large relief, plateaus are high but flat-topped, and plains are low and flat.
cer.evidence: At the common scale, the readout shows the mountain with the greatest highest point and the greatest relief, the plateau with a high top but small relief across it, and the plain low with small relief. The basin's lowest point sits below the land around it.
cer.reasoning: Elevation measures height above a reference, while relief measures the difference between the highest and lowest points in an area. A plateau can be high but have gentle relief on top, with its steepest slopes only at its edges.

labs.title: River erosion
labs.hook: Flowing water can detach and transport material from a river’s bed and banks.
labs.objective: Explain how river erosion forms waterfalls, gorges and potholes, and distinguish the retreat of a waterfall from the direction of flow.
standards: OCR GCSE A Landscapes of the UK

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Follow the water downstream, then find the lip, the resistant cap and the plunge pool.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Change Retreat to move the lip upstream, then set Feature to Pothole close-up or V-shaped valley.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain why a waterfall can retreat upstream while the water continues to flow downstream.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: As a waterfall (a nick point) retreats, it leaves…
choices: A delta at the river’s mouth
A meander just below the fall
A wide plunge pool far downstream
A gorge downstream of the new fall
questions.explain: Erosion and collapse can make a waterfall retreat upstream. The narrow, steep-sided valley left between its former and current positions forms a gorge.

questions.prompt: Potholes form by…
choices: Pebbles swirling and abrading the bed
Acidic water slowly dissolving the rock bed
Frost shattering the river bed
Ice scraping the bed in winter
questions.explain: Eddying water can trap stones and sand in a bedrock hollow and repeatedly move them against its sides. This abrasion deepens and widens a river pothole.

questions.prompt: V-valleys are typical of…
choices: Glacial erosion in uplands
River downcutting in uplands
Lateral erosion in lowlands
Deposition on floodplains
questions.explain: A river cutting down into its bed creates a narrow valley floor while weathering and slope processes lower the sides. Together these processes commonly produce a V-shaped cross-section in upland valleys.

questions.prompt: The Grand Canyon formed mainly by…
choices: A glacier cutting a U-shaped trough
A rift pulling apart
A river incising a plateau
Wind carving a yardang
questions.explain: The Colorado River cut down through rock layers as the regional landscape evolved and the plateau rose. The exposed rocks are much older than the canyon carved through them.

questions.prompt: What is attrition?
choices: Water forcing air into cracks in the bank
Stones colliding and wearing each other down
Sediment dragged along, scraping the bed and banks
Weak acids in the water dissolving rock
questions.explain: Attrition wears down the load itself. As pebbles collide they chip and round each other, so sediment usually becomes smaller and smoother downstream.

why: Flowing water can detach and transport material from a river’s bed and banks. Hydraulic action and abrasion contribute to erosion, while differences in rock resistance can influence the resulting forms.

Water and stones in the plunge pool wear back the weaker rock beneath the resistant cap. The unsupported cap overhangs and collapses, so the lip moves upstream even though the water keeps flowing downstream, and a gorge is left behind.
The stages show how the landforms change; they are not timed by a measured erosion rate.

misconceptions.claim: Weathering and river erosion describe the same process.
misconceptions.truth: Weathering breaks down or alters rock in place, while erosion wears away and removes material. A river can exploit rock weakened by weathering and use transported sediment to abrade its bed. The processes can work together without being interchangeable.

misconceptions.claim: Rivers cut their valleys with water alone.
misconceptions.truth: Clear water erodes hard rock only slowly. Most river erosion of bedrock is abrasion by the sand, pebbles and boulders the river carries, helped by hydraulic action on weak or cracked rock.

teacher.script:
Follow the water downstream, then find the lip, the resistant cap and the plunge pool.

Change Retreat to move the lip upstream, then set Feature to Pothole close-up or V-shaped valley.
pitfalls: Compare valley shapes and rock conditions rather than describing every river valley as a canyon.
Students often think a waterfall moves downstream with the water. Show that undercutting and collapse move the lip upstream while the flow stays downstream.
Distinguish the age of the rocks from the time over which the river excavated the valley.

modelNotes: Retreat moves the lip up to 25 m upstream in chosen steps, not a dated rate; the falling water and plunge pool move with it.
Vertical relief is enlarged 2.2 times in the waterfall view and 1.5 times in the valley view; Physical scale removes the exaggeration.
The Real: Grand Canyon view uses USGS elevation and aerial imagery to show a river that has cut about 1.5 km into a rising plateau.

predict.prompt: Water flows downstream over a waterfall. Which way do you think the waterfall itself moves over time: downstream or upstream?

cer.prompt: How does a waterfall retreat upstream and leave a gorge, even though the water flows downstream?
cer.claim: A waterfall retreats upstream because water undercuts the soft rock beneath a resistant cap until the cap collapses, leaving a gorge downstream.
cer.evidence: In Waterfall and gorge, the lip is made of resistant rock above softer beds, with a plunge pool at the foot. Raising Retreat moves the lip and plunge pool up to 25 m upstream, and the gorge lengthens behind it, while the water still flows downstream.
cer.reasoning: Falling water and swirling stones erode the plunge pool and the weaker rock under the cap faster than the cap itself. Without support the overhanging cap breaks off, so the position of the fall moves upstream step by step.

labs.title: River deposition
labs.hook: Sediment is deposited when transport conditions no longer keep it moving.
labs.objective: Explain where rivers deposit sediment and compare the formation of point bars, natural levees and deltas.
standards: OCR GCSE A Landscapes of the UK

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the point bar on the inside of the bend and the river cliff (cut bank) on the outside.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Environment to Overbank floodplain and toggle Overbank water, then switch to Delta mouth. Change Grain diameter, press Play and open How to read these results to compare settling speeds.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can a river erode its outer bank while depositing sediment on the inner bank?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A slip-off slope is…
choices: The cliff on the outer bend
Deposition on the inner bend
Erosion on the inner bend
A ridge beside the channel
questions.explain: Flow around a meander transports sediment toward the inner bend, where near-bank velocities and transport capacity are often lower. Deposition there builds a point bar and its gently sloping surface.

questions.prompt: Levees form when…
choices: Waves build ridges at the coast
The river slowly erodes its own banks upward
Floodwater drops coarser load by the banks
Fine clay settles in the channel bed
questions.explain: When floodwater leaves the channel, it slows and deposits much of its coarser suspended sediment near the banks. Repeated floods can build raised natural levees alongside the river.

questions.prompt: Chesapeake Bay and the Hudson end in estuaries, not deltas, because…
choices: These rivers carry no sediment at all to the sea
These rivers flow too slowly to drop any load
Waves are too weak to move sediment there
Tides and drowned valleys outpace delta building
questions.explain: Strong tidal exchange can redistribute river sediment, while rising relative sea level can drown a river valley. These conditions favor an estuary where sediment supply is insufficient to build a delta outward.

questions.prompt: The outer bank of a meander is mainly a site of…
choices: Erosion of a cut bank
Deposition of a point bar
Levee building by floodwater
Slack water with little change
questions.explain: Faster flow and greater shear stress commonly occur near a meander's outer bank. Undercutting and bank collapse then help the bend migrate outward.

questions.prompt: Why does a river drop much of its load where it enters the sea or a lake?
choices: It slows down and loses energy.
Salt water dissolves the sediment.
Waves push the sediment back upstream.
The bed suddenly becomes much steeper.
questions.explain: When river water enters a large, still body of water it spreads out and slows down. It can no longer carry as much sediment, so deposition builds features such as deltas.

why: Sediment is deposited when transport conditions no longer keep it moving. Inner bends, floodplains and river mouths create different settings for sorting and storing sediment.

On a bend, the fastest, deepest flow swings toward the outer bank and undercuts it, while a spiraling (helicoidal) current sweeps bed sediment toward the slower, shallower inner bank, where it builds a point bar. When floodwater spills out of the channel, or a river enters the sea, the flow spreads and slows, so coarser grains settle first: near the banks they build levees, and at the mouth they build a delta.
The separate settling experiment describes small quartz spheres in still water; river turbulence and flocculation can change their behavior.

misconceptions.claim: A river deposits all its sediment as soon as the water slows down.
misconceptions.truth: Deposition depends on the ability of the flow to keep particular particles moving. Coarser material often settles or stops first as transport capacity falls, while finer particles may remain suspended farther downstream. Sediment size, turbulence, water depth and incoming supply all affect the result.

misconceptions.claim: Floodplains are flat because people leveled them for farming.
misconceptions.truth: Floodplains are built naturally. Each flood spreads a thin layer of fine sediment across the valley floor, and migrating meanders rework the deposits, producing a wide, flat surface.

teacher.script:
Find the point bar on the inside of the bend and the river cliff (cut bank) on the outside.

Compare Overbank floodplain (toggle Overbank water) with Delta mouth, then change Grain diameter in the settling tube.
pitfalls: Distinguish sediment accumulation in a delta from processes operating in a tidal estuary.
Locate inner-bank deposition and outer-bank erosion correctly when interpreting a meander.
Explain that levees can form naturally during floods as well as being built or enlarged by people.

modelNotes: A separate Stokes calculation uses isolated 10–50 μm quartz spheres, still fresh water at 20 °C, density 998 kg/m³ and dynamic viscosity 1.002 mPa·s.
It estimates terminal settling speed and the distance traveled at 0.1 m/s through 2 m depth.

predict.prompt: On a river bend, where do you think the water flows fastest: on the inside or the outside of the bend? Where would sand be dropped?

cer.prompt: Why does a river build point bars on the inside of bends, levees on its banks, and a delta at its mouth?
cer.claim: A river deposits sediment wherever it slows down: on the inside of bends, at the edge of the channel during floods, and where it enters still water at its mouth.
cer.evidence: The point bar lies on the slower inside of the bend, opposite the eroding cut bank on the outside. With Overbank water on, the coarsest sediment drops nearest the channel and builds levees. In the settling tube, larger grains settle faster: a 50 μm grain sinks much faster than a 10 μm grain.
cer.reasoning: Slower water has less energy to carry sediment, so it drops the heaviest grains first. Settling speed rises with grain size, so coarse grains settle close to where the flow slows and fine grains travel farther.

labs.title: River capture
labs.hook: Headward erosion can extend one river into a neighboring basin and divert its headwaters.
labs.objective: Explain how headward erosion can divert a river’s headwaters and identify evidence left in the old channel.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify the two separate water routes and their outlets.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Formation stage to Approaching the divide, then After capture, and play the new water route.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does diverting the headwaters affect the captured river and the abandoned part of its old valley?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: An elbow of capture is…
choices: A meander loop on a wide floodplain
A waterfall at a rock band
A sharp bend at the capture point
Where two equal rivers meet
questions.explain: When a stream is diverted into a neighboring drainage system, it may turn sharply at the capture point. That abrupt change in course can form an elbow of capture.

questions.prompt: A beheaded stream…
choices: Gains extra water
Cuts down faster than before
Takes over a neighboring river
Loses its headwaters and shrinks
questions.explain: A beheaded stream loses part of its upstream drainage area and therefore often loses discharge. The remaining stream may be too small to account for the size of its inherited valley.

questions.prompt: Capture is more likely when…
choices: One river cuts headward faster than its neighbor
Both rivers erode their valleys at the same rate
The divide between them is made of resistant rock
Strong tides push seawater up both valleys
questions.explain: A stream with a greater erosive advantage can extend its headwaters back toward a neighboring basin. If it breaches the divide, it may divert the neighboring headwaters into its own channel.

questions.prompt: What does the Mississippi Old River Control Structure illustrate?
choices: Natural river capture by headward erosion
Engineering that limits a river diversion
A waterfall retreating upstream
A meander cut off to form an oxbow
questions.explain: The Old River Control Structure regulates how Mississippi flow divides toward the Atchafalaya. This is an example of managing potential river diversion, which differs from the headward erosion shown in the capture model.

questions.prompt: What is a wind gap?
choices: A notch in a ridge carved by strong winds
A dry notch left after a river was captured
A waterfall at the point of capture
A pass cut through a ridge by a glacier
questions.explain: A wind gap is a valley notch through a ridge that no longer has a river flowing through it, usually because the stream that cut it was captured upstream. The ‘wind’ is just a name: wind did not carve it.

why: Headward erosion can extend one river into a neighboring basin and divert its headwaters. The new route may leave an elbow of capture and a former valley carrying a much smaller stream.

The captor has a steeper course to a lower outlet, so it erodes headward faster than its neighbor. Once its valley head breaks through the divide, the neighboring headwaters take the lower, steeper route. Beyond the elbow the old valley is left with a dry wind gap and a much smaller misfit stream.
The chosen stages show one capture mechanism; their spacing does not represent an erosion rate or dated sequence.

misconceptions.claim: A drainage divide is permanent, so one river cannot gain another river’s headwaters.
misconceptions.truth: Erosion, tectonic change or other landscape adjustment can shift a divide and divert flow into a neighboring basin. The capturing river gains drainage area while the former channel may carry a smaller stream. Landforms such as wind gaps can help reconstruct the change.

misconceptions.claim: River capture happens suddenly, during a single storm.
misconceptions.truth: Capture usually follows thousands of years of headward erosion as one stream cuts back into its neighbor’s basin. The final breach of the divide can be quick, but the build-up is slow.

teacher.script:
Identify the two separate water routes and their outlets.

Set Formation stage to Approaching the divide, then After capture, and play the new water route.
pitfalls: Present river capture as the result of evolving drainage and erosion rather than an instantaneous change without a cause.
Explain how a drainage divide can migrate as neighboring river systems erode their headwaters.
Use features such as a wind gap to discuss the evidence for an earlier drainage pattern.

predict.prompt: Two rivers start on either side of the same hill. If one erodes back toward the hill much faster, what might happen to the other river?

cer.prompt: How can one river capture the headwaters of another?
cer.claim: A river that erodes headward faster can cut back through the divide and divert another river's headwaters into its own course.
cer.evidence: At Separate catchments, two rivers drain to different outlets. At Approaching the divide, the faster-eroding river has cut back close to the other's channel. After capture, the upper river turns sharply at an elbow of capture into the new route, and the beheaded river below is left smaller, with a dry notch called a wind gap.
cer.reasoning: Headward erosion lengthens a river at its source. A steeper river, or one on weaker rock, erodes back faster; once it breaks through the divide, the water takes the lower, steeper route, so the other river loses its headwaters.

labs.title: Coasts
labs.hook: Waves erode rock, transport sediment and deposit it along the coast.
labs.objective: Explain how coastal erosion forms caves, arches and stacks, and how longshore drift and groynes change the movement of beach sediment.
standards: OCR GCSE A Landscapes of the UK

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Set Headland stage to Cave, look into the sea cave and find its back wall. Then change Headland stage to compare the arch, stack and stump on the wave-cut platform.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Environment to Beach transport and switch on Groyne, then choose Spit and bay and change Spit extent.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How can retaining sediment at one groyne affect beaches farther along the coast?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Longshore drift moves sediment…
choices: Straight out to sea
Up the beach, then straight back down
Along the beach against the wind
Along the beach in the swash direction
questions.explain: Waves approaching at an angle carry sediment diagonally up the beach in the swash. Backwash returns more directly downslope, producing a net movement along the coast over repeated waves.

questions.prompt: A stack is…
choices: A pillar left when an arch collapses
A cave cut into a headland
A ridge of sand joined to land
A low rock stump covered at high tide
questions.explain: Wave erosion can enlarge a cave into an arch through a headland. When the arch roof collapses, an isolated pillar remains as a stack.

questions.prompt: Groins (UK: groynes) along a New Jersey beach…
choices: Add sand all along the coast
Trap sand up-drift, starving down-drift
Stop all erosion on the coast
Push the sand offshore into deeper water
questions.explain: Groynes interrupt sediment transported along the beach and encourage accumulation on their up-drift side. Unless sediment is supplied from elsewhere, less may reach the coast down-drift.

questions.prompt: How should a sea wall be assessed within a whole-coast budget?
choices: As a permanent fix for the whole coast
Only by its cost per meter
By its effects on nearby coasts too
Only by how tall it is
questions.explain: A sea wall protects a particular frontage but can alter wave reflection, local scour and sediment exchanges. Its effects should therefore be assessed within the connected coastal sediment system.

questions.prompt: Where does a spit form?
choices: Where longshore drift carries sand past a bend in the coast
Where waves erode a cave right through a headland
Where a river drops its load into a lake
Where two neighboring arches collapse and their rubble piles up
questions.explain: Where the coastline changes direction, for example at a river mouth, longshore drift keeps carrying sand out into open water. It builds a narrow ridge of sand or shingle, such as Sandy Hook in New Jersey or Spurn Point in England.

why: Waves erode rock, transport sediment and deposit it along the coast. The resulting landforms depend on rock structure, wave direction, sediment supply and the balance of material entering and leaving a coastal section.

Waves attack joints in a headland, enlarging a cave until it breaks through as an arch; the roof later collapses to leave a stack, which is worn down to a stump. Where waves arrive at an angle, swash carries sediment diagonally up the beach and backwash returns it straight down, so material drifts along the coast. A groyne traps this drift on its up-drift side, and where the coast turns inland the drift carries on to build a spit.
The scene demonstrates selected coastal processes; a real shoreline’s response also depends on its wider sediment budget.

misconceptions.claim: Groynes create new beach sediment without affecting nearby coasts.
misconceptions.truth: Groynes interrupt alongshore sediment movement and can retain material on one side. They redistribute an existing supply rather than create it, potentially reducing delivery farther along the coast. Their effects therefore need to be considered within the wider sediment budget.

misconceptions.claim: Longshore drift always moves sand in the direction the wind is blowing that day.
misconceptions.truth: Sediment moves in the direction set by the angle of the waves, which mainly reflects the prevailing wind and distant storms over weeks and seasons. On any single day, drift can run the opposite way.

teacher.script:
Look into the sea cave and find its back wall. Change Headland stage to compare the arch, stack and stump on the wave-cut platform.

Set Environment to Beach transport and switch on Groyne, then choose Spit and bay and change Spit extent.
pitfalls: Consider sediment inputs and outputs when explaining how a coastal landform changes.
Distinguish a stack of resistant rock from a spit built by sediment deposition.
Ask how a sea wall or other defense affects neighboring sections of coast rather than judging only the protected site.

modelNotes: The chalk headland, with flint bands, stands on a wave-cut platform. The cave and arch are real openings through the rock, drawn at a common scale (1 unit = 10 m).

predict.prompt: Waves hit a headland of hard rock. What shapes do you think the sea will carve over thousands of years?

cer.prompt: How does a headland change from a cave to a stump over time?
cer.claim: Waves erode weaknesses in a headland to form a cave, which becomes an arch, then a stack when the arch collapses, and finally a stump.
cer.evidence: Stepping Headland stage shows a cave cut into the base of the cliff, an opening right through the headland (arch), a pillar standing apart after the roof falls (stack), and a low remnant on the wave-cut platform (stump).
cer.reasoning: Wave attack concentrates on joints and faults, enlarging them into caves. When caves on both sides meet, an arch forms. Erosion at its base and weathering of the roof make it collapse, and the isolated stack is worn down further.

labs.title: Glacial landforms
labs.hook: Glacier ice flows downslope under gravity, even when its margin is retreating.
labs.objective: Explain how moving ice shapes a valley, and distinguish the direction of ice flow from the advance or retreat of its margin.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Press Play and follow the orange markers as ice flows down-valley from the accumulation area, past the equilibrium line, to the snout.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Lower Ice extent and watch the snout move up-valley. Press Play: the markers still move down-valley while the margin has retreated.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain how a glacier’s margin can retreat even while its ice continues to flow down the valley.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: An arête is…
choices: A bowl-shaped hollow below a peak
A knife-edge ridge between cirques
A pointed peak with three faces
A ridge of debris left by ice
questions.explain: Glaciers eroding neighboring cirques can steepen the valley walls on both sides of an intervening ridge. The narrow ridge left between them is an arête.

questions.prompt: A horn is…
choices: A narrow ridge between two cirques
A bowl-shaped hollow on a mountain
A peak cut by three or more cirques
A rock step in a valley floor
questions.explain: When several cirques erode back toward the same summit, they steepen its sides from different directions. The remaining sharply pointed summit is a horn or pyramidal peak.

questions.prompt: How does a U-shaped trough differ from a V-shaped valley?
choices: Both are carved the same way
Rivers widen and deepen; ice cuts down
Both are formed by weathering only
Ice widens and deepens; rivers cut down
questions.explain: A valley glacier abrades and plucks both the floor and sides of a pre-existing valley, widening and deepening it. A river more commonly concentrates erosion within a narrower channel, helping produce a V-shaped profile.

questions.prompt: Yosemite Valley is mainly…
choices: A glacial U-trough in granite
A river canyon like the Grand Canyon
A limestone pavement
A barchan field
questions.explain: Glaciers repeatedly enlarged an earlier river valley in Yosemite's granitic bedrock. Their erosion produced the broad floor and steep walls characteristic of its glacial trough.

questions.prompt: How fast do valley glaciers typically move?
choices: Not at all, because ice is solid
Meters to hundreds of meters a year
Several kilometers every hour
Only on days when the ice is melting
questions.explain: Ice can deform slowly like a very stiff fluid, and meltwater at the base helps it slide. Most valley glaciers move from a few meters to a few hundred meters a year.

why: Glacier ice flows downslope under gravity, even when its margin is retreating. Erosion by ice and carried debris can deepen valleys and shape cirques, arêtes and horns.

Above the equilibrium line, snow that survives each summer is compacted into ice; below it, more ice melts each year than falls as snow. Ice deforms and slides downslope under its own weight, carrying ice from the accumulation zone toward the snout. When melting at the snout removes ice faster than flow delivers it, the snout retreats up-valley even though the ice itself keeps moving down-valley.
Changing ice extent compares margin positions; it does not reverse ice flow or calculate the glacier’s mass balance.

misconceptions.claim: A retreating glacier must be flowing uphill.
misconceptions.truth: Glacier ice generally moves downslope under gravity even when its terminus retreats. The front moves back when local ice loss exceeds the supply of ice moving toward it. Ice velocity and the change in the terminus position describe different aspects of glacier behavior.

misconceptions.claim: Glaciers are frozen in place and do not move.
misconceptions.truth: Glaciers flow downhill under their own weight, deforming internally and sliding on their beds. Valley glaciers typically move meters to hundreds of meters a year, and some outlet glaciers move several kilometers a year.

teacher.script:
