Ask students to point to where the glacier gains ice and where it loses it, then press Play and follow one orange marker from the accumulation area past the equilibrium line to the snout.

Lower Ice extent: the snout moves up-valley but the markers still move down-valley. Ask how both can be true (melting at the snout outpaces the ice arriving). Switch off Ice to show the U-shaped trough and the earlier moraine.
pitfalls: Compare Yosemite’s glacial trough with a predominantly river-cut canyon to distinguish the processes shaping them.
Explain that glaciers can occur in high mountains as well as polar regions.
Consider the thickness and movement of the ice when explaining erosion and deposition.

sources.label: NPS ice flow and glacier margin change

modelNotes: Default relief is enlarged 1.5 times; Physical scale restores a common kilometer scale.
The Real: Yosemite Valley view uses USGS elevation and aerial imagery; its north–south cross-section shows the real U shape. Heights are exaggerated ×1.5 unless Compare physical scale is on.

predict.prompt: If a glacier's snout is retreating up the valley, do you think the ice inside the glacier is moving up-valley or down-valley?

cer.prompt: How can a glacier's snout retreat while its ice keeps moving down-valley?
cer.claim: The ice always flows down-valley; the snout retreats when melting at the front removes ice faster than flow delivers it.
cer.evidence: Pressing Play moves the orange markers down-valley from the accumulation area past the equilibrium line to the snout. Lowering Ice extent moves the snout up-valley, yet the markers still move down-valley.
cer.reasoning: A glacier is a moving conveyor of ice. Its margin position depends on the balance between ice arriving and ice melting at the snout, not on the direction of flow.

labs.title: Karst
labs.hook: Water containing dissolved carbon dioxide can dissolve calcite along joints and bedding planes.
labs.objective: Explain how water dissolves limestone along joints to form surface grooves, sinkholes and underground passages.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the clints, grykes and the doline (a surface hollow).

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Drag Joint opening and watch the grykes widen. With Cutaway on, follow the dashed water route from the doline down through the rock to the spring, and find the stalactites and stalagmites.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do joints and slightly acidic water influence the development of limestone passages?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Grykes are…
choices: Dissolved fissures in limestone pavement
Flat blocks between pavement fissures
Caves running beneath the pavement
Hollows formed when roofs collapse
questions.explain: Weakly acidic water dissolves limestone along joints, widening them into grykes. The remaining blocks between those fissures are called clints.

questions.prompt: A swallow hole is…
choices: Where a stream rises from underground
Where a surface stream sinks underground
A hollow formed by roof collapse
A column where stalactite meets stalagmite
questions.explain: A swallow hole is an opening where surface water enters an underground drainage route. Enlarged joints and solution passages in limestone commonly provide that route.

questions.prompt: Karst develops mainly on carbonate rocks because…
choices: Carbonate rocks are especially soft
Carbonate rocks have no joints or cracks at all
Carbonic acid dissolves calcium carbonate
Carbonate rocks freeze more easily
questions.explain: Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid, which reacts with calcium carbonate. Flow through joints gradually enlarges openings in carbonate rocks and develops karst drainage.

questions.prompt: The caves in this lab are…
choices: Lava tubes
Tunnels cut by glacial meltwater
Faults pulled open
Solution caves in carbonate
questions.explain: These caves form as flowing water dissolves carbonate rock along fractures and other openings. Their origin is chemically distinct from a lava tube left by flowing molten rock.

questions.prompt: Why do streams often disappear into the ground on limestone?
choices: The water soaks into tiny pores, like a sponge.
It sinks through joints widened by dissolving.
It evaporates quickly from the pale rock.
It freezes inside the rock and stays there.
questions.explain: Limestone itself has few pores, but its joints and bedding planes are enlarged by solution. Streams sink through swallow holes into these passages and flow underground.

why: Water containing dissolved carbon dioxide can dissolve calcite along joints and bedding planes. Connected openings can develop into underground drainage routes, while calcite may later precipitate where carbon dioxide escapes.

Water sinks through the doline and enlarged joints, then follows a passage dissolved along a bedding plane until it emerges at a spring. Where drips enter the cave air, carbon dioxide escapes and calcite is deposited as stalactites and stalagmites.
The cutaway illustrates connected passages and the reaction; it does not calculate cave growth rates or water quality.

misconceptions.claim: An underground drainage basin must have exactly the same boundary as the surface basin.
misconceptions.truth: Water in soluble rock can follow connected fractures and passages beneath a surface divide. Its underground route may therefore lead to a different outlet from the one suggested by topography. Dye tracing and other observations can help establish the actual groundwater connections.

misconceptions.claim: Limestone dissolves quickly, so caves form within a few years.
misconceptions.truth: Rainwater is only weakly acidic, so dissolving a cave passage usually takes tens to hundreds of thousands of years. A limestone pavement surface may be lowered by only a few centimeters in a thousand years.

teacher.script:
Start with Cutaway off: students name the clints, grykes and doline from the surface alone and predict where the water goes.

Drag Joint opening to show that dissolution concentrates along joints. Then switch Cutaway on and trace the dashed route from the doline to the passage and spring. Ask why calcite dissolves on the way in but is deposited as stalactites and stalagmites in the cave (carbon dioxide escaping into cave air).
pitfalls: Connect solution landforms with water moving through soluble rock rather than assuming every hollow is volcanic.
Distinguish limestone solution caves from lava tubes formed during volcanic activity.
Use an appropriate soluble rock, such as limestone, when explaining the development of karst.

modelNotes: Water containing dissolved carbon dioxide can dissolve calcite: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca²⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻.
The 60 × 30 m block has its relief exaggerated 1.3 times unless Physical scale is selected.

predict.prompt: Rainwater is slightly acidic. What do you think happens when it flows through cracks in limestone for thousands of years?

cer.prompt: Why do streams often disappear into the ground in limestone country?
cer.claim: Streams disappear because slightly acidic water has dissolved and widened the joints in the limestone, letting water sink underground.
cer.evidence: Raising Joint opening widens the grykes between clints. With Cutaway on, the dashed water route runs from the doline down through widened joints into a cave passage and out at a spring, past stalactites and stalagmites.
cer.reasoning: Water with dissolved carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid, which dissolves calcite: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca²⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻. Dissolution is fastest along joints, so they grow into fissures, sinkholes and caves.

labs.title: Folds and faults
labs.hook: Rock layers may bend into folds or break and move along faults.
labs.objective: Compare the rock deformation caused by compression, tension and sideways motion, using folds and faults as evidence.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Choose Anticline and find the oldest bed. Then choose Syncline and explain why bed age, not shape alone, defines each fold.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Choose Normal fault and name the hanging wall before pressing Play. Choose Reverse fault to see the opposite slip, then Strike-slip fault to see sideways movement.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Use the movement of the hanging wall to distinguish a normal fault from a reverse fault.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: In this upright example, an anticline is…
choices: A downfold with younger beds in its core
An upfold with younger beds in its core
An upfold with older beds in its core
A break where rocks slide past
questions.explain: An anticline has older strata toward its core, even if later deformation overturns the fold. In the upright example, this age arrangement coincides with an upward arch.

questions.prompt: A normal fault forms in…
choices: Compression; hanging wall up
Shearing; blocks slide sideways
Compression; beds fold upward
Extension; hanging wall down
questions.explain: Extension pulls the crust apart, allowing the hanging-wall block to move down relative to the footwall along a normal fault. The movement lengthens the crust across the fault system.

questions.prompt: The San Andreas Fault is…
choices: Strike-slip
Normal
Reverse
Thrust
questions.explain: The San Andreas mainly accommodates horizontal movement between adjacent plate blocks. This sideways displacement makes it a strike-slip fault and a transform plate boundary.

questions.prompt: The hanging wall is…
choices: Always the downthrown block
The block above the fault plane
The block below the fault plane
Only found in folds
questions.explain: The hanging wall is the rock block above an inclined fault plane, while the footwall lies below it. These names identify geometry and do not depend on which block moved upward.

questions.prompt: What kind of force folds rock layers into anticlines and synclines?
choices: Compression squeezing the layers
Tension pulling the crust apart
Erosion removing the top layers
Rain soaking into the layers
questions.explain: Folds form when rock is squeezed, for example where plates converge. Tension instead tends to produce normal faults, and erosion only exposes folds that already exist.

why: Rock layers may bend into folds or break and move along faults. Layer age, orientation and relative movement help distinguish structures that can look similar from one viewing angle.

The type of stress decides the structure. Compression shortens the crust: rock that deforms slowly, often when warm and deeply buried, bends into folds, while colder, brittle rock breaks along reverse faults where the hanging wall moves up. Tension stretches the crust, so the hanging wall slides down a normal fault. Where blocks are pushed past each other sideways, a strike-slip fault forms with mostly horizontal movement.
The deformation is set in advance to show the structure; the model does not calculate stresses or when rocks break.

misconceptions.claim: The hanging wall is always the side of a fault that moves down.
misconceptions.truth: The hanging wall is defined by its position above an inclined fault plane. It moves down relative to the footwall in a normal fault and up in a reverse fault. Identify the plane and blocks before using their displacement to name the fault type.

misconceptions.claim: Rock is too rigid to bend, so folded layers must really be broken pieces.
misconceptions.truth: Deep in the crust, high temperature and pressure acting over millions of years let rock deform slowly without breaking. Near the surface, where rock is cold and brittle, the same stresses are more likely to cause faults.

teacher.script:
Choose Anticline and find the oldest bed. Then choose Syncline and explain why bed age, not shape alone, defines each fold.

Choose Normal fault and name the hanging wall before pressing Play. Choose Reverse fault to see the opposite slip, then Strike-slip fault to see sideways movement.
pitfalls: Identify the hanging wall and footwall from their positions relative to the fault plane before describing movement.
Explain how rock can deform over geological time; a soft classroom material only helps visualize the resulting shape.
Distinguish horizontal movement along the San Andreas system from subduction at Cascadia.

modelNotes: In the faults, a 60° dipping plane separates the footwall below it from the hanging wall above.
The maximum relative fault slip is 700 m, and the readout separates that slip from its vertical throw.

predict.prompt: If rock layers are squeezed from the sides, do you think they will fold, break, or both? What if they are pulled apart?

cer.prompt: How can you tell from rocks whether the crust was squeezed, stretched or moved sideways?
cer.claim: Folds and reverse faults show compression, normal faults show extension, and strike-slip faults show sideways motion.
cer.evidence: In the anticline the oldest beds are in the core, and in the syncline the youngest are. In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down the 60° fault plane; in a reverse fault it moves up; in a strike-slip fault the blocks slide sideways. The readout separates slip from vertical throw.
cer.reasoning: Squeezing shortens the crust by folding layers or pushing one block up over another. Stretching lengthens it, so the hanging wall slides down. Sideways shear moves blocks horizontally past each other, as along the San Andreas Fault.

labs.title: Wind landforms
labs.hook: Wind transports particles by suspension, saltation and surface creep.
labs.objective: Explain how wind erodes rock and transports sand, then identify the wind direction from the shape of a barchan dune.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the wind arrow and the dune horns pointing downwind.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Change Dune position, then compare Barchan dune with Yardang ridges. Play shows enlarged grains moving downwind.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do erosion and deposition produce different landforms under the action of wind?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A barchan’s horns point…
choices: Upwind, into the oncoming wind
Downwind, the way the wind blows
Across the wind, at right angles
Toward the nearest supply of sand
questions.explain: A barchan forms under a dominant wind direction with a limited sand supply. Its thinner margins move faster than the thicker center, extending the horns downwind.

questions.prompt: A yardang is…
choices: A crescent-shaped sand dune
A flat sheet of loose sand
A wind-carved rock ridge
A hollow scoured in a desert
questions.explain: Wind-driven abrasion and the removal of loose material can carve elongated ridges from susceptible ground. These streamlined erosional landforms are called yardangs.

questions.prompt: Wind erosion and transport need…
choices: Dense vegetation and moist soil cover
Steep slopes, frequent heavy rain and running water
Frozen ground under a snow cover
Loose sediment, strong wind, little vegetation
questions.explain: Wind can entrain and transport sediment when exposed particles are loose and the wind is strong enough. Vegetation and soil moisture usually make that removal more difficult.

questions.prompt: The main process in the Dust Bowl was…
choices: Deflation of bare, plowed topsoil in drought
A barchan dune sea spreading over the plains
Gullying by heavy summer thunderstorms
Flooding of the big river valleys
questions.explain: Drought and cultivation left extensive areas of soil exposed during the Dust Bowl. Strong winds removed and transported the vulnerable topsoil, rather than simply building desert dune fields.

questions.prompt: How do most sand grains move during a desert sandstorm?
choices: Carried high in the air, often for hundreds of kilometers
By bouncing along within about a meter of the ground
By rolling uphill against the wind
Dissolved in the occasional rain
questions.explain: Sand moves mainly by saltation: grains are lifted briefly, then fall back and knock other grains into motion. This is why wind abrasion is strongest close to the ground.

why: Wind transports particles by suspension, saltation and surface creep. Where sand supply and wind conditions allow accumulation, deposition builds dunes whose shapes reflect transport and local obstacles.

Erosion and deposition make different landforms. Where loose sand is plentiful but limited, saltating grains climb the gentle windward slope, cross the crest and avalanche down the steep slip face, so the whole dune creeps downwind and its thinner horns move fastest. Where the ground is rock, sand-laden wind abrades it and deflation removes the loosened debris, carving streamlined yardang ridges aligned with the wind.
The examples show selected forms and transport directions; dune migration speed requires additional wind and sediment evidence.

misconceptions.claim: Every desert is covered by dunes.
misconceptions.truth: Many deserts expose bedrock, gravel or other surfaces with little loose sand. Dunes require a suitable sediment supply and wind conditions that allow accumulation. Wind can erode one area while depositing material elsewhere, so aridity alone does not determine the landform.

misconceptions.claim: Wind lifts sand grains high into the air and carries them across continents.
misconceptions.truth: Sand grains are too heavy to stay up for long, so most bounce along within about a meter of the ground by saltation. The fine dust that travels thousands of kilometers is silt and clay carried in suspension.

cases.label: Grand Canyon: weathering in a dry climate

teacher.script:
Find the wind arrow and the dune horns pointing downwind.

Change Dune position, then compare Barchan dune with Yardang ridges. Play shows enlarged grains moving downwind.
pitfalls: Explain that deserts can have rocky or gravel surfaces as well as areas covered by dunes.
Check that the horns of a barchan dune point downwind when students describe its shape.
Distinguish the movement of individual grains from the slower migration of an entire dune.

modelNotes: The example dune has a gentle windward (stoss) slope and a 32° slip face on its lee side at true scale.
The Real: Great Sand Dunes view uses USGS elevation and aerial imagery; its dunefield is shaped by winds from two directions, unlike the single-wind barchan model.

predict.prompt: A crescent-shaped sand dune has two pointed horns. Which way do you think the wind is blowing: toward the horns or away from them?

cer.prompt: How can you tell the wind direction from the shape of a barchan dune?
cer.claim: A barchan's horns point downwind, and its gentle slope faces into the wind.
cer.evidence: The model barchan has a gentle windward (stoss) slope and a steep 32° slip face on its lee side, with its horns pointing the way the wind arrow blows. Play shows enlarged grains bouncing up the gentle slope and over the crest.
cer.reasoning: Wind pushes sand up the windward slope; at the crest the grains fall onto the sheltered lee side until it reaches the angle of repose and slips. The thinner edges of the dune move faster than its middle, so they run ahead as horns.

labs.title: Rock cycle
labs.hook: Rocks can change through melting, crystallization, weathering, deposition, burial and metamorphism.
labs.objective: Trace several possible routes through the rock cycle and explain how melting, cooling, pressure and weathering transform rock.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify three rock groups, loose sediment and magma. In the landscape, notice where each one forms: on the sea floor, deep in the mountains or under the volcano.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Use Material pathway to try several routes, including a metamorphism path (no melting) and a melting path, and watch where each one happens. Then move Selected temperature and Selected pressure: where the orange temperature line crosses the white depth line, those conditions occur in the crust. Switch View to Rock specimens to compare the rocks up close.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Choose a pathway that does not involve melting and explain how it transforms the original rock.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Metamorphism normally means…
choices: Change in solid rock’s minerals or texture.
Complete melting of rock into magma.
Laying down and pressing of new layers of sediment.
Cooling of lava flows at the surface.
questions.explain: Metamorphism changes minerals or rock texture in response to conditions such as heat, pressure and fluids while the rock remains largely solid. Melting produces magma and begins a different transformation pathway.

questions.prompt: Melt becomes an igneous rock through…
choices: Heating alone.
Cooling and solidification.
Weathering alone.
An increase in pressure alone.
questions.explain: As melt loses heat, minerals can crystallize and form an igneous rock. Very rapid cooling can instead preserve some or all of the material as volcanic glass.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the rock cycle is sound?
choices: Every rock follows the same ordered circuit, in one direction.
All sedimentary rocks have identical layers.
Different paths can skip stages or repeat changes.
All metamorphic rocks are foliated.
questions.explain: A rock can follow many paths depending on burial, uplift, weathering, heating and melting. The rock cycle describes possible transformations rather than a fixed sequence that every rock must complete.

questions.prompt: Temperature and pressure on their own…
choices: Fix the exact amount of melting that occurs.
Fix the final minerals found in every rock.
Tell you exactly how old the rock is.
Are not enough without composition and fluids.
questions.explain: Temperature and pressure help constrain the possible changes, but the starting composition, fluids and duration also matter. Two rocks at the same temperature and pressure need not develop identical minerals or textures.

questions.prompt: Which rock forms from layers of sediment that are pressed and cemented together?
choices: Granite
Sandstone
Marble
Basalt
questions.explain: Sandstone is a sedimentary rock made of sand grains that were buried, compacted and cemented. Granite and basalt are igneous, and marble is metamorphic.

why: Rocks can change through melting, crystallization, weathering, deposition, burial and metamorphism. These processes form a network of possible routes rather than a compulsory journey through every rock type.

Each route needs its own conditions. Weathering and deposition happen at the surface; burial compacts and cements sediment; deeper and hotter rock recrystallizes while still solid (metamorphism); only when it is hot enough for part of the rock to melt does a route lead to magma, which must cool to become igneous rock again.
The pathways connect processes at different depths and timescales; the animation does not assign one duration to the whole cycle.

misconceptions.claim: Metamorphic rock forms when an existing rock melts completely.
misconceptions.truth: Metamorphism changes a rock’s minerals or texture while it remains largely solid, under changed temperature, pressure or fluid conditions. Complete melting produces magma; subsequent crystallization forms igneous rock. The rock cycle includes different possible pathways rather than one compulsory sequence.

misconceptions.claim: Rocks never change once they have formed.
misconceptions.truth: Rocks are constantly being changed, but usually very slowly. They are weathered and eroded at the surface, buried and squeezed into metamorphic rock, or melted and recrystallized, over thousands to millions of years.

teacher.script:
Ask students to identify the three rock groups, loose sediment and magma, and to follow the arrow on each arc to see which way a change runs.

Compare a metamorphism route with a melting route, then set temperature and pressure for each. Students should find that metamorphism needs heat and pressure below melting, while the melting routes need roughly 650 °C or more, depending on the rock and its water content.
pitfalls: Distinguish molten material from igneous rock, which forms after the melt cools and solidifies.
Explain that some metamorphic rocks are foliated while others are not.
Consider composition and geological history alongside temperature and pressure when identifying a rock.

modelNotes: The pressure readout gives an equivalent depth using a uniform 2800 kg/m³ overburden and 9.81 m/s² gravity.

predict.prompt: Can a sedimentary rock become an igneous rock without first becoming a metamorphic rock? Explain your guess.

cer.prompt: Does every rock follow the same path around the rock cycle?
cer.claim: No: rocks can take many routes, skipping or repeating stages, depending on the temperature, pressure and surface conditions they meet.
cer.evidence: Material pathway offers routes such as Melting: sedimentary rock straight to magma, Metamorphism: igneous rock without melting, and Weathering of any rock group to sediment. The readout shows that metamorphism needs heat and pressure below melting, while melting needs roughly 650 °C or more.
cer.reasoning: Each change is driven by the conditions a rock meets. Burial and heating can change a rock in the solid state or melt it; uplift exposes any rock to weathering. So the cycle is a network of possible paths, not a single loop.

labs.title: Soil profile
labs.hook: A soil profile exposes horizons formed by organic inputs, weathering and material movement.
labs.objective: Identify the horizons in a soil profile and compare how water, organic matter and parent material influence their development.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Choose Temperate brown soil and read the depth scale. Name the O, A, Bw and C horizons, then explain why a soil need not have E or R horizons.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Choose Mollisol example and compare its thick, dark topsoil. Then choose Oxisol example and discuss its gradual boundaries and intense weathering.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do the profiles show that a soil need not contain every possible horizon?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The R horizon is…
choices: Leaf litter
The layer of washed-in clay
Bedrock
Weathered parent material
questions.explain: The R horizon is coherent bedrock beneath the soil and weathered parent material. Roots and water may enter its fractures, but it is not a loose soil horizon.

questions.prompt: A thick, dark A horizon is typical of…
choices: Oxisol
Young soils on sand dunes
Desert soils
Mollisol (grassland)
questions.explain: Grassland roots supply organic matter through a substantial surface layer, and soil organisms mix it with mineral material. This helps form the thick, dark surface horizon characteristic of many Mollisols.

questions.prompt: An Oxisol is…
choices: A deeply weathered tropical soil
A waterlogged upland peat soil
A young soil on fresh volcanic ash
A frozen soil over permafrost
questions.explain: Oxisols develop under prolonged intense weathering and contain abundant iron and aluminum oxides. Many occur in tropical regions where warm, moist conditions promote deep chemical weathering.

questions.prompt: The E horizon is…
choices: A dark layer rich in humus
A leached, often paler layer
Where washed-down clay builds up
Weathered parent rock
questions.explain: Eluviation removes materials such as clay, iron compounds or organic matter from the E horizon, often leaving it paler. An E horizon is not present in every soil profile.

questions.prompt: Roughly how long can it take to form a few centimeters of soil?
choices: Hundreds of years or more
A few days after heavy rain
One wet winter
Exactly ten years
questions.explain: Soil forms slowly as parent material weathers and organic matter builds up. A few centimeters can take hundreds of years, which is why eroded soil is hard to replace.

why: A soil profile exposes horizons formed by organic inputs, weathering and material movement. Their colors and textures can provide clues, but not every soil contains every horizon.

Under grassland, dense roots grow and die deep in the soil and soil organisms mix their remains with mineral grains, so a Mollisol builds a thick, dark A horizon. In an Oxisol, long and intense chemical weathering in warm, wet conditions has broken down most minerals and leached nutrients, leaving a thick red subsoil rich in iron and aluminum oxides with gradual boundaries.
The selected profiles are examples; identifying a soil order also requires diagnostic properties beyond a color match.

misconceptions.claim: Every soil contains the same sequence and thickness of horizons.
misconceptions.truth: Soil profiles develop through interactions among parent material, climate, organisms, relief and time. Some horizons may be absent, weakly developed or altered by erosion and land use. Color helps describe a profile, but classification also depends on diagnostic properties and processes.

misconceptions.claim: Soil is just ground-up rock.
misconceptions.truth: Soil is a mixture of mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and living organisms. It develops slowly as rock weathers and plants, animals and microbes add and mix organic material.

teacher.script:
Choose Temperate brown soil and read the depth scale. Name the O, A, Bw and C horizons, then explain why a soil need not have E or R horizons.

Choose Mollisol example and compare its thick, dark topsoil. Then choose Oxisol example and discuss its gradual boundaries and intense weathering.
pitfalls: Compare the selected profile with other environments rather than presenting it as a universal sequence of horizons.
Distinguish surface topsoil from the underlying horizons and from the bedrock represented by the R horizon.
Connect a deeply weathered tropical soil with its formation conditions rather than equating it with peat.

predict.prompt: Why do you think grassland soils, like those of Iowa, have such a thick, dark top layer?

cer.prompt: Why do soils in different places develop different horizons?
cer.claim: Climate, vegetation, parent material and time control how a soil develops, so different places build different horizons.
cer.evidence: The temperate brown soil has O, A, Bw and C horizons. The Mollisol example has a thick, dark A horizon. The Oxisol example has a deep red, strongly weathered subsoil with gradual boundaries.
cer.reasoning: Under grassland, dense roots die and decay deep in the soil, building a thick, dark, organic-rich A horizon. In warm, wet tropics, intense chemical weathering over a long time removes most minerals and leaves iron and aluminum oxides that color the soil red.

labs.title: Soil texture triangle
labs.hook: Soil texture describes the proportions of sand, silt and clay.
labs.objective: Use the proportions of sand, silt and clay to classify a soil, then explain how its texture affects water movement.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Read the sand, silt and clay axes (sand along the base, clay up the left edge, silt down the right edge) and locate the selected mixture in the texture triangle. Check that its fractions add to 100%.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Change Sand % and Clay % and follow the point between texture classes; silt makes up the rest. Explain how the particle sizes differ, then distinguish texture from soil structure.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain why changing one particle-size fraction requires at least one of the other fractions to change. Then predict whether a sand or a clay soil drains faster, and explain why using particle and pore size.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Clay particles are…
choices: The finest of the three
The coarsest particles
Between sand and silt in size
The same size as silt
questions.explain: Clay is the smallest mineral particle-size fraction used in the soil texture triangle. Its large surface area and mineral properties help explain why many clay-rich soils are sticky when wet.

questions.prompt: Loam is…
choices: Mostly clay with little sand
A balanced mix of sand, silt and clay
Mostly sand that drains freely
Mostly organic matter, with almost no minerals
questions.explain: Loam occupies a texture class containing appreciable sand, silt and clay rather than being dominated by one extreme. Its mix can balance drainage and water retention, although soil productivity also depends on structure, nutrients and management.

questions.prompt: A soil with 90% sand is…
choices: Sandy clay loam
Silt loam
Sand or loamy sand
Clay loam
questions.explain: With 90% sand, only 10% remains for silt and clay, placing the composition near the sand corner of the triangle. The precise sandy class depends on how that remaining fraction is divided.

questions.prompt: Sand, silt and clay on the triangle must…
choices: Sum to 50%
Ignore silt
Always be equal
Sum to 100%
questions.explain: Sand, silt and clay represent the complete mineral fine-earth sample classified by the triangle. Their percentages must total 100%, so increasing one fraction requires reducing one or both of the others.

questions.prompt: Which soil usually drains fastest after heavy rain?
choices: Sandy soil with large pores
Clay soil with tiny pores
Silty clay soil
Clay loam soil
questions.explain: Water moves easily through the large spaces between sand grains. Soils with more clay have much smaller pores, so water drains through them slowly.

why: Soil texture describes the proportions of sand, silt and clay. These fractions sum to 100%, and their mixture influences properties such as water retention and drainage.

Sand grains are far larger than clay plates, so sandy soils have large pores that drain quickly and hold little water, while clay-rich soils have tiny pores that hold water tightly and drain slowly. Because the fractions must total 100%, raising one fraction always lowers another and moves the point toward that fraction's corner.
Texture is one influence on soil behavior; structure, organic matter and compaction also affect water movement.

misconceptions.claim: A soil’s color determines whether it is sand, silt or clay.
misconceptions.truth: Texture depends on the proportions of mineral particles in defined size classes. Color reflects other properties, including organic matter, iron compounds and drainage conditions. Two soils can therefore look similar while having different textures, and texture differs from the way particles are grouped into structure.

misconceptions.claim: Clay soils drain quickly because their particles are so small.
misconceptions.truth: Small particles leave tiny pores that hold water tightly, so clay soils drain slowly and can become waterlogged. Sandy soils, with larger pores, drain quickly.

teacher.script:
Read the sand, silt and clay axes and locate the selected mixture in the texture triangle. Check that its fractions add to 100%.

Change Sand % and Clay % and follow the point between texture classes; silt makes up the rest. Explain how the particle sizes differ, then distinguish texture from soil structure.
pitfalls: Classify mineral texture using the proportions of sand, silt and clay, not the soil’s color or a commercial label.
Check that the three mineral fractions total 100% before plotting a point on the triangle.
Explain that peat is dominated by organic material and is not a fourth corner of the mineral texture triangle.

modelNotes: The USDA texture triangle is a ternary plot: the three percentages must sum to 100.
Silt is calculated as the remainder, so the three always sum to 100.

predict.prompt: Which do you think drains faster after heavy rain: a sandy soil or a clay soil? Why?

cer.prompt: How do the proportions of sand, silt and clay affect how a soil holds water?
cer.claim: Sandy soils drain quickly and hold little water, while clay-rich soils drain slowly and hold water tightly.
cer.evidence: With 90% sand, the point lies near the sand corner of the triangle (sand or loamy sand). Raising Clay % moves the point toward the clay corner. Sand grains are 0.05–2 mm, silt 0.002–0.05 mm and clay smaller than 0.002 mm.
cer.reasoning: Large sand grains leave large pores that water drains through quickly. Tiny clay particles leave very small pores and a large surface area, which hold water tightly and let it move only slowly.

labs.title: Weathering
labs.hook: Weathering changes rock in place.
labs.objective: Compare how freezing water, weakly acidic water and growing roots break down rock in place.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Choose Freezing in a joint and compare the volume before and after freezing. Use Compare physical scale to separate the real widening from the ×10 exaggeration.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Choose Carbonate dissolution and read the reaction and the mass totals. Then choose Root growth and name its mechanical and chemical effects.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does each weathering process change rock in place, and what would be needed to transport the fragments away?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Frost shattering is…
choices: Chemical
Biological
Salt crystal growth
Mechanical
questions.explain: Water freezing within cracks, including the growth of ice as more water is drawn in, can exert stress on the surrounding rock. This breaks the rock physically without requiring a chemical change in its minerals.

questions.prompt: Carbonation attacks…
choices: Carbonate rocks, via carbonic acid
Granite, through frost action
Iron minerals, through rusting in air
Salt crystals in sandstone
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide dissolved in water forms weak carbonic acid, which reacts with carbonate minerals. This dissolution helps enlarge fractures and form karst features in limestone.

questions.prompt: Biological weathering includes…
choices: Only animals digging their burrows
Roots, lichens and burrowing animals
Only plant roots growing in cracks
Rain dissolving limestone pavements
questions.explain: Organisms can disrupt rock physically, for example through root growth, or chemically through acids and other compounds. Biological weathering therefore includes more than one breakdown mechanism.

questions.prompt: Weathering versus erosion…
choices: Two words for exactly the same process
Erosion breaks rock; weathering moves it away
Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion moves it
Weathering happens only in hot deserts
questions.explain: Weathering alters or breaks down material where it is exposed. Erosion removes material from its original position through agents such as water, wind, ice or gravity.

questions.prompt: Which of these is chemical weathering?
choices: Ice expanding in a crack
Rain slowly dissolving limestone
Roots prying rock apart
Rock flaking as it heats and cools
questions.explain: Chemical weathering changes the minerals themselves. Rainwater containing carbon dioxide reacts with calcium carbonate and carries it away in solution.

why: Weathering changes rock in place. Freezing water, chemical dissolution and biological activity can weaken it through different mechanisms, often acting together before erosion transports the material.

Freezing water and growing roots push joint walls apart, breaking rock physically without changing its minerals. Carbonic acid instead reacts with calcite, so the solid shrinks while the same mass of calcium carbonate is carried away in solution as dissolved ions.
The water and calcite masses shown are conserved, but the volume of water grows by about 9% as it freezes. The animations do not calculate how fast weathering happens.

misconceptions.claim: Chemical and mechanical weathering are separate alternatives that cannot act together.
misconceptions.truth: Several weathering processes can affect the same rock. Mechanical cracking exposes new surfaces to chemical reactions, while chemical alteration can weaken material for later breakage. Temperature, water, organisms and rock properties influence which processes are most effective in a particular setting.

misconceptions.claim: Weathering is too slow to see within a human lifetime.
misconceptions.truth: Some weathering is visible within decades. Old limestone gravestones lose their lettering, sandstone buildings flake and crumble, and frost can split rock in a single winter.

teacher.script:
Choose Freezing in a joint and compare the volume before and after freezing. Use Compare physical scale to separate the real widening from the ×10 exaggeration.

Choose Carbonate dissolution and read the reaction and the mass totals. Then choose Root growth and name its mechanical and chemical effects.
pitfalls: Distinguish weathering in place from erosion that removes and transports material.
Explain how water, temperature, organisms and rock type influence which weathering processes are effective.
Use a carbonate rock such as limestone to demonstrate carbonation rather than assuming all rocks react in the same way.

modelNotes: Using densities 1000 kg/m³ for liquid and 917 kg/m³ for ice, freezing increases occupied volume by about 9%.
The joint starts 20 mm wide. The teaching view exaggerates its widening ten times; Compare physical scale shows the real change.
Solid calcite plus dissolved calcite always adds up to the starting mass (calcite density 2710 kg/m³).

predict.prompt: Water seeps into a crack in a rock and freezes overnight. Predict what happens to the crack over many winters.

cer.prompt: How can water break rock apart without moving it anywhere?
cer.claim: Water breaks rock in place by freezing in cracks (mechanical weathering) and by dissolving minerals such as calcite (chemical weathering).
cer.evidence: In Freezing in a joint, water expands by about 9% as it turns to ice and pushes the joint walls apart (shown ×10 unless Compare physical scale is on). In Carbonate dissolution, calcite dissolves while solid plus dissolved calcite always adds up to the starting mass.
cer.reasoning: Ice is less dense than water (917 compared with 1000 kg/m³), so freezing water takes up more space and wedges cracks open. Weak carbonic acid reacts with calcite and carries it away in solution. Both break down rock without transporting it, which is the difference from erosion.

labs.title: Soil erosion
labs.hook: Raindrops and flowing water can detach and carry soil.
labs.objective: Compare soil loss under different vegetation cover and explain how runoff carries sediment away from a slope.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify the bare and covered plots, then find the three sediment stores: in place, in transport and exported.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Press Play or drag Process and compare the two plots. Then switch on Dry wind transport.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why does detached sediment not necessarily leave the plot immediately?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Exported sediment is…
choices: All material detached so far
Material that has left the plot
Soil newly formed by rainfall
Sediment still moving within the plot
questions.explain: Detachment releases sediment from the soil, but that sediment may remain in motion or settle within the plot. Export counts only the material that crosses the plot boundary.

questions.prompt: The 85% reduction in detachment on the covered plot is…
choices: A universal vegetation constant.
A measured Dust Bowl value.
A value chosen for this model.
A guaranteed erosion-control outcome.
questions.explain: The 85% reduction is a chosen model coefficient that isolates the effect of cover in this comparison. A measured reduction would depend on soil, vegetation, rainfall, slope and management.

questions.prompt: Compare physical scale (the T key) changes…
choices: The calculated mass of soil lost from the plot.
The physical size of the plot.
How the soil is detached by rain.
How much surface lowering is exaggerated.
questions.explain: The scale control changes how strongly the vertical surface lowering is exaggerated on screen. It leaves the calculated sediment transfers and their total unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which method reduces soil erosion on a sloping field?
choices: Plowing up and down the slope
Plowing along the contours
Removing hedgerows around the field
Leaving the soil bare through winter
questions.explain: Furrows that follow the contours slow water running downhill and trap soil. Plowing up and down the slope makes channels that speed runoff and erosion.

questions.prompt: Why does bare soil lose more particles in heavy rain than soil under crops?
choices: Raindrops hit it directly and splash particles loose.
Bare soil is always made only of sand.
Crops attract the rain away from the soil.
Bare soil warms in the sun, so its particles dissolve faster.
questions.explain: Plant leaves and litter absorb the impact of raindrops. On bare ground each drop strikes the soil and splashes particles loose, ready to be carried away by runoff.

why: Raindrops and flowing water can detach and carry soil. Ground cover reduces exposure and can slow transport, while deposited sediment remains within the catchment until it moves again.

Detachment and export are separate steps. Raindrop impact, runoff or wind first loosens soil; that sediment then spends time in transport, moving downslope or settling for a while, before some of it crosses the plot edge. Export therefore lags behind detachment, and the in-transport store holds the difference.
The selected sediment budget is a classroom comparison; local erosion rates require evidence about rainfall, soil and land management.

misconceptions.claim: Vegetation prevents all soil erosion.
misconceptions.truth: Plant cover can intercept raindrops, protect the soil and slow surface flow, reducing erosion. Its effectiveness depends on cover density, roots, soil condition, slope and the event itself. Even a vegetated slope can lose sediment during intense runoff or other disturbances.

misconceptions.claim: Soil forms as quickly as it is eroded, so losses are always replaced.
misconceptions.truth: Soil usually forms at a fraction of a millimeter a year. Bare farmland on a slope can lose soil many times faster than that, so erosion can strip in decades what took centuries to form.

teacher.script:
Identify the bare and covered plots, then find the three sediment stores: in place, in transport and exported.

Press Play or drag Process and compare the two plots. Then switch on Dry wind transport.
pitfalls: Treat the selected coefficients as model inputs rather than measurements from a particular field.
Distinguish soil detached at the surface from sediment that is eventually exported from the plot.
Use the numerical readings for quantities; enlarged raindrops and grains help show the process rather than their actual sizes.

sources.label: NRCS RUSLE2: a different erosion-estimation method

modelNotes: Each plot’s model surface layer is 20 mm thick with a dry bulk density of 1500 kg/m³, giving 6000 kg per plot.
Every transfer is subtracted from one store and added to another, so the total stays at 6000 kg.
Process runs through 60 model minutes.
The chosen detachment coefficient is 0.004 per minute for rain and runoff, or 0.002 for dry wind; cover multiplies it by 0.15.
Sediment leaves the transport store at 0.15 per minute for rain and runoff, or 0.3 for wind.
The teaching view exaggerates surface lowering 30 times; Compare physical scale shows the true lowering.

predict.prompt: Two identical slopes get the same heavy rain. One is bare and one is covered by plants. How much less soil do you think the covered slope loses?

cer.prompt: Why does a bare field lose more soil in heavy rain than a field covered by plants?
cer.claim: Bare soil loses far more sediment because nothing shields it from raindrops or slows the runoff.
cer.evidence: Over 60 model minutes, the bare plot exports much more sediment than the covered plot, where plant cover multiplies the detachment rate by 0.15. Each plot starts with 6,000 kg of surface soil, and the in-place, in-transport and exported stores always add up to that total.
cer.reasoning: Raindrops hitting bare ground knock particles loose, and fast runoff carries them away. Leaves and residue absorb the impact and roots hold the soil, so fewer particles are detached and less is carried off. The value 0.15 is a model choice, not a measured constant.

labs.title: Earthquakes
labs.hook: An earthquake releases energy when rock slips along a fault.
labs.objective: Locate the focus and epicenter of an earthquake and compare how different seismic waves travel through Earth.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the hypocenter, the epicenter and the fault scarp, which is in a different place. Set Focus depth to 20 km and predict which wave front reaches the seismometer first.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Drag the Process slider past both arrivals and read the times. Increase Focus depth, then explain why the ray path gets longer.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does increasing the focus depth change the wave path and arrival time at a fixed station?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The focus (hypocenter) is…
choices: The point underground where slip begins
The point on the surface above the slip
The place where shaking is strongest
The seismometer that records it
questions.explain: The focus is the location inside Earth where earthquake rupture begins. The epicenter is the point on the surface directly above it.

questions.prompt: P-waves…
choices: Are the slowest of the seismic waves
Are fastest and cross solids and liquids
Travel only through solid rock layers
Travel only along Earth’s surface
questions.explain: P-waves transmit alternating compression and expansion, which both solids and liquids can support. They are the fastest major seismic wave type and usually arrive first.

questions.prompt: Surface waves…
choices: Arrive first, well before P-waves
Travel straight through the liquid outer core
Arrive later and often cause most damage
Are just another name for S-waves
questions.explain: Love and Rayleigh waves travel along Earth's surface and can produce large, sustained ground motion. They arrive after the faster body waves and can contribute substantially to damage.

questions.prompt: Magnitude versus intensity…
choices: They are the same number in different units
Intensity is source size; magnitude is local shaking
Intensity is measured only at the epicenter
Magnitude is source size; intensity is local shaking
questions.explain: Magnitude measures the size of the earthquake source, while intensity describes shaking and effects at a particular location. One earthquake can therefore produce different intensities at different sites.

questions.prompt: Where do the world’s largest earthquakes usually happen?
choices: In the middle of stable continents
Along mid-ocean spreading ridges
On subduction-zone megathrust faults
Close to the North and South Poles
questions.explain: The largest earthquakes, above magnitude 9, have all occurred on megathrusts where one plate sinks beneath another, such as off Chile in 1960 and Japan in 2011. The faults there are long and wide, so they can slip over huge areas.

why: An earthquake releases energy when rock slips along a fault. The focus is the source at depth and the epicenter lies above it; different seismic waves transmit the disturbance through and along Earth.

P-waves travel faster than S-waves (about 6 km/s against 3.5 km/s here), so the P-wave always reaches a seismometer first and the gap between the two arrivals grows with distance. A deeper focus makes the path from focus to station longer, so both waves arrive later and the S–P gap widens.
The model shows how each wave type travels; real shaking and damage also depend on the source, distance, ground and buildings.

misconceptions.claim: Earthquake magnitude and shaking intensity are the same measurement.
misconceptions.truth: Magnitude describes the earthquake’s size at its source. Intensity describes shaking and effects at a particular place, so it varies with distance, local ground and buildings. One earthquake can therefore have a single reported magnitude but many different local intensities.

misconceptions.claim: Most earthquake deaths happen when the ground opens up and swallows people.
misconceptions.truth: The ground rarely opens wide. Most deaths and injuries come from collapsing buildings, and from landslides, tsunamis and fires that earthquakes trigger. This is why building design matters so much.

teacher.script:
Find the hypocenter, the epicenter and the fault scarp, which is in a different place. Set Focus depth to 20 km and predict which wave front reaches the seismometer first.

Drag the Process slider past both arrivals and read the times. Increase Focus depth, then explain why the ray path gets longer.
pitfalls: Distinguish earthquake magnitude from the intensity of shaking experienced at a particular location.
Locate the epicenter at the surface above the focus, and explain that S-waves do not pass through the liquid outer core.
Identify the fault setting before interpreting an event; California includes transform movement as well as other tectonic settings.

modelNotes: P-wave fronts spread at 6 km/s and S-wave fronts at 3.5 km/s.
The Process slider covers 30 seconds; play it or drag it, and change Focus depth.
Compare P and S arrivals at the station 50 km horizontally from the epicenter; the straight-ray distance is √(depth² + 50²).
The violet surface-wave ring is simplified: it starts when the S-wave first reaches the epicenter and then travels at 3.2 km/s.

predict.prompt: A seismometer is 50 km from an earthquake. Which wave do you think arrives first, the P-wave or the S-wave? How far apart might they arrive?

cer.prompt: How can the gap between P-wave and S-wave arrivals tell you how far away an earthquake is?
cer.claim: The time gap between the P-wave and S-wave arrivals grows with distance, so a longer gap means a more distant earthquake.
cer.evidence: With Focus depth at 20 km, the station 50 km from the epicenter is about 54 km from the focus. The P-wave (6 km/s) arrives after about 9 seconds and the S-wave (3.5 km/s) after about 15 seconds, a gap of about 6 seconds. Increasing the depth lengthens the path and widens the gap.
cer.reasoning: P-waves travel faster than S-waves, so the two separate as they travel. The gap equals the distance multiplied by (1/3.5 − 1/6) seconds per kilometer, so measuring the gap gives the distance; gaps from three stations locate the epicenter.

labs.title: Volcanoes
labs.hook: Magma composition, gas content and the conditions of ascent influence eruption style.
labs.objective: Explain how magma viscosity influences volcanic form and eruption style, using shield and composite volcanoes as examples.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Move Viscosity to compare a broad shield with a steeper composite cone. Then raise Gas drive on its own: with enough gas, even runny basalt can erupt explosively. Sticky magma with little gas builds a lava dome instead.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Use the Cutaway slider to look inside. Follow the magma from the chamber up the conduit and watch its gas bubbles grow; in an explosive eruption, find where the froth shatters into ash. Then turn on Fissure vents: a fissure is a crack in the ground, not a type of magma.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can viscosity alone not decide whether an eruption is explosive or produces lava flows?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Shield volcanoes form from…
choices: Runny basalt in long, gentle flows
Sticky rhyolite in explosive eruptions
Layers of ash and thick lava
Ice melting over a magma chamber
questions.explain: Low-viscosity basaltic lava can travel far from a vent before solidifying. Repeated spreading flows build the broad, gently sloping form of a shield volcano.

questions.prompt: Stratovolcanoes are steep because…
choices: They are older and more eroded
Sticky, gassy magma builds lava and ash layers
Runny lava flows a long way before cooling
Their magma rises from much greater depths in the mantle
questions.explain: More viscous lava tends to travel shorter distances, while explosive eruptions add layers of fragmented material. Repeated eruptions can therefore build a relatively steep composite cone.

questions.prompt: A rift eruption…
choices: Always needs a hotspot below
Always produces a steep cone
Can erupt basalt along a long fissure
Happens only where one plate sinks under another
questions.explain: Extension at a divergent boundary opens fractures and allows magma to rise. Basalt may then erupt along an elongated fissure rather than from a single central vent.

questions.prompt: Sticky magma explodes more readily because…
choices: It is hotter than runny magma
It contains less dissolved gas than basalt
It erupts only under water
Gas cannot escape, so pressure builds
questions.explain: Viscous magma can impede gas escape as pressure falls during ascent. Expanding trapped gas can then fragment the magma and drive an explosive eruption, although viscosity is only one control.

questions.prompt: Which volcanic hazards have caused the most deaths in history?
choices: Slow-moving lava flows
Falling volcanic bombs near the vent
Pyroclastic flows and volcanic mudflows
Sulfur smells from fumaroles
questions.explain: Pyroclastic flows are fast, hot clouds of gas and rock, and lahars are mudflows that can travel tens of kilometers down valleys. Both move too fast to escape, unlike most lava flows.

why: Magma composition, gas content and the conditions of ascent influence eruption style. Comparing volcano shapes links these processes to lava flows, ash layers and how a volcano is built up over time.

Magma collects in a chamber in the crust and rises through a conduit or crack because it is less dense than the rock around it. As it nears the surface the pressure falls and dissolved gas forms bubbles. In runny basalt the bubbles escape easily, so lava flows or fountains; in sticky, silica-rich magma they are trapped until the magma shatters into ash. A large gas supply can make even basalt erupt explosively.
The eruptions shown illustrate a few processes; a volcano’s shape alone cannot predict its next eruption.

misconceptions.claim: A volcano’s size alone predicts how explosive its next eruption will be.
misconceptions.truth: Eruption behavior depends on magma properties, gas, ascent conditions and possible interaction with water or ice. Large shield volcanoes often produce fluid lava flows, but basaltic eruptions can also be explosive. The existing landform records earlier activity without determining every future event.

misconceptions.claim: Lava flows are the deadliest volcanic hazard.
misconceptions.truth: Most lava moves slowly enough for people to walk away, although it destroys property. Pyroclastic flows, volcanic mudflows (lahars), ash and gases have caused far more deaths.

teacher.script:
Move Viscosity to compare a broad shield with a steeper composite cone. Then raise Gas drive on its own: with enough gas, even runny basalt can erupt explosively. Sticky magma with little gas builds a lava dome instead.

Use the Cutaway slider to look inside. Follow the magma from the chamber up the conduit and watch its gas bubbles grow; in an explosive eruption, find where the froth shatters into ash. Then turn on Fissure vents: a fissure is a crack in the ground, not a type of magma.
pitfalls: Compare effusive and explosive activity rather than assuming every volcano erupts in the same way.
Include hotspot and divergent-boundary examples as well as volcanoes around subduction zones.
Explain how repeated fluid lava flows build a shield volcano rather than describing it as an eroded stratovolcano.

modelNotes: Eruption styles follow simple rules rather than a simulation: gas drives fragmentation, and sticky magma traps its gas, so less gas is needed for an explosive eruption. Lava lakes, fountains, domes, eruption columns and pyroclastic flows are drawn to show the processes, not to scale.
Turn on Real volcanoes to compare Mauna Loa and Mount St. Helens from USGS elevation data at the same scale (heights from sea level, exaggerated ×3 unless Compare physical scale is on).

predict.prompt: Do you think runny lava or thick, sticky lava builds a steeper volcano? Which is more likely to explode?

cer.prompt: Why do Mauna Loa and Mount St. Helens look so different and erupt so differently?
cer.claim: Mauna Loa is a broad shield built by runny basalt lava flows, while Mount St. Helens is a steep composite cone built by sticky, gas-rich magma that erupts explosively.
cer.evidence: Low Viscosity builds a broad, gently sloping shield; high Viscosity builds a steeper cone of lava and ash layers. Raising Gas drive makes eruptions more explosive. With Real volcanoes on, Mauna Loa rises about 4 km above sea level over a very wide base, while Mount St. Helens is much smaller and steeper.
cer.reasoning: Runny lava flows far before it cools, spreading into gentle slopes. Sticky magma flows a short distance and traps gas, so pressure builds until it escapes explosively, piling ash and lava into a steep cone.

labs.title: Tsunami
labs.hook: A tsunami has a long wavelength and travels faster in deeper water.
labs.objective: Explain how seafloor displacement generates a tsunami and why its speed and height change as it enters shallow water.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Drag Process through the first stage, where the seafloor rises and lifts the water above it. How does this differ from a wind-driven storm surge? Then follow the wave in the second stage as it travels toward the shelf.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Read the wave’s speed in deep water and again in shallow water. Use the chart, drawn in meters, to compare wave heights.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does decreasing water depth change the speed and height of a long wave approaching the coast?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A tsunami starts with…
choices: Strong winds over the open sea
Sudden seafloor movement
An unusually high spring tide
Low air pressure in a storm
questions.explain: A tsunami begins when a large volume of water is displaced rapidly, often by vertical movement of the seafloor during an earthquake. Landslides and other disturbances can also generate tsunamis.

questions.prompt: In deep water a tsunami is…
choices: A 30 m wall everywhere
Slow until it reaches the coast
Fast and often unnoticed at sea
Only a few kilometers long
questions.explain: A tsunami's long wavelength allows it to travel rapidly through deep water while its offshore height may remain small. A ship can therefore experience little noticeable change even as the wave passes.

questions.prompt: It grows at the coast because…
choices: The Moon’s pull is stronger near the land
Its speed increases in shallow water
Onshore winds keep pushing it higher and higher
Slowing bunches its energy into a taller wave
questions.explain: As a tsunami enters shallower water, it slows and its wavelength shortens. Its height can increase through shoaling, with the final coastal response also shaped by refraction, seabed geometry and energy loss.

questions.prompt: The coastal flooding from hurricanes Katrina and Sandy was mainly…
choices: Storm surge from wind and low pressure
A tsunami from a megathrust earthquake
A spring tide on its own
A landslide-generated tsunami
questions.explain: Katrina and Sandy raised coastal water levels through storm winds and atmospheric pressure, combined with tides and waves. That storm-surge mechanism differs from the rapid water-column displacement that generates a tsunami.

questions.prompt: Why should people stay away from the beach after the first tsunami wave?
choices: The first wave is always the largest one.
The sea is calm once one wave has passed.
More waves can follow for several hours.
Tsunami water drains away almost instantly.
questions.explain: A tsunami is a series of waves that can be tens of minutes apart, and a later wave may be the biggest. People should stay on high ground until officials say it is safe.

why: A tsunami has a long wavelength and travels faster in deeper water. As it crosses into shallower water, it slows and its amplitude can increase as energy is concentrated into a smaller depth.

Long-wave speed depends only on water depth: c = √(g h). In 4000 m of water a tsunami travels at about 200 m/s, as fast as a jet airliner; on a 100 m shelf it slows to about 30 m/s. The back of the wave, still in deeper water, catches up with the front, so the wavelength shortens and the same energy is squeezed into a shorter wave, which grows taller.
This long-wave calculation ends offshore and excludes breaking, run-up and inundation on land.

misconceptions.claim: A tsunami and a storm surge are the same kind of coastal wave.
misconceptions.truth: A tsunami is a sequence of long waves generated by rapid water displacement, such as seafloor movement or a landslide. Storm surge is an abnormal water-level rise driven mainly by storm winds and atmospheric pressure. Their causes, propagation and warning evidence differ.

misconceptions.claim: A tsunami is a single giant breaking wave, like a surfing wave.
misconceptions.truth: A tsunami is a series of very long waves that can keep arriving for hours. Often it comes ashore as a fast, rising flood of water rather than a curling breaker, and the first wave is not always the largest.

teacher.script:
Drag Process through the first stage, where the seafloor rises and lifts the water above it. How does this differ from a wind-driven storm surge? Then follow the wave in the second stage as it travels toward the shelf.

Read the wave’s speed in deep water and again in shallow water. Use the chart, drawn in meters, to compare wave heights.
pitfalls: Distinguish a tsunami from astronomical tides and wind-driven storm surge, such as Hurricane Katrina’s surge or the 1953 North Sea flood.
Explain why a tsunami can have a small wave height in deep water and change greatly as it enters shallow water.
Connect coastal flooding to the generating process instead of identifying the hazard from water level alone.

modelNotes: The traveling stage starts with a set 20-minute wave packet with a 0.5 m amplitude in deep water.
Along a 500 km transect, depth stays at 4000 m for the first 180 km, then declines smoothly to 100 m.

In the first 15% of Process the seafloor rises by up to 1 m and lifts the water above it; the gold block and arrow show the uplift, enlarged. The hump then splits into two waves of about half its height, and the model follows the one heading for the coast (0.5 m).
In the teaching view depth is enlarged ×20 and wave height a further ×600; Physical scale shows both at true scale.
Gradually varying depth, no reflection and no lateral spreading are strong assumptions; the transect ends in 100 m water before the coast.

predict.prompt: Out in the deep ocean, do you think a tsunami is tall or short, fast or slow? What happens as it reaches shallow water?

cer.prompt: Why does a tsunami that is barely noticeable at sea become dangerous at the coast?
cer.claim: A tsunami slows down in shallow water, and the slowing squeezes its energy into a shorter, taller wave.
cer.evidence: In 4,000 m of water the wave travels at about 200 m/s with an amplitude of about 0.5 m. Over the shelf it slows to about 30 m/s at 100 m depth, and the chart shows its height growing as the water shallows.
cer.reasoning: Tsunami speed depends on water depth: c = √(g h). The back of the wave, still in deeper water, catches up with the slower front, so the wavelength shortens. The same energy is packed into a shorter wave, so the wave grows taller.

labs.title: Tropical cyclone
labs.hook: A tropical cyclone draws moist air inward near the surface, with strong ascent in the eyewall and outflow aloft.
labs.objective: Identify the eye, eyewall and rainbands of a tropical cyclone and explain how warm ocean water supports its circulation.
standards: OCR GCSE A Environmental threats to our planet

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the eye, eyewall and rainbands. Follow the arrows for inflow, rising air and outflow, and find the sinking air in the eye.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Read the wind profile and find its peak at 30 km. Change Intensity and watch the center pressure: why is that number only a model estimate?

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How are the strongest winds near the eyewall related to the pressure change toward the center?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The eyewall is…
choices: The calm, clear center of the storm
The outer bands of heavy showers
The cold front trailing behind it
The ring of strongest wind and rain
questions.explain: The eyewall surrounds the relatively calm eye and contains vigorous rising air and deep convection. The strongest near-surface winds commonly occur in or close to this ring.

questions.prompt: Tropical cyclones need…
choices: Warm ocean water and low wind shear
Cool water and strong wind shear
A strong temperature contrast between air masses
Dry air over land
questions.explain: Warm ocean water can supply heat and moisture, while low vertical wind shear helps organized convection remain aligned with the circulation. These favorable conditions do not by themselves guarantee that a cyclone will develop.

questions.prompt: A winter blizzard over the Great Plains is usually…
choices: A tropical cyclone
A midlatitude cyclone
An anticyclone
A large tornado outbreak
questions.explain: Winter storms over the United States, like those over Europe, are usually extratropical cyclones associated with contrasts between air masses and with fronts. Their structure and energy sources differ from those of a tropical cyclone over warm water.

questions.prompt: The Saffir–Simpson scale rates…
choices: Every US winter storm and nor’easter
Hurricanes by the total rain they drop
Tropical cyclones, by wind speed
Storm surge height only
questions.explain: The Saffir–Simpson scale assigns hurricane categories using maximum sustained wind speed. It does not classify extratropical storms such as nor’easters or represent a storm's rainfall and surge hazards.

questions.prompt: Why does a tropical cyclone usually weaken after it moves over land?
choices: Mountains reflect its winds back out to sea.
Land is too dry to make the air spin.
It loses its supply of warm, moist ocean air.
Daylight heats the storm until it evaporates.
questions.explain: A tropical cyclone is powered by heat and moisture from warm sea water. Over land that supply is cut off and friction slows the winds, although heavy rain and flooding can continue far inland.

why: A tropical cyclone draws moist air inward near the surface, with strong ascent in the eyewall and outflow aloft. Its eye has weaker winds and often descending air, distinct from a tornado funnel.

Air turns faster as it moves toward the center, so the wind is strongest at the eyewall and falls away outside it. To keep fast-moving air on a tight circular path, pressure must drop steeply toward the center: a stronger maximum wind needs a deeper low, which is why the model's center pressure falls as Intensity rises.
The ideal vortex links wind and pressure through stated assumptions; it does not calculate storm development, rainfall or a track.

misconceptions.claim: The calm eye means a tropical cyclone has passed and the danger is over.
misconceptions.truth: The eye is surrounded by the eyewall, where winds and convection are strong. If the eye crosses a location, the opposite eyewall may arrive after a temporary lull, with a changed wind direction. Rainfall, flooding and coastal water levels can also remain hazardous beyond the strongest winds.

misconceptions.claim: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are different kinds of storm.
misconceptions.truth: They are all tropical cyclones. The name depends on the ocean: hurricane in the Atlantic and north-east Pacific, typhoon in the north-west Pacific, and cyclone in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

teacher.script:
Find the eye, eyewall and rainbands. Follow the arrows for inflow, rising air and outflow, and find the sinking air in the eye.

Read the wind profile and find its peak at 30 km. Change Intensity and watch the center pressure: why is that number only a model estimate?
pitfalls: Distinguish a tropical cyclone from a midlatitude windstorm and apply intensity scales only to the storms they describe.
Locate the strongest winds around the eyewall rather than in the relatively calm eye.
Explain storm surge as a rise in sea level driven by the storm, separate from both tsunami waves and ordinary wind waves.

modelNotes: The ideal wind profile increases linearly from a calm center to a maximum at radius 30 km, then decreases inversely with radius.
Intensity selects maximum tangential wind from 38 to 80 m/s.
Pressure comes from a steady gradient-wind balance with air density 1.15 kg/m³, a Coriolis parameter of 0.00005 per second and 101300 Pa at 300 km radius.

Cloud depth is 12 km, drawn five times taller in the teaching view (Physical scale, or the T key, shows it 1:1). The cloud tops are a NASA MODIS image of Hurricane Katrina (28 August 2005) at the model's scale; their heights are illustrative, and the clouds are not simulated droplets or rainfall.

predict.prompt: Why do you think hurricanes form over warm oceans and weaken after they move over land?

cer.prompt: Where are a hurricane's strongest winds, and why does a stronger storm have lower central pressure?
cer.claim: The strongest winds are in the eyewall around the calm eye, and a stronger storm needs a deeper low-pressure center to keep its fast winds circling.
cer.evidence: The wind profile rises from a calm center to its maximum at 30 km, the eyewall, then falls away outward. Raising Intensity raises the maximum wind from 38 to 80 m/s and lowers the model's center pressure.
cer.reasoning: Air spirals inward and speeds up as it gets closer to the center. To keep fast-moving air on a tight circular path, pressure must drop steeply toward the center. Warm ocean water supplies the moisture whose condensation releases heat to power the eyewall.

labs.title: Graticule and coordinates
labs.hook: Latitude measures an angle north or south of the equator, while longitude measures an angle east or west of the prime meridian.
labs.objective: Use latitude and longitude to locate a point on Earth, and relate longitude to differences in local solar time.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Locate the equator and prime meridian, then follow a parallel and a meridian around the globe.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Change Latitude first: the marker slides north or south along its meridian and the gold arc grows from the equator. Then change Longitude: the globe turns to carry the marker east or west, and the blue arc grows along the equator from the prime meridian. Read the hemisphere letters and the local solar-time difference.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Move Latitude from 0° toward 80° and watch the readout for the length of 1° of longitude. Why does one degree of longitude cover less ground near the poles than near the equator?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Latitude measures…
choices: Angle east or west of Greenwich
Distance from the North Pole in km
Angle north or south of the equator
Height above sea level
questions.explain: Latitude locates a point north or south of the equator using an angle up to 90°. Lines of equal latitude are parallels, with the North Pole at 90° N.

questions.prompt: The Greenwich meridian is…
choices: The equator
180° longitude
The Tropic of Cancer
0° longitude
questions.explain: The prime meridian is the agreed zero reference from which longitude is measured east or west. Choosing that reference is a mapping convention rather than a physical boundary on Earth.

questions.prompt: 15° of longitude is about…
choices: One hour of rotation
One minute of rotation
One day of rotation
15 km at the equator
questions.explain: Earth turns through 360° relative to the Sun during a mean solar day of 24 hours. Dividing gives about 15° of longitude for each hour of local solar-time difference.

questions.prompt: A point at 0°, 0° sits…
choices: In London, at the Greenwich meridian
In the Gulf of Guinea, south of Ghana
At the North Pole, where lines meet
In the Pacific, near the date line
questions.explain: Zero latitude identifies the equator and zero longitude identifies the prime meridian. Their intersection lies in the Gulf of Guinea in the Atlantic Ocean, south of Ghana.

questions.prompt: Why do lines of longitude get closer together toward the poles?
choices: Earth is wider at the poles than at the equator.
Map makers draw them closer on purpose.
Longitude is measured in kilometers, not degrees.
All meridians meet at the two poles.
questions.explain: Every meridian runs from the North Pole to the South Pole, so they converge there. The distance represented by one degree of longitude therefore shrinks with latitude.

why: Latitude measures an angle north or south of the equator, while longitude measures an angle east or west of the prime meridian. Parallels and meridians form the coordinate grid called the graticule.

Latitude is measured along a meridian, from the equator toward a pole, so it can only reach 90°. Longitude is measured along the equator, east or west from the prime meridian, up to 180°. Because Earth turns 360° in about 24 hours, every 15° of longitude east puts local solar time about one hour ahead of Greenwich.

These are angular coordinates on a sphere. Every meridian meets at the poles, so the ground covered by 1° of longitude shrinks with latitude: about 111 km at the equator, 84 km at 40.7° N (New York) and 56 km at 60°, falling to zero at the poles. A degree of latitude stays close to 111 km everywhere.

misconceptions.claim: The coordinates 0 degrees latitude and 0 degrees longitude locate Greenwich.
misconceptions.truth: Greenwich is close to zero longitude but about 51.5 degrees north of the equator. Zero latitude lies on the equator, so the two zero coordinates meet in the Gulf of Guinea. Latitude and longitude identify separate angular directions and must both be specified.

misconceptions.claim: Lines of longitude are the same distance apart everywhere.
misconceptions.truth: Meridians meet at the poles. One degree of longitude is about 111 km wide at the equator, about 84 km at New York’s latitude and zero at the poles. Lines of latitude, by contrast, stay roughly 111 km apart.

teacher.script:
Locate the equator and prime meridian, then follow a parallel and a meridian around the globe.
