Change Latitude first, then Longitude. Ask students which arc grows with each slider (gold for latitude, blue for longitude), then set Latitude to 0°, 40.7° and 80° and compare the readout's length of 1° of longitude.
pitfalls: Check the east–west convention using a known location; New York is west of Greenwich.
Distinguish the prime meridian from the International Date Line, and place 0° latitude, 0° longitude on the equator.
Explain that time zones are human conventions for clocks, while Earth’s rotation produces day and night.

modelNotes: The four mainland US time zones (Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific) span about 60° of longitude; their boundaries bend around state lines, but sunrise and sunset do not.
Dallas is about 15° east of Phoenix, so the Sun rises there roughly an hour earlier.
Railway timetables drove the adoption of standard time zones, usually based on meridians 15° apart.
The equator plays no part in time zones: it is 0° latitude, the other set of lines in the grid.
Latitude is the angle from the equator, 0° to 90° north or south.
Longitude is the angle from the Greenwich meridian, 0° to 180° east or west.
The equator is 0° latitude, not a line of longitude.
Greenwich is 0° longitude by agreement; Earth’s rotation does not depend on which meridian we call zero.

predict.prompt: The point 0° latitude, 0° longitude is often thought to be in London. Where do you think it really is?

cer.prompt: How do latitude and longitude locate a place, and why does 1° of longitude cover less ground near the poles?
cer.claim: Latitude gives the angle north or south of the equator and longitude the angle east or west of the prime meridian; a degree of longitude shrinks toward the poles because all meridians meet there.
cer.evidence: Moving Latitude slides the marker along a meridian and grows the gold arc from the equator; moving Longitude grows the blue arc along the equator. The readout shows 1° of longitude as about 111 km at the equator, 84 km at 40.7° N (New York) and 56 km at 60°. The point 0°, 0° lies in the Gulf of Guinea.
cer.reasoning: Latitude and longitude are angles measured from Earth's center. Meridians converge at the poles, so the distance between them falls with the cosine of latitude, while degrees of latitude stay about 111 km apart.

labs.title: Map projections
labs.hook: A map projection transfers positions from a curved surface to a plane.
labs.objective: Compare how map projections represent a curved Earth on a flat surface, identifying the distortions each introduces.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Compare Greenland and Africa on the globe before flattening it. Predict which properties may change on the map.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Drag Flatten to 1.00 for each choice in Projection. Compare the equal-sized gold circles at the equator and at 60° N and S, then describe the trade-off between area and shape.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Choose a map use and explain which distortion would matter most for that purpose.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: On a Mercator world map Greenland looks…
choices: Much smaller than it really is
At its true size, compared with Africa and Europe
About as large as Africa, which is far bigger
Squashed flat, as if near the equator
questions.explain: Mercator's scale increases strongly toward the poles, enlarging high-latitude areas on the map. Greenland therefore appears far larger relative to Africa than its actual area warrants.

questions.prompt: An equal-area projection is built to…
choices: Keep compass bearings
Show shortest routes as straight lines
Keep shapes correct everywhere
Keep relative sizes of regions
questions.explain: An equal-area projection preserves area ratios between mapped regions. Flattening the curved surface still requires distortion of other properties, including local shapes or distances.

questions.prompt: Why was Mercator widely used for navigation at sea?
choices: Lines of constant bearing are straight
It shows true areas
It shows true distances everywhere
It has the least overall distortion
questions.explain: A rhumb line maintains a constant compass bearing, and Mercator represents it as a straight line. This property made the projection useful for plotting sailing directions even though it distorts area.

questions.prompt: The globe in this lab is…
choices: The most distorted view
The undistorted reference
Just another Mercator map
An equal-area flat map
questions.explain: A globe represents positions on a curved surface without first flattening them onto a plane. Comparing it with a flat map reveals the distortions introduced by the projection.

questions.prompt: Which property does the Mercator projection distort most?
choices: Local angles between lines
Compass bearings
Area at high latitudes
Shapes of small areas
questions.explain: Mercator keeps local angles and bearings correct, so small shapes look right. The price is that scale grows toward the poles, so high-latitude areas such as Greenland and Antarctica look far too large.

why: A map projection transfers positions from a curved surface to a plane. Every projection distorts some combination of area, shape, distance and direction, so the right choice depends on the map’s purpose.

On a cylindrical map every parallel is drawn as long as the equator, so at 60° N or S the map is stretched east–west to twice its true length. Mercator stretches north–south by the same amount to keep local shapes and angles, so areas there appear four times too large. The equal-area map squashes north–south by half instead, which keeps areas true but flattens shapes.
Judge each projection when it is fully flat; intermediate shapes are a visual transition rather than a separate projection.

misconceptions.claim: One flat world map can preserve every area, shape, distance and direction.
misconceptions.truth: Flattening Earth’s curved surface necessarily introduces distortion. A projection may preserve a selected property, such as area, while changing others. Compare a map with a globe and choose its projection according to the task, rather than assuming all visual comparisons are equally reliable.

misconceptions.claim: North has to be at the top of a map because that is how Earth really is.
misconceptions.truth: Putting north at the top is a convention. Earth has no up or down in space, and some maps are drawn with south at the top or with the Pacific in the center. What matters is that the map shows its orientation clearly.

cases.label: Greenwich as a meridian, not a map

teacher.script:
Compare Greenland and Africa on the globe before flattening it. Predict which properties may change on the map.

Flatten each projection fully. Compare the equal-sized circles at low and high latitudes, then describe the trade-off between area and shape.
pitfalls: Compare the properties a projection preserves with those it distorts before choosing it for a task.
Use the globe to check area comparisons, including the enlarged appearance of Greenland on a Mercator map.
Distinguish the requirements of a world map from those of a local map covering a much smaller region.

modelNotes: The surface uses Earth imagery and the projection formulas, cut off at 85° N and S because Mercator stretches the poles to infinity.

predict.prompt: On many world maps Greenland looks about as big as Africa. Do you think it really is? Explain your guess.

cer.prompt: Why does every flat map distort something, and why does Mercator make Greenland look so big?
cer.claim: No flat map can keep area, shape, distance and direction all correct; Mercator keeps local shapes and compass bearings but enlarges areas toward the poles.
cer.evidence: With Flatten at 1.00, Mercator's equal-sized gold circles stay round but grow much larger at 60° N and S than at the equator. The cylindrical equal-area projection keeps the circles' areas equal but squashes them flat at high latitudes. On the globe, Greenland is much smaller than Africa.
cer.reasoning: A sphere cannot be flattened without stretching or squashing. A cylindrical map stretches every parallel to the length of the equator, doubling east–west scale at 60°. Mercator stretches north–south by the same amount to keep shapes, so areas there appear about four times too large.

labs.title: Grid references
labs.hook: A grid reference locates a square using eastings followed by northings.
labs.objective: Read and plot a six-figure grid reference on a US National Grid (UTM) map, locating the easting before the northing.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Read the map’s scale and locate its eastings and northings. Distinguish the full 100 km square from the selected 100 m square: the pin marks its southwest corner, because at this scale a 100 m square is far too small to see.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Easting, then Northing, and read the six-figure reference. Explain how the UTM zone and 100 km square letters (such as 18T WL) say which 100 km square it lies in. Then turn on British National Grid to compare the Ordnance Survey version, which uses one letter pair (such as SH).

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain the difference between identifying a grid square and measuring a point’s position accurately.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: You read a grid reference…
choices: Northings, then eastings
Whichever number is larger first
Eastings, then northings
Latitude, then longitude
questions.explain: Eastings identify the position across the grid and northings identify the position up it. Giving them in that order ensures that both coordinates refer to the intended square or location.

questions.prompt: A six-figure reference locates to about…
choices: 1 km
1 m
A county
questions.explain: A six-figure grid reference uses three digits for each direction, identifying a 100 m square within the kilometer grid. It indicates a smaller area than a four-figure reference rather than an exact point.

questions.prompt: The four-figure reference 1234 means…
choices: The 1 km square with SW corner at 12, 34
The exact point 12.34 km east
The 1 km square with NE corner at 12, 34
The 10 km square labeled 1234
questions.explain: The first pair of digits identifies the western grid line and the second identifies the southern grid line. Together they locate the 1 km square extending northeast from that southwest corner.

questions.prompt: The US National Grid printed on USGS topographic maps is…
choices: The same as latitude and longitude
A metric grid based on UTM zones
A worldwide grid of 1° squares
A grid used only for navigation at sea
questions.explain: The US National Grid is based on the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) system, which projects each 6°-wide zone onto a flat grid measured in meters. Britain’s National Grid works the same way on a single projection. Both support grid distances and references, while latitude and longitude describe angular position on Earth.

questions.prompt: A church lies 3 tenths of the way east from easting 45 and 7 tenths of the way north from northing 23. What is its six-figure grid reference?
questions.explain: Write the easting first: 45 plus 3 tenths gives 453. Then the northing: 23 plus 7 tenths gives 237. Together they make 453237.

why: A grid reference locates a square using eastings followed by northings. More digits identify a smaller square, while the zone and letter code identify the 100 km square it lies in.

The easting measures how far east of the square’s western edge you are, and the northing how far north of its southern edge, so you go along before you go up. Each extra pair of figures divides the square by ten: within a 100 km square, two figures give a 10 km square, four give 1 km and six give 100 m. The same numbers repeat in every 100 km square, so letters are needed to say which one: the UTM zone and square letters in the US National Grid (such as 18T WL), or a single letter pair in the British National Grid (such as SH).
The map is fictional, and a more precise reference does not by itself make a measurement more accurate.

misconceptions.claim: A six-figure grid reference identifies an exact point.
misconceptions.truth: A six-figure reference identifies a 100-meter square within the relevant 100 km square. More digits specify a smaller area, but extra precision does not guarantee an accurate observation. Read eastings before northings and include the zone and square letters when the wider location is needed.

misconceptions.claim: Grid north on a USGS topographic map is exactly the same as true north.
misconceptions.truth: UTM grid lines point to true north only along the central meridian of each 6° zone. Elsewhere grid north differs from true north, by up to about 2° in the contiguous United States, and USGS maps show the difference in a declination diagram. Magnetic north, shown by a compass, differs again and changes over time. The British National Grid behaves the same way about its central meridian at 2° W.

teacher.script:
Read the map’s scale and locate its eastings and northings. Distinguish the full 100 km square from a selected 100 m square.

Set Easting, then Northing, and read the six-figure reference. Then explain how the UTM zone and 100 km square letters (such as 18T WL) identify which 100 km square it lies in.

Turn on British National Grid to show that Ordnance Survey maps use the same easting-then-northing method, with a two-letter code (such as SH) in place of the zone and square letters.
pitfalls: Read eastings before northings and distinguish the projected grid from latitude and longitude.
Explain that a six-figure reference identifies a 100 m square rather than an exact point within it.
Check the coordinate system and datum before comparing a grid reference with a GPS location.

modelNotes: A complete US National Grid reference gives the UTM zone and 100 km square letters, then eastings and northings (for example 18T WL 246 513); a British National Grid reference gives one letter pair instead (for example SH 246 513).
Six figures identify a 100 m square, not a surveyed point accurate to one meter.
Four figures such as 1234 identify the 1 km square with southwest corner at easting 12 and northing 34.
Six figures subdivide to 100 m, and eight figures to 10 m.
This fictional map covers one 100 km square; its main grid lines are 10 km apart.

predict.prompt: On a grid map, would you read the number along the bottom edge or the number up the side first? Why might the order matter?

cer.prompt: How does a six-figure grid reference identify a place, and why is it a square rather than an exact point?
cer.claim: A six-figure reference gives the easting then the northing, each to a tenth of a 1 km square, which identifies a 100 m square by its southwest corner.
cer.evidence: Setting Easting and Northing moves the pin, and the readout shows the six figures. The pin marks the southwest corner of the selected 100 m square. A full US National Grid reference adds the zone and 100 km square letters, such as 18T WL 246 513.
cer.reasoning: Eastings increase eastward and northings northward, so you go along before you go up. Each extra pair of figures divides the square by ten, so six figures narrow it to 100 m, not to a single point.

labs.title: Mass movement
labs.hook: Gravity drives a slope downhill while friction and cohesion resist movement.
labs.objective: Identify the main parts of a rotational slump and explain how rainfall can reduce the stability of a slope.
standards: OCR GCSE A Landscapes of the UK

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the crown, the curved shear surface and the toe. Read the starting factor of safety, then open How to read these results for the soil strength values.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Pore pressure and explain why resistance falls as effective stress drops. Once the factor of safety is below 1, press Play to watch the slump rotate.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does increasing pore pressure reduce the resistance to sliding along the selected surface?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A rotational slump moves on…
choices: A straight, flat slip plane underground
The vertical face of the cliff
Nothing: loose rock falls freely
A curved, spoon-shaped slip surface
questions.explain: A rotational slump moves along a curved slip surface, so the displaced block rotates as it descends. The head drops and may tilt backward while material moves outward near the toe.

questions.prompt: Rain makes till more likely to fail because…
choices: Pore-water pressure reduces its strength
It freezes and wedges the cliff apart
It cements the clay particles together
It makes the till lighter
questions.explain: Higher pore-water pressure reduces the effective stress pressing soil particles together. This weakens frictional resistance and can make a slope more likely to fail.

questions.prompt: When pore pressure pushes the factor of safety below 1, Play shows…
choices: The slope stays as it is
The head drops and the toe moves outward
The toe drops and the head moves outward
The whole slope slides as one flat sheet
questions.explain: A factor of safety below 1 means the forces driving movement exceed those resisting it. The rotation shown illustrates that unstable state; it does not predict how fast or how far a real slide moves.

questions.prompt: Before comparing a real coastal slide with this model, check…
choices: Whether both slopes face the open sea
Whether the two cliffs are equally high
Its material, pore pressure and slip shape
How much rain fell in that whole year
questions.explain: Material strength, pore pressure and the geometry of the failure surface determine whether a rotational mechanism is plausible. Two coastal slopes can fail differently despite sharing a similar setting.

questions.prompt: Which change would most improve the stability of a wet clay slope?
choices: Building heavy houses along the top
Cutting into the toe of the slope to widen a road
Removing the trees and shrubs
Installing drains to lower pore pressure
questions.explain: Drains lower the water pressure in the slope, which increases the friction resisting movement. Loading the top, cutting the toe and removing vegetation all make failure more likely.

why: Gravity drives a slope downhill while friction and cohesion resist movement. Rising pore-water pressure can reduce effective stress and resistance, making a chosen slip surface less stable.

Water in the pores pushes soil grains apart, so less of the soil's weight presses the grains together along the slip surface. Friction depends on that effective stress, so resistance falls while the driving weight stays almost the same; when resistance drops below the driving force, the factor of safety falls below 1.
The factor of safety applies to the starting slope and its chosen slip surface; the rotation that follows is illustrative, not a calculated runout.

misconceptions.claim: Rain can destabilize a slope only by making the material heavier.
misconceptions.truth: Added water can increase weight, but rising pore-water pressure can also reduce effective stress and frictional resistance along a potential slip surface. Drainage, cohesion, slope geometry and material properties influence stability, so the effect is not explained by added mass alone.

misconceptions.claim: Landslides always happen without any warning signs.
misconceptions.truth: Many landslides are preceded by signs such as new cracks at the top of a slope, bulging ground near the toe, tilting trees or posts, and springs appearing. Monitoring these signs helps warn people, although some failures are very sudden.

teacher.script:
Find the crown, the curved shear surface and the toe. Read the starting factor of safety, then open How to read these results for the soil strength values.

Increase Pore pressure and explain why resistance falls as effective stress drops. Once the factor of safety is below 1, press Play to watch the slump rotate.
pitfalls: Consider slope material, gravity and water pressure together rather than attributing every failure to wave erosion.
Distinguish a rockfall from a slide or flow by describing how the material moves.
Explain how saturation can reduce slope stability, including on slopes that are not beside the sea.

modelNotes: A simplified Bishop calculation divides the initial sliding mass into 160 vertical slices.
Effective cohesion is 2 kPa, friction angle 15°, and soil unit weight 20 kN/m³.

predict.prompt: After days of heavy rain, do you think a clay slope becomes more or less likely to slide? Why?

cer.prompt: Why can heavy rain make a stable slope fail?
cer.claim: Rain raises the water pressure in the soil's pores, which lowers the friction holding the slope together until the factor of safety falls below 1 and the slope slumps.
cer.evidence: The starting factor of safety is above 1. Raising Pore pressure lowers it; once it drops below 1, Play shows the slump rotating on its curved shear surface, with the head dropping and the toe pushed outward.
cer.reasoning: Friction depends on how hard soil grains are pressed together. Water pressure in the pores pushes the grains apart, reducing this effective stress, while the weight driving the slide stays almost the same. When resistance falls below the driving force, the slope fails.

labs.title: Rain shadow
labs.hook: Rising air expands and cools.
labs.objective: Explain why rising air cools and produces rain on a windward slope, leaving drier conditions on the leeward side.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Predict which side the air rises and cools on. Set Initial humidity to 20% and Ridge height to 900 m: why does no cloud form?

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Initial humidity to 70% and Ridge height to 2100 m, and follow the parcel through cloud base. Compare the temperatures at the windward and leeward feet and explain the difference.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can air arrive at the leeward foot of a mountain warmer and drier than when it began rising?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Air rising on the windward slope…
choices: Warms and dries
Warms and condenses
Sinks and clears
Cools and condenses
questions.explain: Rising air encounters lower pressure, expands and cools. If it cools to saturation, water vapor can condense into cloud droplets.

questions.prompt: A rain shadow sits…
choices: On the leeward side of the barrier
On the windward side of the barrier
On the very summit of the ridge
Anywhere at the same height
questions.explain: Air crossing a mountain can lose moisture on the windward side and then warm as it descends downwind. The resulting lower relative humidity helps create a drier leeward region.

questions.prompt: If the ridge is higher than the parcel’s condensation level…
choices: Both sides get equally wet from the cloud
Cloud forms; the leeward air arrives warmer and drier
Cloud forms; the leeward air arrives colder and wetter
No cloud forms on either side of it
questions.explain: Above its condensation level, the parcel cools more slowly because condensation releases latent heat. Once the moisture has rained out, it descends at the faster dry rate, so it reaches the same height warmer and drier. The model does not calculate rainfall totals.

questions.prompt: Why are Owens Valley (east of the Sierra Nevada) and Penrith (east of the Lake District) both relatively dry?
choices: They are both far inland from the sea
Cold valley air stops clouds forming
Air loses rain over hills upwind, then sinks
Both lie under the subtropical high-pressure belt
questions.explain: Both examples involve moist air rising over a barrier and descending on its sheltered side. Their rainfall contrasts also depend on prevailing winds, moisture supply and the wider regional climate.

questions.prompt: Why is eastern Washington State much drier than the coast near Seattle?
choices: Westerly winds lose much of their rain over the Cascades.
Hot, dry air from Mexico reaches the interior first.
Eastern Washington is farther from the Pacific’s warm currents.
Eastern Washington is higher above sea level.
questions.explain: The prevailing winds come from the Pacific. Moist air rises over the Olympic Mountains and the Cascades, giving heavy rain and snow on their western slopes, and much less is left by the time the air sinks into the Columbia Basin. The same pattern makes eastern England drier than western Scotland or Wales.

why: Rising air expands and cools. If it reaches saturation, condensation can occur; after moisture is lost, descent on the far side of a ridge can bring warmer, drier air to the same elevation.

Below cloud base the rising air cools at the dry rate, about 9.8 °C per kilometer. Above it, condensation releases latent heat, so the saturated air cools more slowly (6 °C/km in this model). Once that water has fallen as rain, the sinking air warms at the faster dry rate all the way down, so it reaches the leeward foot warmer and with lower relative humidity than when it started.
The parcel uses fixed lapse rates and assumes all condensed water rains out; it compares temperatures but does not calculate rainfall.

misconceptions.claim: A mountain creates the moisture that falls as rain on its windward side.
misconceptions.truth: The approaching air already carries water vapor. Forced uplift makes it expand and cool; if it becomes saturated, cloud and rain can form. Having lost moisture, the air warms as it descends, so the leeward side is often warmer and drier.

misconceptions.claim: The leeward side is dry because the mountain blocks the wind completely.
misconceptions.truth: The wind still blows over the mountain. The leeward side is drier because the air has already lost moisture as rain on the windward side, and it warms as it sinks, so clouds evaporate.

teacher.script:
Predict which side the air rises and cools on. Set Initial humidity to 20% and Ridge height to 900 m: why does no cloud form?

Set Initial humidity to 70% and Ridge height to 2100 m, and follow the parcel through cloud base. Compare the temperatures at the windward and leeward feet and explain the difference.
pitfalls: Explain that uplift can cool moist air to condensation; a mountain does not create the water vapor.
Distinguish local windward and leeward contrasts from broad climate patterns associated with latitude.
Use long-term climate evidence before classifying a relatively dry valley as a desert.

modelNotes: Unsaturated air cools at about 9.8 °C per kilometer as it rises.
Above cloud base, the model uses a fixed saturated lapse rate of 6 °C/km; real values vary with temperature and pressure.

Relief is drawn 2.5 times taller than true; Physical scale uses the same scale in every direction. Ground color and trees are schematic: the lee side is drawn drier only in proportion to the water the air loses on the way up.

predict.prompt: Moist ocean air blows over a mountain range. Which side of the mountains do you think will be wetter, and which side warmer?

cer.prompt: Why is the land on the far (leeward) side of a mountain range often drier and warmer?
cer.claim: Air loses its moisture as rain on the windward side, then sinks and warms on the leeward side, arriving warmer and drier than it started.
cer.evidence: At 20% humidity and a 900 m ridge, the air never reaches cloud base, so no cloud forms. At 70% humidity and a 2,100 m ridge, the parcel reaches cloud base, cools more slowly (6 °C/km) above it while rain falls, then warms at 9.8 °C/km all the way down, reaching the leeward foot warmer than at the windward foot.
cer.reasoning: Rising air expands and cools; once saturated, condensation releases latent heat, so it cools more slowly. After the water has rained out, the sinking air warms at the faster dry rate the whole way down, so it ends up warmer with lower relative humidity.

labs.title: Groundwater
labs.hook: Groundwater fills connected pores and fractures below the water table.
labs.objective: Locate water in connected pores and explain how pumping changes the water table and flow toward a well.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Before pumping, find the saturated pores and the water table. Raise Pump and compare the well head with the Boundary head.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Turn on Confined aquifer. Explain why the gold Potentiometric surface sits above the clay layer, and why it shows the level water would rise to in a well, not a lake.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does lowering the water level in a well change the hydraulic gradient around it?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The water table is…
choices: The top of the saturated zone in the pores
An underground lake with a shore
A river flowing under the ground
The boundary between the soil and the bedrock
questions.explain: The water table is the upper surface of the saturated zone in an unconfined aquifer. Beneath it, connected pores and fractures are filled with water rather than air.

questions.prompt: An aquifer is…
choices: Any rock that contains some water
Rock that stores and yields useful water
Rock that water cannot flow through
An open underground lake or river in a cave
questions.explain: An aquifer must both store groundwater and transmit it readily enough to supply useful quantities. High water content alone is insufficient if pore connections or fractures do not allow water to flow.

questions.prompt: In this steady unconfined model, increasing pumping makes the nearby water table…
choices: Rise toward the ground surface
Stay level because the boundary refills it
Lower into a cone of depression
Fall evenly across the whole aquifer
questions.explain: Pumping lowers hydraulic head near the well, creating a gradient that draws groundwater toward it. This steady model balances that inflow against pumping and does not track long-term exhaustion of a finite store.

questions.prompt: In the confined model, pumping lowers the gold surface. What happens to the sand beneath the clay layer?
choices: It drains and fills with air near the well
It turns into an empty cone below the well
It refills at once, so its pressure is unchanged
It stays saturated while the water pressure falls
questions.explain: A confined aquifer stays fully saturated under its aquitard. Pumping lowers the pressure, so the potentiometric surface (the level water would rise to in a well) falls, but the pores remain full of water.

questions.prompt: What is recharge?
choices: Water pumped out of a well
Water flowing out at a spring
Water entering an aquifer from above
Water evaporating back up from the soil
questions.explain: Recharge is water that soaks down from rain, rivers or lakes and reaches the saturated zone. If pumping takes more than recharge replaces, the water table falls.

why: Groundwater fills connected pores and fractures below the water table. Pumping lowers hydraulic head near a well, creating a gradient that draws water toward it.

In a confined aquifer the sand stays fully saturated beneath the clay aquitard, so pumping does not drain the pores. Instead it lowers the water pressure, and the potentiometric surface (the level water would rise to in a well) falls into a cone around the well.
The steady-flow calculation holds the outer head fixed; it does not determine recharge, long-term depletion or sustainable abstraction.

misconceptions.claim: Groundwater usually occupies a single underground lake.
misconceptions.truth: Most groundwater occupies connected pores and fractures in rock or sediment. In an unconfined aquifer, the water table marks the top of the saturated zone. In a confined aquifer, water in a well may rise above the aquifer because of pressure rather than an underground open lake.

misconceptions.claim: Groundwater is always clean and safe to drink.
misconceptions.truth: Soil and rock filter some pollution, but groundwater can be contaminated by fertilizer nitrates, leaking sewage, industrial chemicals or natural arsenic. Once polluted, an aquifer can take decades to recover.

cases.label: Dust Bowl and the Ogallala aquifer

teacher.script:
Before pumping, find the saturated pores and the water table. Raise Pump and compare the well head with the Boundary head: the difference is the drawdown shown in the readout.

Turn on Confined aquifer. The gold potentiometric surface is the level water would rise to in a well; the aquifer below the clay stays saturated even when that level falls.
pitfalls: Show groundwater occupying pores and fractures rather than presenting underground rivers as the usual arrangement.
Explain that pumping removes water from an existing store and can lower the water table.
Distinguish a rock’s ability to store water from its ability to transmit enough water to act as a useful aquifer.

modelNotes: Hydraulic conductivity is 10 m/day, well radius 0.2 m, outer radius 500 m and confined thickness 12 m.

predict.prompt: If a farmer pumps a lot of water from a well, what do you think happens to the water table around the well?

cer.prompt: How does pumping from a well change the groundwater around it?
cer.claim: Pumping lowers the water table around the well into a cone of depression, and groundwater flows toward the well from all sides.
cer.evidence: With Pump at 0, the water table is level with the Boundary head. Raising Pump toward 800 m³/day lowers the head at the well and the drawdown in the readout increases, with the water table sloping down toward the well. In the confined aquifer, the gold potentiometric surface falls but the sand below the clay stays saturated.
cer.reasoning: Groundwater flows from higher to lower head through connected pores. Pumping removes water at the well, lowering the head there, so the water table slopes toward it. In a confined aquifer, pumping lowers the water pressure rather than draining the pores.

labs.title: Isostasy
labs.hook: Adding an ice load changes the equilibrium height of the crust.
labs.objective: Explain how the crust responds to loading and unloading, using an ice sheet to explore subsidence and rebound.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify the crust, the Moho and the solid mantle. Set Ice thickness to 0 m, predict which way the crust will move, then set it to 3000 m.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Calculate 3000 × 917/3300 and compare it with the depression shown in the readout. Switch to Physical scale to remove the ×5 vertical exaggeration; the width of the ice sheet stays schematic.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain why adding an ice load depresses the crust and why removing it allows rebound.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Isostasy means…
choices: The crust is fixed to the core
The crust floats in balance on the mantle
Plates move only at their edges
Mountains stay up because rock is strong
questions.explain: Isostasy describes the tendency toward gravitational balance between lithospheric loads and the material beneath them. The mantle is mostly solid but can deform and flow over geological timescales.

questions.prompt: After an ice sheet melts, the land…
choices: Stays down permanently
Sinks further as water drains
Slowly rises: glacial rebound
Rises instantly once ice melts
questions.explain: Removing an ice sheet reduces the load on the lithosphere, allowing uplift as the underlying mantle readjusts. This response can continue for thousands of years after the ice has melted.

questions.prompt: If you increase Ice thickness, the crustal block should…
choices: Float higher
Stay at the same level
Tilt but keep its average height
Sink, displacing mantle
questions.explain: Adding ice increases the weight supported by the underlying material. In this local balance model, the crustal block sinks farther to displace enough denser mantle to support the added load.

questions.prompt: What process links raised beaches in western Scotland with the rising shore of Hudson Bay?
choices: Both lost ice and are still rebounding
Both are sinking under sediment
Both sit on a rising hotspot
Both are folding upward as plates collide
questions.explain: Both regions carried thick ice sheets whose removal initiated ongoing crustal uplift. Raised shorelines record the resulting change in land level relative to the sea, together with any sea-level changes.

questions.prompt: The land around the Gulf of Bothnia, between Sweden and Finland, is still rising by nearly 1 cm a year. Why?
choices: Mantle rock is still flowing back after the ice sheet melted.
A new volcano is forming beneath the gulf.
River sediment is pushing the land upward.
The Baltic Sea is drying up, so less water weighs on the land.
questions.explain: A thick ice sheet pushed the land down during the last glaciation. It melted around 10,000 years ago, and the slow flow of mantle rock back beneath the region is still lifting the land.

why: Adding an ice load changes the equilibrium height of the crust. In the local Airy model, a denser mantle supports a less dense crustal column, and unloading raises its equilibrium position.

At equilibrium every column must have the same mass above a deep compensation level. Ice adds mass, so the column sinks until it has pushed aside an equal mass of mantle: 1 m of ice (917 kg/m³) displaces about 0.28 m of mantle (3300 kg/m³). Because ice is far less dense than mantle rock, even 3000 m of ice lowers the land by only about 830 m.
The experiment calculates an equilibrium displacement; actual rebound takes time as the solid mantle deforms.

misconceptions.claim: Postglacial rebound shows that the mantle beneath the crust is liquid lava.
misconceptions.truth: The mantle is mostly solid rock that can deform slowly over long timescales. When an ice load is removed, the land rises toward a new balance as mantle rock slowly flows back. This lab calculates the final balance, not how fast rebound happens.

misconceptions.claim: Since the last ice age, coastlines have changed only because sea level rose.
misconceptions.truth: Land levels changed too. Areas that were under thick ice, such as Hudson Bay, Scotland and Scandinavia, are still rising, while some areas beyond the old ice margin, including the Chesapeake Bay region and parts of southern England, are slowly sinking. Coastlines record the combination.

teacher.script:
Identify the crust, the Moho and the solid mantle. Set Ice thickness to 0 m, predict which way the crust will move, then set it to 3000 m.

Calculate 3000 × 917/3300 and compare it with the depression shown in the readout. Switch to Physical scale to remove the ×5 vertical exaggeration; the width of the ice sheet stays schematic.
pitfalls: Explain how the lithosphere responds to loading rather than treating the crust as resting on a rigid floor.
Describe the mantle as predominantly solid material that can flow slowly over long timescales.
Distinguish local changes in relative sea level caused by rebound from changes in global sea level.

modelNotes: This local Airy experiment keeps a 35 km crustal column unchanged and adds up to 3000 m of ice.
Crust, mantle and ice densities are 2800, 3300 and 917 kg/m³.
Equal mass above a compensation depth gives an equilibrium depression of ice thickness × 917/3300.

predict.prompt: A thick ice sheet covers a continent. Do you think the land under it stays where it is, sinks or rises? What happens after the ice melts?

cer.prompt: Why is land that was covered by thick ice during the last ice age still rising today?
cer.claim: The weight of an ice sheet pushes the crust down into the mantle, and after the ice melts the land slowly rises back as mantle rock flows back underneath.
cer.evidence: Raising Ice thickness to 3,000 m lowers the crustal column by about 830 m in the readout, which matches 3,000 × 917 ÷ 3,300. Removing the ice returns the column to its starting level. Land around Hudson Bay and the Gulf of Bothnia is still rising today.
cer.reasoning: The crust floats in balance on the denser mantle. Adding ice adds mass, so the column sinks until it has displaced an equal mass of mantle. Because the mantle flows very slowly, rebound after melting takes thousands of years.

labs.title: Wilson cycle
labs.hook: Continental rifting can open an ocean basin, while subduction can later consume oceanic lithosphere and bring continents together.
labs.objective: Follow the opening and closing of an ocean basin and relate continental collision to the formation of mountain belts.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Choose Continental rift, then Young ocean and Open ocean. Find the ridge and the thin oceanic crust.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Switch to Subduction begins and follow the slab. Compare Ocean closes with Continental collision and find the mountain root.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does subduction turn an expanding ocean into a closing basin?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The Wilson cycle is…
choices: Oceans opening and closing over geological time
The yearly cycle of ocean currents
Continents drifting in one direction forever
The cycle of rock types forming
questions.explain: Continental rifting can open an ocean basin, while later subduction can consume its oceanic lithosphere and bring continents together again. The Wilson cycle summarizes these possible stages over geological time.

questions.prompt: The Caledonides and Appalachians record…
choices: A hotspot track like Hawaiʻi’s islands
An older ocean that opened and then closed
A rift that never became an ocean
A long transform fault like the San Andreas
questions.explain: Parts of the Caledonian and Appalachian mountain belts preserve evidence of convergence and collisions associated with closure of the Iapetus Ocean. Later Atlantic opening separated sections of that older mountain system.

questions.prompt: If you move Formation stage toward Continental collision, the ocean should…
choices: Keep widening
Stay the same width
Close, then collide
Open a new ridge
questions.explain: As subduction consumes oceanic lithosphere, the basin narrows and the bordering continents approach one another. Continental collision then shortens and thickens crust, producing a mountain belt.

questions.prompt: Iceland, on today’s Mid-Atlantic Ridge, shows which stage?
choices: Collision
A closing ocean with trenches
An early continental rift
An actively spreading ocean
questions.explain: Iceland lies on the active Mid-Atlantic spreading ridge, where plates separate and new oceanic crust forms. It therefore represents ongoing ocean-basin opening rather than closure by continental collision.

questions.prompt: Which stage comes first in the Wilson cycle?
choices: Continental collision
Subduction at a trench
Rifting of a continent
A mountain belt eroding
questions.explain: The cycle begins when a continent is stretched and splits apart in a rift. Spreading then opens an ocean, which may later close by subduction and end in collision.

why: Continental rifting can open an ocean basin, while subduction can later consume oceanic lithosphere and bring continents together. Mountain belts can preserve evidence of oceans that have closed.

Old oceanic lithosphere is cold and dense, so it can sink beneath a continent at a trench. Once subduction consumes plate faster than the ridge makes it, the basin narrows. Continental crust is too buoyant to sink far, so when the continents meet the crust crumples and thickens into a mountain belt with a deep root.
The six stages organize possible tectonic changes; they are not a fixed schedule followed by every ocean basin.

misconceptions.claim: Every ocean basin follows the same fixed timetable from opening to closure.
misconceptions.truth: The Wilson cycle organizes possible stages of rifting, ocean spreading, subduction and collision. Real basins differ in geometry, plate motions and duration, and some rifts stop developing. The framework helps interpret geological evidence without prescribing one schedule for every ocean.

misconceptions.claim: The Atlantic Ocean has always existed.
misconceptions.truth: The Atlantic began opening around 180 million years ago as Pangaea broke apart. Before that, an older ocean called Iapetus closed, joining the rocks that now form parts of Scotland, England and North America.

teacher.script:
Choose Continental rift, then Young ocean and Open ocean. Find the ridge and the thin oceanic crust.

Switch to Subduction begins and follow the slab. Compare Ocean closes with Continental collision and find the mountain root.
pitfalls: Use Pangaea as one example within a longer history of continental assembly and breakup.
Place Iceland at a divergent boundary rather than using it as an example of continental collision.
Connect the closing of an ocean with later mountain building while allowing for more complex histories in real regions.

modelNotes: The unstretched reference continent is 35 km thick and the oceanic crust about 7 km thick; both overlie solid mantle. Collision thickens the crust to about 65 km beneath peaks about 5–6 km high. Lithosphere and slab thicknesses are simplified to fit the section.
Physical scale removes the ×2 vertical exaggeration. The 300 km section shows only part of a basin.

predict.prompt: The Atlantic Ocean is getting wider today. Do you think oceans can also close? What would happen when the continents meet?

cer.prompt: How do oceans open and close, and how does that build mountain ranges?
cer.claim: Oceans open when a continent rifts apart and close when oceanic crust is subducted; when the continents collide, the crust thickens into a mountain belt.
cer.evidence: The stages run from Continental rift through Young ocean and Open ocean, with a ridge and thin (about 7 km) oceanic crust, to Subduction begins and Ocean closes. At Continental collision the crust thickens to about 65 km beneath peaks about 5–6 km high.
cer.reasoning: Spreading at the ridge widens the ocean. Old, dense oceanic crust eventually sinks at a subduction zone, closing the ocean. Continental crust is too buoyant to subduct, so it crumples and stacks up, forming high mountains with a deep root, as in the Himalaya and the old Appalachians.

labs.title: Soil catena
labs.hook: Soils along a slope are linked by movement of water and sediment.
labs.objective: Compare soil profiles from the crest to the foot of a slope and explain how water and sediment movement connect them.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Locate the crest, backslope and toe, which share one parent material. Read the three soil thicknesses.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Slope and watch the backslope soil thin while the toe soil thickens. Use Compare physical scale to tell soil thickness apart from the height of the slope.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How can movement of water and sediment connect soil differences along a single slope?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A catena is…
choices: A single horizon within one soil
A class on the soil texture triangle, like loam
The same soil across a whole region
A sequence of linked soils down one slope
questions.explain: A catena links soils along a slope where drainage and the transfer of material vary with topographic position. These differences can produce distinct profiles even where the parent material is similar.

questions.prompt: Why may an upper-slope soil be thinner than the toe soil?
choices: Soil moves downslope and collects below
It has been forming for longer than the toe soil
More rain falls on the upper slope
It sits on different bedrock
questions.explain: Erosion can remove material from upper slopes while deposition adds it near the foot of a slope. The resulting thickness pattern also depends on soil formation, drainage and local conditions.

questions.prompt: In this model, steepening the slope makes the backslope soil…
choices: Thicker
Thinner
Unchanged
Waterlogged
questions.explain: The model is set up so that the backslope soil thins as the slope steepens. This shows a likely relationship; it does not calculate an erosion rate.

questions.prompt: An Iowa loess hill and a Yorkshire valley side are paired in this lab because…
choices: Both have exactly the same climate
Both are formed entirely from loess
Both show soils changing down a slope
Both are slopes made of glacial till
questions.explain: Both examples compare soils at different positions along a slope rather than assuming a whole region has one profile. Keeping parent material similar helps reveal the effects of drainage and downslope transport.

questions.prompt: Where on a hillslope are soils most likely to be waterlogged?
choices: On the crest of the hill
On the steepest backslope
At the foot, where water collects
Equally everywhere on the slope
questions.explain: Water drains downslope through and over the soil and collects near the foot. Poor drainage there can produce gray, gleyed soils, while the crest and backslope drain freely.

why: Soils along a slope are linked by movement of water and sediment. Upper slopes may lose material while lower slopes receive it, creating differences even where parent material is similar.

On the steeper backslope, soil creep, rainsplash and surface wash move soil downslope faster than weathering can replace it, so the soil stays thin. At the toe this colluvium builds up, and water draining from upslope keeps the subsoil saturated for long periods, so it becomes gray and mottled (gleyed).
The selected thickness pattern is one example; climate, drainage and land use can produce a different catena.

misconceptions.claim: Soils on one hillside must be identical because they share a climate.
misconceptions.truth: Position on a slope affects drainage, erosion, deposition and the movement of dissolved material. These differences can produce contrasting soils even on similar parent material under the same regional climate. The pattern depends on local conditions rather than a universal sequence of thicknesses.

misconceptions.claim: The thickest soil is always found on the top of a hill.
misconceptions.truth: Hilltops and steep slopes often have thinner soils, because material is washed and moved downslope. The deepest soils frequently build up at the foot of a slope, where eroded material collects.

teacher.script:
Locate the crest, backslope and toe, which share one parent material. Read the three soil thicknesses.

Increase Slope and watch the backslope soil thin while the toe soil thickens. Use Compare physical scale to tell soil thickness apart from the height of the slope.
pitfalls: Consider slope position, drainage and material movement alongside climate when comparing soils along a hillslope.
Use evidence of erosion and accumulation rather than assuming that the thickest soil must occur at the crest.
Distinguish a catena’s sequence of soil profiles from a texture triangle that classifies mineral particle proportions.

modelNotes: The model hillslope is 120 m long, with soils shown at the crest, backslope and toe.

predict.prompt: On a hillside, do you think the soil will be thicker at the top, on the steep middle slope, or at the bottom? Why?

cer.prompt: Why do soils change from the top to the bottom of the same slope?
cer.claim: Soil and water move downslope, so soils are thin on the steep backslope and thicker and wetter at the toe, even though they formed from the same parent material.
cer.evidence: The crest, backslope and toe profiles share one parent material. Raising Slope thins the backslope soil and thickens the toe soil, as the readout's soil thicknesses show.
cer.reasoning: On steeper slopes, gravity, runoff and soil creep move soil downhill faster than it forms. The material collects at the foot of the slope, where water also gathers, giving deeper and often waterlogged soils.

labs.title: Periglacial landforms
labs.hook: Permafrost is ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years.
labs.objective: Explain how repeated freezing and thawing produce ice wedges and patterned ground in cold landscapes.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Define permafrost and explain how ground ice differs from a glacier. Play one year and watch the active layer thaw down to the dashed line.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Wedge development and trace the tapering wedge of ice. Explain how winter cracking, meltwater and refreezing make it grow, then set View to Polygon network.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain how repeated thermal cracking and refreezing build an ice wedge over many years.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Periglacial means…
choices: Land that is always buried under glacier ice
Cold-climate processes without glacier ice
Areas that glaciers once covered
Only land with permanent snow cover
questions.explain: Periglacial environments are dominated by cold-ground processes such as seasonal freezing and, in some settings, permafrost. They do not require a glacier to occupy the site.

questions.prompt: An ice wedge grows because…
choices: Meltwater erodes a channel downward
Frost heave pushes stones to the top
Frozen cracks refill with ice each year
The ground thaws and then slumps
questions.explain: Strong winter cooling can crack frozen ground, and meltwater entering the cracks can freeze. Repeated cracking and ice addition over many years can build a wedge of ground ice.

questions.prompt: What does Wedge development change here?
choices: The years needed for growth
The rate of yearly growth
The ground temperature
How wide the wedge has grown
questions.explain: Wedge development sets the wedge width so that different stages of growth can be compared. It does not assign a growth rate or a number of years.

questions.prompt: Alaskan ice-wedge polygons and Cairngorm blockfields are grouped together because…
choices: Both are linked to cold ground, not glacier ice
Both were carved by valley glaciers in the last ice age
Both formed beneath thick ice sheets
Both are active only during summer
questions.explain: Blockfields and ice-wedge polygons illustrate different processes associated with cold ground. Neither requires the local landscape to have been carved by an actively flowing valley glacier.

questions.prompt: What is the active layer?
choices: Permanently frozen ground far below
Snow that falls each winter
A layer of old glacier ice buried beneath the soil
Ground above permafrost that thaws each summer
questions.explain: The active layer sits on top of the permafrost and thaws and refreezes every year. Because water cannot drain down into the frozen ground below, it is often waterlogged in summer.

why: Permafrost is ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years. Seasonal thaw affects its active layer, while repeated thermal cracking and refreezing can build ice wedges.

Each winter, intense cold makes frozen ground contract and crack, usually along the same line. In spring, meltwater trickles into the crack and freezes in the permafrost as a thin vertical vein of ice. Repeated over hundreds of years, the veins build a wedge that is widest at the top, and the cracks join up into a network of polygons with troughs above the wedges.
The annual cycle and accumulated wedge width are separate comparisons; the width slider does not specify a growth rate.

misconceptions.claim: Permafrost is simply a glacier buried beneath the soil.
misconceptions.truth: Permafrost is ground that remains at or below zero degrees Celsius for at least two consecutive years. It may contain ground ice, but it need not be entirely frozen water. Seasonal thaw can affect the active layer above it, while glaciers are separate bodies of accumulated, flowing ice.

misconceptions.claim: Permafrost exists only in the Arctic.
misconceptions.truth: Permafrost underlies much of Alaska, and is also found in Antarctica and in high mountains such as the Tibetan Plateau, the Rockies, the Andes and the Alps. Britain has none today, but features such as blockfields record colder periglacial conditions in the past.

teacher.script:
Define permafrost and explain how ground ice differs from a glacier. Play one year and watch the active layer thaw down to the dashed line.

Increase Wedge development and trace the tapering wedge of ice. Explain how winter cracking, meltwater and refreezing make it grow, then set View to Polygon network.
pitfalls: Distinguish processes in cold ground from erosion and deposition by moving glacier ice.
Explain ice wedges through repeated cracking and freezing rather than describing them as river channels.
Consider whether a landform records past cold conditions when interpreting relict features in the Cairngorms.

modelNotes: Permafrost is ground at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years.
The section is 10 m wide and 5 m deep at a common geometric scale.
It assumes permafrost lies beneath an active layer that thaws to a maximum depth of 0.7 m each summer.
Wedge development sets the top width between 0.1 and 0.9 m; it does not convert to a number of winters or a growth rate.

predict.prompt: In Alaska, the ground stays frozen for years at a time. What do you think happens to the top layer of soil each summer?

cer.prompt: How do ice wedges grow in permafrost?
cer.claim: Ice wedges grow because the frozen ground cracks in winter, meltwater fills the crack in spring and freezes, and the cycle repeats over many years.
cer.evidence: Playing a year thaws the active layer down to about 0.7 m each summer while the permafrost below stays frozen. Raising Wedge development widens a tapering wedge of ice from 0.1 m to 0.9 m at the top, and the Polygon network view shows the wedges joining into polygons.
cer.reasoning: Very cold ground contracts and cracks in winter. Meltwater trickles into the crack and freezes because the permafrost below stays at or below 0 °C. Each year adds a thin vein of ice, so the wedge widens and the cracks join into a pattern of polygons.

labs.title: Storm surge
labs.hook: Onshore winds push water toward the coast, while lower atmospheric pressure also raises the water surface.
labs.objective: Explain how strong winds and low atmospheric pressure can raise coastal water levels, especially over a shallow shelf.
standards: OCR GCSE A Environmental threats to our planet

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Set Onshore wind and Pressure drop to zero: the water lies on the reference sea level (dashed line). Raise Onshore wind, then compare the setup at the coast for two values of Shelf depth.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Onshore wind to zero and Pressure drop to 3000 Pa to see the pressure effect alone. Then combine both, and switch to Physical scale (1:1) to see how small the rise is beside the shelf.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can the same onshore wind produce a larger rise in water level over a shallower shelf?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A storm surge is…
choices: A fast wave set off by a seafloor earthquake
An unusually high spring tide
Water piled up by wind and low pressure
A wave from a coastal landslide
questions.explain: Onshore winds can push seawater toward a coast, and low atmospheric pressure can also raise sea level. Shallow shelves and coastal geometry can amplify the resulting storm surge.

questions.prompt: A tsunami starts with…
choices: Strong winds over the sea
Low atmospheric pressure
Very heavy rainfall
Sudden seafloor movement
questions.explain: Rapid displacement of a large volume of water generates a tsunami, often following vertical seafloor motion. Storm surge instead develops through atmospheric forcing by winds and pressure.

questions.prompt: If you raise Onshore wind, the water should…
choices: Pile up higher toward the coast
Flatten
Rise evenly across the whole shelf
Drain away offshore
questions.explain: Stronger onshore wind applies greater stress to the water surface and drives more water toward the coast. In the model, the resulting setup also depends on shelf depth.

questions.prompt: Hurricane Katrina and the 1953 North Sea flood are paired because…
choices: Both were tsunamis from earthquakes
Both were surges from wind and low pressure
Both were caused by river floods
Both were caused by unusually high spring tides alone
questions.explain: Both events involved storm winds and low pressure raising coastal water levels over shallow margins. Their different storm types and coastlines affected the timing, extent and severity of the flooding.

questions.prompt: Why is a storm surge often higher over a wide, shallow continental shelf?
choices: Shallow water is warmer, so it expands much more.
Deep water has much stronger tides.
Wind piles water up more where it is shallow.
Shallow seas have no waves at all.
questions.explain: In deep water, water pushed by the wind can return at depth. Over a shallow shelf it has nowhere to go but up against the coast, so the surge builds higher, as along the northern Gulf of Mexico, in the southern North Sea and in the Bay of Bengal.

why: Onshore winds push water toward the coast, while lower atmospheric pressure also raises the water surface. Shallow shelves can produce a larger setup for the same forcing.

Wind drags the surface water toward the coast. At the coast the water cannot escape, so it piles up until the sloping sea surface pushes back as hard as the wind pushes forward. The slope needed is larger in shallow water, so a shallow shelf builds a bigger rise. Falling pressure adds about 1 cm of rise for every hectopascal.
This steady shelf experiment excludes tides, waves and inundation, which are needed to assess a real coastal flood.

misconceptions.claim: A hurricane’s wind category fully describes its coastal flood threat.
misconceptions.truth: Coastal water rise also depends on storm size, track, duration, atmospheric pressure and the shape and depth of the coast. Tide, waves and river flow further affect flooding. A wind category therefore cannot specify the water level or inundation at a particular location.

misconceptions.claim: A storm surge is just a set of very big waves.
misconceptions.truth: A surge raises the whole sea surface, sometimes by several meters, for hours. Storm waves ride on top of that higher water, which is why surges can flood land that waves alone would never reach.

teacher.script:
Set Onshore wind and Pressure drop to zero and find the reference sea level (dashed line). Raise Onshore wind, then compare two values of Shelf depth.

Set Onshore wind to zero and Pressure drop to 3000 Pa to see the pressure effect alone. Then combine both, and switch to Physical scale (1:1) to see how small the rise is beside the shelf.
pitfalls: Distinguish storm surge from a tsunami by explaining the process that raises the water level.
Consider wind-driven water accumulation and atmospheric pressure as well as waves on the surface.
Use water depth and coastal shape to explain why shallow shelves and narrowing bays can amplify a surge.

modelNotes: This steady experiment has a flat 100 km shelf, an offshore sea level held at zero and a closed coast. The pressure drop is assumed to grow steadily from zero offshore to its full value at the coast.
Wind stress uses air density 1.225 kg/m³ and a constant drag coefficient of 0.0015.

predict.prompt: A hurricane approaches two coasts: one with deep water offshore and one with a wide, shallow shelf. Which coast gets the higher storm surge?

cer.prompt: Why is storm surge highest where strong onshore winds blow over a shallow shelf?
cer.claim: Onshore wind piles water against the coast, and a shallow shelf makes the pile-up much higher; low air pressure adds a smaller extra rise.
cer.evidence: Raising Onshore wind raises the setup at the coast, and with the same wind a shallow shelf gives a much larger setup than a 100 m shelf. With wind at zero, a 3,000 Pa pressure drop raises the sea by only about 0.3 m, roughly 1 cm per hectopascal.
cer.reasoning: Wind drags surface water toward the coast until the sloping sea surface pushes back as hard as the wind pushes forward. In shallow water the same wind stress needs a steeper slope to balance it, so the water piles up higher. Lower air pressure lets the sea surface bulge up slightly.
